title: We Asked About Play-Action Passing; Packers Provided Explosive Answer
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Before the Green Bay Packers faced the Chicago Bears last week, we asked why the Packers weren’t leaning into their play-action passing game more.
At the time, Jordan Love had some of the best play-action stats but coach Matt LaFleur used it less than most teams.
“I think you have to stay in manageable situations,” LaFleur said last week. “If it’s second-and-20 and you run a play-action, it’s probably not going to be as effective as if it’s even second-and-7. I think that [not needing an effective run game to have an effective play-action game] could hold true for some of the first-down situations, but it’s more when you’re in get-back-on-track (situations) that I think it’s less effective.”
On Sunday, LaFleur and Love dropped a series of play-action bombs on Chicago’s secondary. The result was one of the best games of Love’s career and a combined 330 receiving yards from Christian Watson, Matthew Golden and Tucker Kraft.
Love’s play-action numbers were downright absurd. Even with limited success running the football again, Love according to Pro Football Focus was 12-of-14 passing for 245 yards with one touchdown and a 142.6 passer rating.
According to Sumer Sports, Love was 10-of-12 for 212 yards. That’s not just the most play-action yards for a quarterback this season but the most in a regular-season game since Jared Goff in 2024.
Why? And how? It’s not as if the Packers ran the ball well. They finished the day with 2.7 yards per carry, though a solid 4.0-yard average in the first half helped. They finished last in the league last week with 1.1 yards per first-down carry.
Taking out Tyrod Taylor’s kneel-down to end the game, the Packers had as many first-down runs that gained 0 yards or worse as 3 yards or better (four apiece). MarShawn Lloyd, Pierre Strong and Kaleb Johnson combined for 11 carries for 14 yards.
But the Packers kept dialing up play-action passes and Love kept answering with big-play completions.
“Ultimately you’ve got to go out and you’ve got to execute, though,” LaFleur said before practice on Wednesday. “Whether you’re dropping back, screening, throwing the quick game, play action, you’ve got to go out there and execute. And our guys went out there and did a really good job.
“It all starts up front, just giving Jordan the time to be able to allow some of those long-developing plays to develop. It starts up front. It’s not just the O-line. MarShawn (Lloyd) had a key block on the first one in terms of when they brought the corner blitz.”
Even without run-game support, Love had 66 more play-action yards than any other quarterback last week, according to Pro Football Focus. Among quarterbacks with more than five play-action dropbacks, he was first in completion percentage (85.7) and yards per attempt (17.5).
“I felt like we were rolling, definitely, play after play, drive after drive, making big plays,” Love said after the game. “It’s definitely a good feeling when you’re having a lot of explosive plays (and) putting up a lot of points. Obviously, defense played a huge part in that, getting us the ball back with all those turnovers, keeping them out of the end zone.
“It’s one of those things we’ve talked about. It’s flow state – feels like you’re flowing out there – just play after play we’re making those. It felt good to be able to do that at home.”
With Love flowing, Watson and Golden were exploding. They combined for 266 yards.
Highest yards per route run among WR in Week 5 so far Christian Watson       4.77 Matthew Golden        4.56 Mike Evans                   4.35 Xavier Hutchinson    4.06 George Pickens          3.42 pic.twitter.com/ru4ZR7M9fM
“I’ve said this a million times, I feel like – every week’s a new week,” LaFleur said on Monday. “Obviously, we’re always trying to get our playmakers the ball and those two guys are our best playmakers in that room right now. So, if their number’s called and the coverage presents itself the way that it did, then they’re going to get opportunities.
“You can’t control what the defensive call is, but you want to try to as much as possible put those guys at the point of attack and in position that if the coverage plays out the way you want it to, they have opportunities to go make plays. I can’t say enough about those two guys, just the plays that they made.”
While the data shows teams don’t need a successful run game to have a successful play-action attack, it doesn’t hurt. Whether it’s the mere threat of the run or the difference between second-and-7 and second-and-10, the Packers probably know that last week’s success against Chicago isn’t sustainable until they build some semblance of a relevant run game.
“We’re inconsistent, but yeah, there’s been some good ones,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said. “I think we still need to just be more consistent. We’ve had some negative runs put us behind the sticks in every game, so we just got to make sure we’re finding yards in those plays and not losing yards. I think once we do that, we’ll be able to get more runs called, we’ll be able to be more consistent and just be better as an offense.
According to PFF, 29 quarterbacks have at least 100 total dropbacks. Comparing play-action passes to standard dropbacks, Love is plus-19.8 in completion percentage (second), plus 4.1 yards per attempt (second) and plus-67.8 in passer rating (first).
Ten quarterbacks are averaging at least 1.7 yards more per play-action dropback than traditional dropbacks. Two of those quarterbacks have top-10 rushing attacks, three have bottom-10 rushing attacks and the other five are in the middle.
Why doesn’t it matter? Because linebackers are trained to stop the run.
“What I like to say is that you don't have to establish the run because the run was established in Pop Warner,” said Aaron Schatz, a founder of Football Outsiders and now with FTN Fantasy.
Can the Packers keep it going against the Cowboys? If so, it will be up a lot more than Love, Watson and Golden.
“It’s everybody,” LaFleur said. “It falls on everybody who’s in protection, and then obviously the wideouts have got to go do their thing, and those guys were making plays. They made some tough contested catches, and that’s part of the reason it was so effective.”

title: Grading the Six Players From Packers’ Top-10 Draft Class With Huge Test Looming
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Who says you need a first-round pick to have an impactful draft class?
Having sent two first-round picks to Dallas in the Micah Parsons trade, Green Bay Packers general manager Brian Gutekunst has turned lemons into lemonade with his six-man draft class.
In his recent draft-class rankings , NFL Draft On SI’s Justin Melo ranked the Packers ninth. He gave them a B-plus, saluting in particular cornerback Brandon Cisse and edge player Dani Dennis-Sutton.
Going through each individual, here is our grade for the six players. Plus, it’s a look ahead to ahead to their challenges on Sunday night against the Cowboys.
It didn’t take long for Brandon Cisse to emerge as the no-doubt-about-it starter. With 1.5 sacks and two pass breakups, there’s been a lot more good than bad in his five starts.
According to Pro Football Focus, 109 cornerbacks have played at least 68 coverage snaps. Cisse is 70th with a completion rate allowed of 68.8 percent and 90th with 16.9 yards allowed per catch. Those numbers seem terrible, but he’s only been targeted 16 times and given up 11 catches. That makes him 19th with 16.1 coverage snaps per reception allowed.
Of the 14 rookie cornerbacks to play at least 40 coverage snaps, Cisse is No. 1 in snaps per reception.
Cisse has given up more than two catches in only one game – Week 3 against Atlanta – and was charged with three receptions allowed for 20 yards the last two weeks combined. He’s missed too many tackles but the mentality is there, which is a good starting point.
He’ll obviously face a much, much bigger challenge on Sunday night against Dak Prescott and premier receivers CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. We’ll know a lot  more about Cisse after this game and then next week at Detroit.
Chris McClellan has played a lot as defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has leaned on a rotation to minimize everyone’s workload. Playing 29 snaps a game, the box-score production hasn’t been there with only five tackles and one quarterback hit.
The Packers drafted McClellan over Vikings run-stuffer Domonique Orange because of his ability to be a three-down player. They’re still waiting for that to show up because he hasn’t produced in either phase.
Of the 100 defensive tackles with 53 pass-rushing opportunities, McClellan ranks 89th in PFF’s pass-rush productivity, which measures sacks, hits and hurries per pass-rushing snap, and 91st in pass-rush win rate.
Of the 13 rookie defensive tackles with 20 pass-rushing snaps, McClellan is eighth in both categories. Two of his three pressures came against the Bears.
During one run play against the Bears, he wound up being pushed about 8 yards downfield. There were some impactful reps, though.
Chris McClellan is off to a quiet start. Without Javon Hargrave, they'll need more of this. pic.twitter.com/W0dpIs6HrN
With Javon Hargrave out for the rest of the season with a torn Achilles and with Warren Brinson on injured reserve, the Packers need more from their five remaining players. McClellan is front and center in that conversation. He will face a huge test against the Cowboys, who feature three-time Pro Bowl left guard Tyler Smith and 2025 first-round right guard Tyler Booker.
The Packers were thrilled that Dennis-Sutton fell into their laps in the fourth round. That optimism seems warranted. He has 13 tackles, 1.5 sacks, four quarterback hits and two tackles for losses. Barryn Sorrell, a fourth-round pick last year and a starter this year, has 13 tackles, a half-sack, one quarterback hit and no tackles for losses.
Third of three clips on Dennis-Sutton. Here's his sack. pic.twitter.com/716KYQ8yI9
Of the 99 edge players with at least 50 pass-rushing opportunities, Dennis-Sutton is 47th in pass-rushing productivity – just behind T.J. Watt and Khalil Mack – but 87th in pass-rush win rate.
Of the 16 rookie edge players with 20 pass-rushing snaps, Dennis-Sutton is sixth in PRP and 12th in win rate. Of his nine pressures, four came against the Jets and three against Chicago.
He has used his length and strength against the run. In fact, his average distance of tackle vs. the run has produced a loss of 0.7 yards; only the Vikings’ Andrew Van Ginkel is better. His aggressive play has worked against him in the bootleg game …
First of three clips on Dennis-Sutton. He has been suckered frequently by bootlegs, like this one. pic.twitter.com/vhFyUwiTPi
But this play against a receiver screen was impressive.
Second of three clips on Dennis-Sutton. The awareness and hustle here is excellent. I don't think an offense schemes for an edge player to ruin a receiver screen. pic.twitter.com/6KdjjkAmkq
Dennis-Sutton played a lot on the right side of the defense against Chicago. If he stays there, that would mean a match against the Cowboys’ excellent young left tackle, Tyler Guyton.
Jager Burton’s starting debut was a disaster as he allowed 10 quarterback pressures against the Falcons. Burton allowed five quarterback hits in that game. Only one guard has allowed more hits this season.
The team quickly pivoted by signing veterans Laken Tomlinson and Kevin Zeitler to the 53-man roster and Mekhi Becton to the practice squad. At this rate, Burton might not be heard from for the rest of the season.
That doesn’t mean his career is over, obviously. The Packers were bullish on him throughout training camp; one bad game shouldn’t change the outlook.
With Keisean Nixon and Carrington Valentine entering the final season under contract, the Packers took a flier on Domani Jackson with the 201st pick, hoping to get the best out of a touted prospect who had a disappointing senior season at Alabama.
Jackson didn’t make the roster and is on the practice squad. Taken a few picks later, Lions defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard has 13 pressures. All of Green Bay’s defensive tackles have 21 pressures, led by Javon Hargrave with six.
Grade: F (for now, obviously).
Trey Smack was the only kicker who was drafted and is one of three on a roster. He missed two kicks in the first four games – a missed extra point and a blocked field goal – but had three against Chicago. Smack, fellow rookie Drew Stevens of Washington and veteran Eddy Pineiro have each missed a league-worst five kicks.
“It’s something we can build off of,” special teams coordinator Cam Achord said on Tuesday. “We talked about it (that it) wasn’t always going to be perfect. Whether you’re a kicker or another position, you’re a rookie. There’s going to be a bump in the road, and he’s got the right mental makeup to trust the process, trust what we’re doing in practice, trust what he did the first four weeks. Good contact on the ball, and just trust it. And I think he’s going to be fine. I have no fear about that.”
For field goals among the rookies, Smack is 7-of-10 (70.0 percent), the Giants’ Dominic Zvada is 11-of-14 (78.6 percent) and Stevens is 9-of-11 (81.8 percent).
The stats suggest the grade should be an F, but he’s really only had one bad game.
The Packers have been hit harder than most teams by injuries. Their injuries keep hitting key players with big contracts. ⬇️ https://t.co/0mPPEUNkPJ

title: Packers Broke the Bank for These 12 Players; Six of Them Are Broken
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The hits just keep coming for the Green Bay Packers.
The Packers are one of the most injured teams in the NFL , with many of the ailments being significant injuries to key players.
Including defensive tackle Javon Hargrave’s torn Achilles in the waning moments of Sunday’s game against the Bears, six of Green Bay’s 12 players with average salaries of at least $10 million are out of the lineup. They total $128 million in average annual salary.
In terms of cap dollars, they are consuming $72.08 million. That’s almost 24 percent of the cap not contributing to the lineup.
Here they are, with the dollar figures being their average annual salaries.
The Packers hoped Micah Parsons would be back for this week’s game against the Dallas Cowboys. Parsons no doubt wanted to be back to face his former team, as well. Instead, he hasn’t even started practicing.
His brother said the “best bet” would be Parsons returning in Week 10 against the Vikings or Week 12 against the Rams, the games bridging this year’s bye.
“First of all, you’ve got to get him back on the practice field,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “There’s a lot of testing that goes on before he gets medically cleared to get out there, and then I’m sure we’re going to want to give him some time to get back to playing football. As you see with most guys that are coming off a major injury, it takes a little bit of time.”
When healthy, Bako-Bewele is one of the best right tackles in the NFL. The Packers gave him a huge contract extension at the start of training camp in 2023, only for him to completely tear the patellar ligament that he partially tore last year. He’ll wind up playing 676 of about 2,100 snaps in 2025 and 2026.
Fortunately for the Packers, Anthony Belton is playing better. He has allowed zero pressures the last two games, according to PFF.
“He’s done a nice job,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said on Tuesday. “He’s firmed the pocket up. I think that was the biggest thing the first couple weeks was just the push that we were feeling in the pocket.
“I think him and Laken (Tomlinson at left guard) have done a really nice job just firming that up, allowing Jordan (Love) to see and not have that pocket pushed in his face. There were a couple reps in the game that, obviously, we got to clean up with him but, for the most part, he’s out there competing and doing a nice job.”
We might be able to erase Aaron Banks from this ledger at some point. Banks was inactive in Week 1 with a knee injury and started Week 2 but suffered a toe injury that held him out of the second half and then each of the last three games.
Banks has played 22 snaps this season. He returned to practice on Friday, though, so a decision will have to be made at some point whether Banks or Laken Tomlinson will start at left guard.
“One thing we have to keep in mind too is where do we fit those guys into the best five,” Adam Stenavich said. “We’ll evaluate that but, yeah, that’s going to be an interesting thing as we go through the next few weeks, for sure.”
After an injury-plagued 2025 season, the Packers gave Jayden Reed a three-year, $50.25 million contract extension in April. However, he wound up suffering a season-neck injury that required surgery. It ended his season after 41 snaps.
The Packers believed Skyy Moore could pick up the slack but he suffered an ankle injury early against Chicago and could miss a little time.
“Losing Skyy for however long he’s going to be out, that’s going to be interesting,” Adam Stenavich said. “We’ll see where Savion (Williams) is at this week. But J-Mike (J. Michael Sturdivant) is definitely going to have a bigger role, for sure.”
Josh Jacobs’ NFL future remains in limbo. Green Bay’s running game without him is averaging 60.4 yards per game – almost 20 yards worse than any other team – and ranks 31st with 3.05 yards per carry.
Javon Hargrave was averaging 30 snaps per game as a valuable role player on the defensive line. Even while missing the Week 2 game, he led Green Bay’s defensive tackles in pressures and pass-rush win rate.
The Packers are down to five defensive tackles: Devonte Wyatt and Karl Brooks are the starters, Jonathan Ford is the nose tackle, Chris McClellan is a rookie and Anthony Campbell is a first-year player who made his NFL debut in Week 2 but suffered an ankle injury and hasn’t played since.
“We see who we have, we see who they have and see if we can put the pieces together,” defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon said on Tuesday. “But whoever’s up on gameday, I truly believe this, they have to play in some role for your team or why are you up on gameday? So, if they’re up, they’re going to be up and playing.”
The Packers have 28 players with average salaries of more than $2.0 million per season. They’re not big-ticket items, but cornerback Benjamin St-Juste ($4.9 million), receiver Skyy Moore ($2.5 million), running back Chris Brooks ($2.43 million), linebacker Edgerrin Cooper ($2.15 million) and tight end Luke Musgrave ($2.12 million) add another $14.1 million of average salary to the ledger.
Combined with the six expensive players listed above, those 11 players on the sideline have average salaries totaling $142.1 million. That’s 37.4 percent of the team total.
Not counting Hargrave, who remains on the 53-man roster, the Packers have almost $99 million of average salary on injury lists (injured reserve, physically unable to perform or non-football injury), according to OverTheCap.com . That’s $11 million more than the next team, Carolina, which the Packers will host in a few weeks. Their next two opponents are Dallas and Detroit, which have a combined $66.4 million on the shelf.
A formula at OverTheCap.com shows the Packers have the lowest contract utilization in the NFL, a byproduct of so many high-priced players being out of action.
“It truly is a next-man-up mentality and guys got to get ready to play,” coach Matt LaFleur said on Monday. “That’s just the nature of the beast and I think that’s one of the luxuries of having a 70-man roster. And we tell our players this all the time: Whether you’re on the active or you’re on the P-squad, you got to get ready to play.”

title: Packers Don’t Sign Short Cornerbacks, But They Just Did to Practice Squad
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers have definite height requirements that they haven’t veered from in decades.
However, they did make a noteworthy exception to the rule by signing cornerback Elijah Culp to the practice squad following a Monday workout, a source confirmed what originally was reported by Easton Butler .
The Packers made it official on Tuesday afternoon and released guard Josh Gesky.
Culp ended his college career at James Madison. At pro day, he measured only 5-foot-9 3/4. That’s just fractionally taller than Ahmad Carroll, the Packers’ first-round pick in 2004. He was 5-foot-9 5/8. Carroll was a bust and the Packers haven’t taken another corner shorter than 5-foot-10 since.
What Culp lacks in height, he makes up for in speed with a 4.39-second time in the 40-yard dash and other physical attributes.
“I knew I had to run fast, man,” Culp said after pro day .
Short corners usually find a home as a nickel, and that is how Green Bay views him.
Culp is well-traveled. He opened his college career at Austin Peay in 2020 before transferring to Troy for 2021 and 2022. He transferred to Charlotte, where he redshirted in 2023 and started nine games in 2024.
At James Madison in 2025, he was third-team all-Sun Belt Conference with one interception and eight pass breakups in 13 starts. The interception came against Oregon in the College Football Playoffs.
PFF charged him with a 44.4 percent completion rate and only 9.9 yards per catch in 2025. That includes 1-of-2 for just 5 yards against Oregon and 1-of-5 for 7 yards in the opener against Louisville.
“I really like, honestly, his growth off the field at this point in time, even better than his growth on,” Dukes coach Bob Chesney said last season . “We knew what he could do on the field, but what he's doing off the field now and how he's growing into it, just a really good young man that's going to make a lot of people proud later in life when football is done.”
Culp, who was the No. 44 cornerback prospect in this year’s draft, according to The Athletic’s Dane Brugler, went undrafted and signed with the Cardinals, where he competed for a job in training camp. He recently served a stint on the Colts’ practice squad.
“My whole career I’ve been the underdog,” he told The Touchdown before the draft . “Even at high school, some of my coaches didn’t think I could make it – I was 5’7” back then, and so getting on the field was tough. But when I did get on, I brought that dog mentality, and they couldn’t take me off.
“So, really, I only started playing varsity in the 11th grade. And then by my junior year, I started to see the hard work pay off. It took some time to get there, but I reached the top. As a senior, I had 26 pass breakups. You just don’t see that. But my body grew as my game got better.”
That underdog mentality powered him through the draft process.
“That's my number one motivation,” Culp said at pro day . “Two is just like God gave me this blessing. I don't want to let him down. I'm grateful and I'm blessed for the opportunity. So that's why I wake up every day, even the days I don't want to.”
On the active roster, the Packers have starters Keisean Nixon and Brandon Cisse along with Carrington Valentine, Benjamin St-Juste and Kamal Hadden. St-Juste dropped out of Sunday’s game against Chicago with a hamstring injury, meaning the team could be a man down at corner for this week’s game at Dallas. The only player on the practice squad is Domani Jackson, a sixth-round pick this year.
The Packers had a full practice squad so had to make another move. With the additions on the offensive line and with guards Jacob Monk and Aaron Banks returning to practice late last week, the team opted to release Josh Gesky, who signed with the Packers after going undrafted.
“Man, it would mean a lot,” to make it in the NFL, Culp told The Touchdown. “My family has been very supportive of me, helped me chase my dreams through four different schools. And reaching the NFL would change a lot of people’s lives, and it would definitely change ours.
“So I feel like everybody – me, my mom, pops, brothers – would all be very emotional when that call comes. They obviously know how much I’ve invested in this and I know what they’ve put in too. It would be a dream come true.”

title: 3 Storylines I'm Watching Most in Texans' Week 6 Matchup vs. Jaguars
full_text:
The Houston Texans have their third AFC South matchup of the 2026 season on the horizon for Week 6, as they'll be making the trek overseas to London for a date against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
Last year, these two had split their season series 1-1. Jacksonville got the best of this group in Week 3, which sunk them to a brutal 0-3 through three games, while Week 10 back at home marked the Texans' first victory of an eventual eight-game win streak to finish the season at 12-5.
The Texans are certainly hoping that this game looks a little more like that second meeting from 2025 as opposed to the first. And in the process of their first matchup against Jacksonville for this season, there are a select few storylines worth keeping a close eye on from now until these two take the field at Wembley Stadium on Sunday morning.
Let's break down three of the bigger storylines surrounding the Texans' Week 6 matchup against the Jaguars that I'll be watching the closest:
The Texans will get their first look at Marvin Harrison Jr. within their offense in Week 6 as the team has confirmed that he will be making the trip to London to face the Jaguars, and he will be getting on the field.
The bigger question for Harrison Jr.'s Week 6 showing, though, is just how involved he'll be from the jump.
DeMeco Ryans has already emphasized that the Texans won't be rolling out their new wideout for a huge chunk of snaps for this game earlier in the week, and will likely only have a select few designed plays where he'll be able to get on the field.
So how much will Harrison Jr. be utilized? How does he look in his first game as a part of the Texans, catching passes from his college quarterback against a pretty stout Jaguars defense? All eyes will be on the 2024 No. 4 pick in this one, even if on the field for a limited amount of time.
Veteran running back David Montgomery won't be making the trip to London as he recovers from a groin injury suffered in Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans . That means Woody Marks is due to be the Texans' primary runner throughout the day against Jacksonville, as he was for virtually the entire second half last weekend.
And Marks had a solid game when given the opportunity against Tennessee. He had a season-high 15 carries to turn in 62 yards on the ground, and paired that with four receptions for 23 yards.
But this Jaguars run defense is a force to be reckoned with. Jacksonville has allowed the lowest yards per game (63.8 yds/gm) and the lowest rushing yards over expected (-0.84) through the first five weeks of this season, meaning there aren’t many better at stuffing the run in the NFL than this team.
If Marks is able to overcome the tough matchup, and be the explosive threat in the backfield that this Texans offense could really benefit from, it'll pay off some major dividends for this offense entirely.
The first four weeks of the season for the Texans' defense was a far cry from what they had been used to throughout all of their 2025 campaign.
After some electric performances from the likes of Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills in Week 1, along with CeeDee Lamb and the Dallas Cowboys in Week 4, the Texans decided to shift their defensive play-calling duties to head coach DeMeco Ryans, who had held onto the role for the first two seasons at the helm in Houston.
And that shift was able to work quite well against the Titans in Week 5 . Houston limited Cam Ward and their offense to just three points on the day, and looked a whole lot similar to the form Texans fans had gotten used to over the course of last season, and thus landed them win number one on the season.
Now though, the Texans have a much tougher date against another AFC South opponent in the Jaguars, who have been an above-average scoring attack en route to their own 4-1 start to the season, and can be a true test of whether or not this Houston defense really is back to where they left off last season.

title: Tank Dell Injury Update: Where Texans WR Stands for Week 6 vs. Jaguars
full_text:
It's been a little over a week since the Houston Texans first activated the 21-day practice window returning from injured reserve for wide receiver Tank Dell, who hasn't played in an NFL game dating back to when he first suffered his severe knee injury in December of 2024.
But now that Dell is back at practice–– and as of Wednesday's injury report, was able to be a full participant–– the big question for the Texans' wideout is when he'll be able to get back on the field for a game, and whether or not it could be as soon as Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
And while Dell's full participation in practice is certainly a great sign for how he's progressing, there's no clear determination just yet on whether he'll be good to play this weekend.
Texans general manager Nick Caserio recently appeared on 95.7 The Fan with Seth Payne and Sean Pendergast heading into their Week 6 game in London, where Caserio dove into the status of Dell and what his availability could look like moving forward.
And overall, Dell seems to be "trending in the right direction." However, there remains no clear determination just yet on when the Texans might be activating him from the injured reserve.
"With those players, you have 21 days. So, he practiced last week. He'll practice again here this week. We'll kind of evaluate where he is. Unless he has a setback––he's trending in the right direction," Caserio said of Dell.
"So, whether it's this week or next week, some of this is going to be like: 'Okay, how does this practice go? What does that look like?' Make sure he's loaded properly, make sure that he's prepared so that when he does go out there and actually play, he's ready to go for that."
Dell has been showing some really positive signs when it comes to getting back to 100%. Returning to practice is a big part of that, and participating in full for multiple sessions will be the next step for his availability to look even more promising moving forward.
But Dell also has two key factors to clear within his recovery and return to practice before he's officially deemed ready to be activated from injured reserve : that's handling contact, and getting back his top-end speed that made him such a potent offensive weapon before his injury.
The longer that Dell is able to get his feet wet in practice and get more comfortable back in pads, the better his chances will be to finally be activated after a nearly two-year wait to return to the field.
However, seeing those aspects of his recovery develop in practice might end up extending his absence an extra one or two weeks before the Texans do activate him from injured reserve, and would thus sideline him for Week 6 against the Jaguars .
What might end up being the most ideal approach for the Texans to take is to wait until their Week 8 bye before activating Dell from injured reserve.
The Wednesday of Houston's bye in Week 8 marks the end of Houston's 21-day window to elevate Dell to the active roster, and doing so then could essentially allow Dell one more full week of practice before their next game in Week 9 against the LA Chargers.
When Caserio was asked about the possibility of waiting until the bye week to activate Dell, he didn't shoot the idea down. But the focus was simply on how this week's practice looks before Week 6. Then the team would re-evaluate from there.
"Look, you have 21 days. So, within that 21-day period, you're either going to activate him, or you're not. So, we'll kind of handle this week, we'll kind of see how this week goes, and make an assessment at the end of the week," Caserio continued.
"But, he's certainly done everything we've asked him to do, and he's turning in the right direction."
The main takeaway from all of this? Dell's moving in the right direction to get back on the field in the coming weeks. As to when his return to the field might be, though, could be anywhere from Week 6 in London, all the way until Week 9 on the road in Los Angeles.

title: Why Texans Must Temper Expectations for Marvin Harrison Jr. vs. Jaguars
full_text:
The Houston Texans will be getting their first look at Marvin Harrison Jr. in his new jersey following his move from the Arizona Cardinals, as head coach DeMeco Ryans confirmed on Wednesday that the team is planning on their new wide receiver being active for Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
It's bound to be an exciting moment for Harrison Jr. and everyone watching, as the Texans' newest pass-catcher will be bringing in balls from his college quarterback, C.J. Stroud, once again , and potentially mark the beginning of a fresh start in the NFL with a new situation in Houston.
But when it comes to Harrison Jr.'s chances to make an impact in Week 6 against the Jaguars, just how involved will the Texans' newest receiver be in the overall game plan?
Of course, Harrison Jr. is bound to get on the field for his fair share of plays, but having been in the building for less than a week, there's a good chance that the Texans' newest wideout will be a bit limited in his debut.
Now, in a few weeks' time, Harrison Jr. will slowly find himself as a bigger and more important piece of the Texans' game plan. Houston invested a premium second-round pick for the talent he brings to the table , and will be hungry to squeeze some of that production out of him as soon as this season.
But the turnaround that Harrison Jr. has to face–– going from an entirely new team and offensive system with different plays in a one-week span–– it's hard to expect the Texans' newest wideout to catch onto and adjust the entire playbook in such a short amount of time.
Instead, the Texans will likely take things a bit slower when it comes to Harrison Jr.'s involvement; letting him learn a select number of plays before this weekend's matchup in London, getting him involved in those specific reps, and hoping that he can have a smoother transition as a result.
DeMeco Ryans even addressed the Texans' plans for Harrison Jr. in terms of workload on Wednesday after revealing Houston's new receiver was set to play against the Jaguars, where it was clear he wasn't exactly going to be an every-snap player just yet.
"When you get a player to come in late as Marvin has, like, what is he able to pick up on? We go through the entire playbook, we'll have set plays, and we'll make sure it's as easy as possible for him to get lined up so he can play fast," Ryans said.
"Don't expect him to come out and play all 60 snaps in the game, but we'll make sure he gets what he needs, and make sure he's confident in what we're asking him to do."
While Week 6 against the Jaguars could see Harrison Jr.'s workload on the lighter side, it's only a matter of time before those snaps and opportunities grow larger.
Keep an eye on the Texans' Week 9 against the LA Chargers as a potential turning point for Harrison Jr.'s involvement. Houston has their bye sitting in Week 8 after facing the New York Giants next weekend, and could set up the right amount of time necessary for the 2024 No. 4 pick to really get an understanding of his new offense.
Until then, the Texans will make it an emphasis to ensure Harrison Jr. has a smooth transition within his new home, and hope it can set up to pay some dividends for this offense in due time.

title: 4 Noteworthy Quotes From Marvin Harrison Jr.'s First Texans Presser
full_text:
The Houston Texans finally got Marvin Harrison Jr. in the building for his first practice with the team on Wednesday, only a few days out from his first game in uniform against the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 6.
And after that Texans' practice, Harrison Jr. was able to speak to the media for the first time since the deal to ship him out from the Arizona Cardinals went down earlier this weekend.
Let's sort through four of the more notable points to come out of Harrison Jr.'s first presser as a part of the Texans:
One thing Texans fans will notice pretty quickly about Harrison Jr. is that he's a pretty reserved personality.
However, even while not your typical alpha, outspoken NFL wide receiver, he made sure to express the excitement he has in store with his new situation, along with pairing up next to his college quarterback in C.J. Stroud .
"I'm excited to be here," Harrison Jr said. "I'm excited to help this team win games. I'm excited to be with C.J. again, and help C.J. to the best of my abilities."
"Always watched the Texans from afar. Obviously, just watching C.J. So, it's pretty surreal to be able to play with him now again, and just help him out the best I can."
As for Harrison's biggest goals for both now and the future, he kept things pretty simple:
"Help the team win. Period."
While the process for Harrison Jr.'s move out of Arizona was a bit different than your typical trade, it seems Harrison Jr. himself found out Houston was his ultimate destination a little bit before the entire world did–– or at least until DeMeco Ryans made it clear during his post-game presser after beating the Tennessee Titans.
"My agent told me, obviously, before the news broke to you guys," Harrison Jr. said of how he found out about the trade to Houston. "DeMeco kind of did his thing as well. But, yeah, before that."
As to whether or not Houston was the place he wanted to be, he set the record straight that he really had no control over where he would be headed after the Cardinals.
"When you get traded, you don't really have that option, you know?"
Harrison Jr. was also asked about how he felt about some viral clips circling around social media showcasing some of his routes run during his time with the Cardinals: some of which might've not looked the most polished or with 110% effort that you'd expect.
look at the effort on this route from Marvin Harrison Jr. on 2nd and 6 pic.twitter.com/xu6jK6VJwe
However, Harrison Jr. simply brushed off those types of comments or concerns. Simply put, everybody has their own opinion, and he knows the player and person he can be.
"I mean, everybody has their own opinions," Harrison Jr. said. "That's really the best way I can put that. Everybody has their own opinions and what they're going to gather from information."
"I know who I am as a player. I know who I am as a person. However people want to label me or think of me, that's their opinion."
Harrison Jr.'s first team session in the Texans' facility on Wednesday also meant he was able to be coached up by DeMeco Ryans for the first time .
And based on first impressions, Harrison Jr. had one clear takeaway on what Ryan’s brings to the table: energy.
"Energy, man. Energy. That's one thing you can always pinpoint, especially with a defensive guy," Harrison Jr. on what he's noticed about DeMeco Ryans. "They always want to bring the energy. You can kind of see that throughout the whole team, and the energy he brings day in and day out."

title: Texans Make Marvin Harrison Jr. Plans Clear for Week 6 vs. Jaguars
full_text:
The Houston Texans finally got their new wide receiver addition Marvin Harrison Jr. in the building for his first team practice on Wednesday, coming just a day before the team is set to take the flight overseason to face off against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London for Week 6 .
And it seems like for the Texans, they won't be waiting long at all before they're able to see their new trade acquisition on the field for a regular season game.
Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans spoke to the media after Wednesday's team practice, where he was asked about what Harrison Jr.'s availability would look like for the week ahead. Ryans noted that the team will be playing their new wide receiver in Week 6 against the Jaguars.
Texans HC DeMeco Ryans said newly-acquired WR Marvin Harrison Jr. will make his Houston debut Sunday in London vs. the Jaguars. pic.twitter.com/qfcrSg3SWC
It's a quick turnaround for the Texans' new wideout after being less than a week removed from his time with the Arizona Cardinals .
In just a week's time, Harrison Jr. was notified he'd be traded from the Cardinals, was deemed inactive for Week 5 against the Detroit Lions, saw the trade go down on Sunday afternoon , and he's now seemingly ready to go for his first game with Houston––albeit a little far away from home in London.
As to how much the Texans wind up utilizing Harrison Jr. in his first game with the team? To this point, that remains a bit of a mystery.
There remains a chance that while the 24-year-old will be active and on the field for Week 6 against the Jaguars, he might not be a true featured part of the game plan until closer to the second half of the season.
However, from the initial signs that the Texans and DeMeco Ryans have seen from their new pass-catcher at Wednesday's practice, he appears to be pretty confident that Harrison Jr. has caught onto his new system and situation quite well.
"I thought Marvin did a really good job today getting acclimated," Ryans said of Harrison Jr.'s first Texans practice.
"Coaches have done a great job in the background, just really working with him, getting him caught up to speed on our plays, the verbiage of what we're doing. He got in, ran some plays today, did a good job."
Harrison Jr. also seemed to take it upon himself to get further adjusted with the Texans' offense a little earlier upon his arrival this week.
Ryans explained that Harrison Jr. had come into the Texans' facility for individual work during his first night in town with assistant wide receivers coach Tiquan Underwood, thus allowing him and his acclimation process to get a day ahead of schedule.
"Getting a player caught up, it isn't hard when the player is attentive and he's locked in on getting the details down. So Marvin's first night here, he was with our assistant wide receiver coach, Coach Tiquan [Underwood], and they were grinding," Ryans said of how Harrison Jr. is adjusting.
"They were working late at night. They were in the playbook, grinding, and that allowed him to get a day ahead. Now, he was able to go out there today and just fit right in seamlessly. So, when you put the work in and you're dialed in, you can make it work."
Now, that urgency and hard work to get on the same page as this Texans' offense early seems to already be paying off for Harrison Jr.
He'll be on the field this weekend against the Jaguars in a brand-new uniform, catching passes from his college teammate C.J. Stroud , and might end up being a key part of the Texans' offensive game plan a bit earlier than expected if he's able to keep up at this pace.

title: Texans' Braden Smith Return Creates Intriguing O-Line Dilemma
full_text:
The Houston Texans are getting some reinforcements on their offensive line this week.
According to an announcement from the Texans, the team is officially activating veteran offensive tackle Braden Smith from injured reserve.
We have activated Braden Smith from the Reserve/Injured list and made other roster moves. pic.twitter.com/iGGwgOV2QE
Smith––one of the Texans' big offensive line additions from this offseason–– has been stuck on the injured reserve list since the start of the 2026 season due to a foot injury he suffered back in August.
The Texans officially activated his 21-day return window for the Wednesday practice before their matchup against the Tennessee Titans, yet felt it would be better to let him rest once more before officially elevating him to the active roster.
Fast forward to their preparation for Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars, and now, Smith is ready to get back in the lineup. And that's good news for the Texans' offensive line: their big $20 million investment from this offseason will finally be able to suit up for a regular season game.
But the Texans have a decision on their hands as it relates to slotting Smith into their offense: is he going to be starting right off the bat, or will they continue to roll with Trent Brown, who's been Houston's right tackle for the first five weeks of the season.
Heading into the 2026 season, the general consensus remained that Smith could have the edge over Brown when it comes to their starting right tackle spot.
After all, the Texans made sure to invest a steep $20 million in his services via free agency just a few months ago with the intent of him being an upgrade upfront.
But Brown had an appealing case himself entering this season: he started the second half of the 2025 season, where he helped the Texans rattle off a perfect 8-0 record, then a Wild Card win against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
So if Houston was confident in Smith's ability, and he performed well in preseason and training camp, keeping him at that right tackle spot isn't a wild idea even if Smith were healthy. With him being placed on injured reserve, though, the Texans essentially had their right tackle decision made for them.
Now though, the Texans have a decision on their hands. Brown, through the first five games of the season, hasn't been the most exemplary tackle: playing 335 snaps to record six penalties, 13 pressures, two sacks, and one QB hit.
The Texans, if they felt there was an ability to improve at their tackle spot opposite Aireontae Ersery, have a clear opportunity to shift things around for Week 6. Smith is healthy, practicing in full a few days out from their trip to London, and should be ready to take on those starting duties if Houston's staff entrusts him with that spot.
Time will tell if the Texans decide to make a pivot within their offensive line unit. So far into the 2026 season, Houston hasn't forced a change upfront unless the move was in the event of injury.
And after finally rattling off a win in Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans in dominant fashion, perhaps a big offensive line change isn't on the radar for Houston.
However, if the Texans' offensive line has a route to perform better than they have through the first quarter of this regular season––and so far, it hasn't exactly been a top unit in the league––it’s something the Houston brass should at least consider.

title: Texans GM Explains Weeks of Work Behind Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade
full_text:
The Houston Texans added a new big name to their wide receiver room over the weekend by adding 2024 No. 4 pick Marvin Harrison via trade with the Arizona Cardinals; ultimately acquiring him and a sixth-round pick in exchange for a second- and seventh-round pick .
And it's a deal for the Texans that's not only significant when diving into what Harrison Jr. could bring to this offense, but the move is seemingly one that's been in the works for some time now–– according to general manager Nick Caserio.
During an interview with Seth Payne and Sean Pendergast on 95.7 The Fan , Caserio broke down what the process looked like when it came to making the move for Harrison Jr. with the Cardinals and their general manager, Monti Ossenfort.
And per Caserio, the two had discussed the move for "a few weeks," and had even agreed to the deal on Friday night, even if initial reports didn't describe things that way.
"We had talked for a few weeks, and then the deal– he and I agreed to the deal Friday night," Caserio said of the Harrison Jr. trade. "Like, the deal was basically done Friday night. We kind of had an agreement in place. I gave him my word, he gave me his word."
"That's how you do business, that's how [Monti Ossenfort] and I do business. But he wanted to handle it a certain way as it pertains to the communication. and some of the other things. So, we certainly didn't have a problem with that at all. We kind of followed his lead there a little bit. I think he communicated with Marvin that he was going to be an active Saturday morning."
#Texans GM Nick Caserio told us how he and Cardinals GM Monte Ossenfort closed the Marvin Harrison Jr. trade. Caserio says the deal was basically done on Friday night and the outcome of the Titans game had no impact on the consummation of the trade. pic.twitter.com/KGe6d2ri5L
So instead of the move being announced a couple of days before Week 5's game for both Arizona and Houston, the two hashed out the agreement, Harrison Jr. was inactive, then got to Sunday afternoon where Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans broke the trade news during his post-game presser.
A common theory that had surfaced surrounding the Texans' negotiations for Harrison Jr. was that Houston had to win their Week 5 game against the Tennessee Titans for the trade to be deemed official.
Caserio, though, explains that wasn't quite the case.
"And so, the trade was done Friday night. We had agreed to the parameters. There was a few things that we had to finalize and work out," Caserio continued. "So what happened in a game had absolutely zero bearing on whether or not we were going to consummate the transaction."
"We're not going to agree to something, and then see what happens in the game, and then back out of it. Like, we're not gonna do that. I don't operate that way. Like, we're not going to operate that way.
Overall, a bit of an unorthodox procedure when it comes to an NFL trade, and one that took a bit longer to develop, all things considered. But in the end, the Texans and Cardinals both checked the boxes they needed to make the trade come to fruition.
The Texans had their eyes on Harrison Jr. and his situation for weeks , and were willing to pay the desired cost to get him on their roster. The Cardinals wanted a second-round pick in exchange for their top-five pick from 2024, and managed to do exactly that. A job well done for both sides.

title: Jalen Pitre Injury Update: Texans DB Could Have Caught a Big Break
full_text:
We now know a bit more about the injury that Houston Texans defensive back Jalen Pitre suffered in Week 5's road trip against the Tennessee Titans.
And it seems like, while there is a chance that Pitre misses some time, the Texans avoided any worst-case scenario surrounding the health of their star defender.
According to NFL insider Tom Pelissero of The Ringer , Pitre has suffered an AC joint sprain in his shoulder that leaves his status as week-to-week.
Texans DB Jalen Pitre suffered an AC joint sprain Sunday and is considered week-to-week, per source. Good news overall for one of Houston's standouts, who avoided a major injury.
Pitre first went down with the shoulder injury during the second half of action in the Texans' Week 5 matchup against the Titans. Pitre would inevitably end up not returning to the action, and head coach DeMeco Ryans had noted that the team was still evaluating his status moving forward.
And now, with a bit more clarity on the severity of Pitre's shoulder issue, it does seem to hint towards a possible absence for him in their upcoming Week 6 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars .
However, without any expectation of a lengthy recovery, or any signs of short-term injured reserve being in play, it's great news for the Texans to hear.
Pitre has long been an integral piece of the Texans' defense as a versatile nickel/safety. He's been on the field for over 90% of Houston's defensive snaps this season as a fifth defensive back to play alongside Houston's strong corner and safety unit.
In the five games that Pitre has played this season, he's put together 24 combined tackles, one tackle for loss, five passes defended, and a forced fumble; really making an impact all over the defensive side as he has since emerging as a full-time starter in his rookie season back in 2022.
The Texans may have to do without his services for a game or two this season––which they had to also navigate in 2025 when Pitre missed three games with a concussion––but a week-to-week status might be the best-case scenario, considering the uncertainty that was surrounding his health after Week 5.
While the length of Pitre's injury absence is far from confirmed, there's a good chance that the Texans end up being without him for just two weeks, simply because of the placement of their bye in Week 8.
Houston could take their trip overseas against the Jaguars in Week 6 , then travel home to face the New York Giants in Week 7 without Pitre, then allow their star defender an extra week of rest before they're back in action in Week 9 against the LA Chargers.
For however long that Pitre does remain out, it feels like a safe bet that fifth-round rookie Kamari Ramsey will be the one called up to take his reps as a similarly versatile contributor at nickel and safety.
Ramsey is one of the few names on the Texans' roster with experience playing both at safety and nickel during his time in college at USC, and already managed to get snaps his way in place of Pitre when he went out in Week 5 against the Titans.
So far this season, Ramsey has played in 40 defensive snaps for the Texans, where he's recorded six tackles and one tackle for loss. If Houston's coaching staff trusts their rookie to claim Pitre's snaps for the time that he's out, Week 6 can be a massive opportunity to see those numbers jump across the board.
The Texans will have a couple of practices at their disposal before traveling to London this week to plan out their defensive plans more in depth without Pitre for Week 6. However, knowing that their star defender won't be sidelined for an extremely long period of time is great news for all involved in Houston.
