Jared Koch is the Publisher of Houston Texans On SI. He has covered the NFL and NBA with On SI since 2023, and is a graduate of Western Kentucky University.

title: Colts-Titans Injury Report: Two Colts Starters Make Significant Progress
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are preparing for a pivotal AFC South matchup against the Tennessee Titans in Week 6.
With Sunday's contest approaching, both teams are working through their final preparations while monitoring several players dealing with injuries. Thursday's practice sessions provided another update on each team's health as the Colts and Titans look to put their best lineups on the field in Nashville.
Let's take a look at the most recent injury developments for both teams.
Indianapolis Colts Injury Report (As of 10/15)
The big news of the day is Matt Goncalves and Jaylhan Tuimoloau being full participants after appearing on the injury report for concussion evaluations on Wednesday . According to James Boyd of The Athletic, neither were practicing in red non-contact jerseys, meaning they are not in concussion protocol. A significant and positive development for Sunday, as both have been evidently cleared and will be good to go this weekend barring a setback.
No practice again for Ashton Dulin. The Colts still consider him week-to-week. Jaylon Carlies missed the game in Pittsburgh and is now in danger of missing his second straight contest after not participating in either practice so far this week.
A number of veterans returned to full participation after getting the day off on Wednesday, including Keenan Allen, Jonathan Taylor and Charvarius Ward. Josh Downs, who was also listed with a hamstring injury on Wednesday, was back in full. Grover Stewart is the only new addition to the report as he gets his usual Thursday rest day.
Will Mallory continues to log full practices, a great sign of his progress working back from a thumb injury. That said, the Colts did sign tight end Pharoah Brown to their active roster from the practice squad earlier this week, bringing the number of tight ends on the roster to four. That’s likely an indication that Mallory is further behind in his rehab than the Colts are letting on.
Thursday's practice report for #TENvsIND pic.twitter.com/cAVnWjK5Lk
Two straight days of full participation for both Daniel Jones and Darius SLayton is a solid indication that both are dealing with minor knocks and are likely on track to play on Sunday. That’s great news for a passing offense that’s dealt with several issues over the first five weeks. If Slayton is healthy for the weekend, he’ll make his long awaited Indianapolis debut unless listed as a healthy scratch on game day.
Limited participation is an improvement for Jalen Travis after missing Wednesday's session. His ankle injury came up during Sunday’s loss to the Steelers, though Travis was able to return to and finish the game. We’ll know more regarding his status tomorrow, but the early indications are at least positive.
Overall, Wednesday’s report brought some worry for the Colts, but Thursday proved to be a significant step in the right direction with several starters either returning to practice or increasing their level of activity. Assuming no new developments arise between now and the final injury report, I’d expect a fairly short list on the Colts’ side of things.
Tennessee Titans Injury Report (As of 10/15)
*-On injured reserve; 21-day practice window currently open
Tennessee’s Thursday report is very similar to the first of the week. All the same names remain, but several players’ participation levels have changed.
Starting with the non-participants, Kevin Winston Jr. is yet to practice this week, indicating he may not be ready for Week 6. Tyjae Spears was limited with a knee injury on Wednesday but was downgraded to no participation on Thursday, making his availability for the weekend unlikely. As a result, the Titans’ run game will lean mostly on Tony Pollard.
Thursday’s Injury Report. pic.twitter.com/aHGH3d327n
Marcus Harris being limited is notable. Tennessee’s starting nickel has been one of the few bright spots for a floundering Titans team, recording an interception and half a sack through five games. David Martin-Robinson is the third of four tight ends listed on the depth chart, ahead of only former Colt Kylen Granson. If Martin-Robinson fails to record a full practice tomorrow, Granson could play a role against his former team.
Nothing much to note with the full participants. Tony Pollard returned from an off-day, as did John Franklin-Myers, and Cor’Dale Flott is on track to play. That said, Amani Hooker didn’t practice after being limited on Wednesday with a concussion. He’ll need to be a full participant in Friday’s practice to have any chance of clearing concussion protocol in time for the game, which seems highly unlikely at this point.
Tennessee’s secondary is the area to monitor as Week 6 approaches. With two starting cornerbacks and both starting safeties dealing with knocks, the Titans could be forced to use some backups.
Considering the wide receiver injuries on the other side for Indianapolis, that could make for a peculiar battle on game day.

title: 3 Burning Questions Facing the Colts Ahead of Week 6
full_text:
There may not be a better get-right opportunity on the Indianapolis Colts' schedule than this one.
Indianapolis is 2-3 and coming off a frustrating loss in Pittsburgh, while the Tennessee Titans enter Lucas Oil Stadium at 0-5 with the NFL's lowest-scoring offense.
This is a game the Colts should win, but it is also a chance to answer a few questions that have followed this team through five weeks.
Moving the football was not the biggest issue against Pittsburgh. Finishing drives was.
Indianapolis scored just one touchdown and settled for five field goals in the 34-22 loss, wasting too many opportunities once the offense reached scoring territory.
The season-long red-zone numbers are actually solid. The Colts have scored touchdowns on 10 of 15 red-zone trips, but Sunday showed how quickly this offense can stall when Jonathan Taylor is not controlling the game.
Taylor was held to 45 yards on 15 carries and did not score against Pittsburgh. Through five games, he has 398 rushing yards and six touchdowns.
Getting him going again, especially near the goal line, has to be priority No. 1.
So far, the answer looks like a resounding yes.
Baltimore, Kansas City and Pittsburgh scored a combined 108 points against Indianapolis. Houston and Washington combined for just 30.
That difference is hard to ignore.
Tennessee now gives this defense another favorable matchup. The Titans are averaging an NFL-worst 11.6 points per game, while Cam Ward has thrown for 896 yards, three touchdowns, and three interceptions.
The biggest key is pressure. Ward has averaged roughly 2.6 yards per attempt when pressured, but Indianapolis has been one of the NFL's worst teams at generating it.
If this pass rush cannot make a struggling rookie quarterback uncomfortable, it's hard to imagine things improving against better competition.
This might be the most interesting question of the week.
Allen played just 11 defensive snaps through the first four games before seeing a career-high 24 against Pittsburgh. For a second-round pick Chris Ballard said would be a green-dot linebacker "from the get-go," his early role has been surprisingly small.
Linebacker has been one of the weakest parts of this defense, and Indianapolis made a clear bet on getting younger at the position this offseason.
Allen does not have to become an every-down star overnight, but Week 5 felt like the first real step toward finding out what the Colts have in him.
Now the question is whether Anarumo keeps the door open.
The Colts have a favorable matchup, a home game and a winless divisional opponent. If they want to get back to .500, these are three areas that need to look different on Sunday.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Four Bold Predictions for the Colts’ Week 6 Battle with the Titans
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are heading into Week 6 looking to put last Sunday's loss to Pittsburgh behind them and get back in the win column. A matchup with the Tennessee Titans presents an opportunity to do just that, with Indianapolis entering as the clear favorite against its division rival.
But divisional games rarely follow a predictable script, and the Colts have plenty to prove as they look to build on their iffy start to the season. With another week of football ahead, here are four bold predictions for Sunday's matchup in Nashville.
Red Zone Struggles Will Continue
Through the first five games, the Colts red zone offense has been ultra-reliable. Indianapolis ranks eighth in the NFL in red zone scoring percentage, finding the end zone 66.7% of the time.
But that efficiency took a hit in Pittsburgh.The Colts drove into the red zone on three separate occasions, but only found the end zone once.
I expect those struggles to continue, despite facing a Tennessee defense that’s allowing red zone touchdowns at a 62.5% clip. The Steelers exposed the blueprint the Colts have been using by loading the defensive front with physical run stuffers and keeping gains to a minimum against the run.
With the Colts’ mangled wide receiver core contributing to issues in the passing game, Indianapolis could struggle to find answers when its rushing attack is bottled up. Defenses can afford to crowd the box and force Daniel Jones to beat them through the air, an especially difficult task with limited options on the perimeter.
The Titans have a stud cornerback in Alontae Taylor, who can easily eliminate a pass catcher in the red zone. If the rest of the secondary does its job, and the run defense holds strong in short yardage, then it could be another long day for the Colts offense.
Titans Double Scoring Average, Amplifying Questions About Colts’ Defense
The Titans rank dead last in the NFL in points scored per game (11.6). The Colts defense is towards the bottom of the league in points allowed per game with 27.6, sixth-most in the NFL.
The Colts defensive issues go deep, with allowing so many points being a symptom of the overall problem. Indianapolis ranks near the bottom of the league in pass rush pressure rate and has repeatedly surrendered explosive plays, which have made it difficult for the defense to stay off the field.
Tennessee has struggled to generate offense all season, but the Colts have shown enough vulnerability to give the Titans an opportunity to find success. I expect Tennessee to take advantage of those weaknesses and score at least 23 points, doubling its season average and raising further concerns about Indianapolis' ability to get stops against even the league's least productive offenses.
And as a result, change could be on the horizon.
The Colts' pass rush has been one of the defense's biggest weaknesses through five games. Indianapolis ranks last in the NFL with a 24% pressure rate, struggling to consistently disrupt opposing quarterbacks without relying on coverage or mistakes from the offense.
Tennessee presents an opportunity to change that narrative after allowing four sacks against Houston last week. However, I expect Indianapolis to continue struggling to generate consistent pressure, even against a vulnerable offensive line. Arden Key is on injured reserve for at least three more weeks, and the pass rush is lacking reliable production.
Without consistent pressure, the Colts will have to rely on their secondary to hold up in coverage for extended periods, giving Cam Ward more opportunities to find open receivers. If Indianapolis can't capitalize on Tennessee's protection issues, it will be another frustrating afternoon for a defense searching for answers.
Colts Win, But Unconvincingly
The Colts will have an opportunity to get back on track against a winless Titans team that has struggled to generate offense. However, Indianapolis cannot afford to mistake a favorable matchup for a sign that its problems have been solved. The 34-22 loss to Pittsburgh exposed recurring issues with tackling, explosive plays allowed and red-zone execution that contributed to the team's struggles.
Indianapolis has yet to demonstrate that it can consistently pair its offensive production with dependable defensive play. The Colts can move the ball and put points on the board, but defensive breakdowns have made it difficult to control games when the offense fails to deliver on every possession. Tennessee offers a chance to correct that imbalance, but the Colts will need to show greater discipline and execution on defense to do so.
I expect Indianapolis to come away with a win, but not necessarily the kind of complete performance that quiets concerns about the team's ability to compete with the AFC's better teams. Beating Tennessee is important for the standings. Showing tangible improvement in the areas that cost them against Pittsburgh would be far more meaningful for the Colts' long-term outlook.

title: The Anthony Richardson Conversation Is Heating Up in Indianapolis
full_text:
The Anthony Richardson conversation is resurfacing, and if the Indianapolis Colts keep losing, it is only going to get louder.
Let me make one thing clear: I still believe Daniel Jones is the better quarterback, and I think he can pilot this offense at a very high level once he fully settles back in from Achilles surgery.
But at 2-3, with the offense taking a clear step backward, it is fair to ask the question.
ESPN's Ben Solak recently floated that very idea in his Week 6 observations, writing, "The Colts should play Anthony Richardson Sr."
Solak pointed to Jones' declining arm strength and Richardson's rushing ability as reasons Indianapolis should consider a change. He stopped short of calling for a permanent benching, but the idea is now out there.
Richardson's fall from favor under Shane Steichen did not happen overnight.
After being benched in 2024, including the infamous moment against Houston when he removed himself from the game, Steichen repeatedly emphasized consistency, details, and professional habits.
Richardson eventually got the job back, but it never felt like he fully regained Steichen's trust. That carried into 2025, when Indianapolis signed Jones and opened a legitimate quarterback competition.
Richardson kept things close throughout training camp, but Jones was ultimately the more consistent option and won the job.
He then proved the Colts right almost immediately.
Jones helped Indianapolis start 8-2, completing 68.0% of his passes for 3,101 yards, 19 touchdowns, and eight interceptions before tearing his Achilles in December. That is part of the reason I am nowhere near ready to give up on him.
Still, the 2026 numbers are ugly. Jones is 108-of-176 for 1,021 yards, three touchdowns and four interceptions through five games, with a 73.6 passer rating after posting a 100.2 mark last season.
He is only about 10 months removed from Achilles surgery, and the explosiveness clearly has not completely returned.
That is where Richardson becomes interesting.
His passing numbers are rough: 50.6% completions, 2,400 yards, 11 touchdowns and 13 interceptions. But he is 8-7 as a starter and has added 634 rushing yards and 10 touchdowns.
There is something to be said for what that rushing threat could do next to Jonathan Taylor. Defenses have to account for Richardson as a runner, which can open things up in the read-option game.
The problem is obvious. If defenses do not fear Richardson's arm, Indianapolis becomes much easier to defend.
Jones has real rushing ability of his own, and I still believe that part of his game can return as he gets healthier. So no, I would not advocate for making the switch any time soon.
But if this season starts going off the rails, the Colts may reach a point where they have nothing left to lose. With Steichen and Chris Ballard under enormous pressure, Richardson could become the ultimate desperation swing.
And as crazy as that might have sounded a month ago, it is becoming increasingly difficult to dismiss the possibility.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts Open Week 6 With Several Key Names on Injury Report
full_text:
At this point, Indianapolis Colts fans are probably tired of watching injuries take a toll on this roster.
It feels like the same story we've seen over the last decade-plus, and through five weeks of the 2026 season, injuries are once again making life considerably more difficult for Indianapolis.
Wednesday's injury report featured several notable names, including two players who left practice for concussion evaluations.
And for a team sitting at 2-3, the last thing Indianapolis needs is more injuries to important contributors.
Offensive lineman Matt Goncalves and rookie defensive end Jaylahn Tuimoloau were both limited Wednesday after leaving practice to undergo concussion evaluations.
Whether either player passed those evaluations remains unclear, but both situations deserve attention heading into Sunday.
Goncalves has been a valuable piece of the offensive line, and with Daniel Jones already struggling to find consistency, losing another contributor up front certainly wouldn't help.
Tuimoloau's situation might be even more frustrating considering the current state of Indianapolis' defensive line.
With Arden Key recently landing on injured reserve, Indianapolis needs its younger pass rushers to step up and produce . Potentially losing another body along the defensive front would only make that challenge more difficult.
Linebacker Jaylon Carlies also missed practice with the rib injury that sidelined him against Pittsburgh. Considering how poorly this linebacker room has performed through five weeks, Indianapolis can hardly afford another week without one of its starters.
Jalen Travis was another nonparticipant after suffering an ankle injury against the Steelers.
Perhaps no position group has been more affected by injuries this season than wide receiver .
Alec Pierce hasn't played since Week 2 against Kansas City, and without his ability to stretch the field, this passing attack has looked considerably less dangerous.
Outside of Josh Downs, there just haven't been many sparks from this group. Downs leads the healthy receivers with 20 catches for 249 yards, but he appeared on Wednesday's report as limited with rest/hamstring listed.
Fortunately, Downs participated in individual drills, suggesting the issue may not be particularly serious.
Keenan Allen did not practice due to rest, while Ashton Dulin remained sidelined with a hamstring injury. One encouraging development was Darius Slayton returning as a full participant after a knee injury kept him out against Pittsburgh.
Slayton hasn't made his Colts debut, but Indianapolis desperately needs someone who can threaten defenses vertically while Pierce remains sidelined.
Right now, opposing defenses simply don't have enough to fear from this passing attack .
Daniel Jones was listed with an ankle injury but practiced fully Wednesday, which is certainly a positive development.
Jonathan Taylor was limited strictly for rest, while Charvarius Ward also received a rest day.
Tight end Will Mallory was another full participant as he continues working toward a potential return from injured reserve.
There's still time for several of these situations to improve before Sunday's divisional matchup against the Tennessee Titans. But the bigger concern remains the same.
Indianapolis is already struggling to find consistency on both sides of the ball, and continuing to lose important contributors certainly isn't making things any easier.
At 2-3, this team needs to start stacking wins. Getting healthy would be a pretty good place to start.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts Have Several Trade Targets to Consider After Marvin Harrison Jr. Miss
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts entered the 2026 season with high expectations, but their offense has developed a glaring weakness at wide receiver . Injuries and a lack of consistent downfield production have limited Daniel Jones' options in the passing game, leaving Indianapolis searching for answers.
With the NFL trade deadline approaching, the Colts must determine whether their current group is capable of getting the job done or if outside help is necessary. The team has playoff aspirations, but its recent performances have exposed some limitations that could become increasingly difficult to overcome as the season progresses.
Acquiring another receiver would give Indianapolis an opportunity to address one of its most pressing concerns. However, making a deal is easier said than done, especially for a team that has already made a significant investment in its present roster.
The question is whether the Colts can find a worthwhile addition at the right price, or if they're better off trusting the players they already have.
The Colts have lacked consistent production from their wide receivers through five games. Josh Downs leads the group with 249 receiving yards, while Keenan Allen has 145 and Laquon Treadwell has 157. Tight end Tyler Warren actually leads the team in receptions with 30, highlighting how much Indianapolis has relied on its tight end to keep the pass game afloat.
Injuries have complicated the picture. Alec Pierce, one of Indianapolis' most important downfield threats, appeared in just two of the team's first five games and is out until further notice Darius Slayton, a midseason addition, is yet to play a game as he deals with a knee injury.
Still, the Colts cannot afford to ignore the position as the trade deadline approaches. The team did its research on a possible trade for Marvin Harrison Jr., but he was moved to Houston after Indy determined the asking price was too steep.
ESPN's Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have identified several wide receivers who could be worth monitoring, giving Indianapolis potential alternatives if it decides its current group needs reinforcement.
One wide out that Graziano threw out as a possible trade candidate is Jacksonville’s Brian Thomas Jr. The third-year player enjoyed a breakout rookie season but regressed in year two and has since fallen behind Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers in the pecking order. While he may be of interest to receiver-needy teams, Jacksonville is reluctant to trade him, especially with their 4-1 start to the season
Another player whose name is generating some buzz is Browns receiver Jerry Jeudy. Cleveland is building around a young core and Jeudy appears to have fallen out of favor with the Browns prioritizing the development of their two rookie receivers, Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion.
Cleveland reportedly set their asking price at a third or fourth-round pick for Jeudy according to Jordan Schultz , but Schultz isn’t convinced they’ll find a partner willing to meet that price. Fowler echoed a similar sentiment, saying “My sense is while they are not actively shopping Jeudy, a strong offer could change that.”
It appears the Browns are simply holding out until they receive a suitable offer.
The third option Graziano and Fowler listed was Chargers’ receiver Quentin Johnston. Johnston has had a rough go of life in the NFL in his first three seasons as drop issues plagued him early on. Now, the Chargers sit winless at 0-5 with a trip to Kansas City on deck before their bye. If Los Angeles is still without a by the time their bye week rolls around, significant change could be on the way.
“Someone the other day mentioned the possibility of a Chargers fire sale,” Graziano said. “Teams will have an eye on potentially helpful players from a Chargers roster that obviously hasn't come together…Johnston is certainly intriguing.”
The price tag for Johnston is unknown, but if the Colts had any interest, a late-round pick could do the trick. Johnston could fit into Shane Steichen’s offense as a possession receiver, but has an $18 million fifth-year option fully guaranteed coming up in 2027.
Working through the rest of the possible trade targets, Rashod Bateman is someone Fowler said he’s keeping tabs on.
“Zay Flowers is the dominant wide receiver in the Ravens' offense, which means Bateman's production comes and goes,” Fowler said. “Bateman's contract is tradable -- he is due $6.5 million this year and $8.25 million in 2027 -- and other teams have had interest in the past. The Ravens are in contention and might not want to move players, but Bateman is at least a name on my list.”
Lastly, Jauan Jennings came up as an option. The former 49ers receiver signed with the Vikings this offseason but has gotten lost in the offense, logging just two catches so far this season. Minnesota is unbeaten and could be hesitant to move anyone. But if the season begins to go the other way for the Vikings, then Jennings could be on the move around the trade deadline.
Jennings’ contract is relatively cheap with a cap hit of $4.3 million, so that’s not an obstacle in the way of a possible move.
Looking at the options listed by Graziano and Fowler, there are definitely some intriguing ones, but there are a number of variables to consider.
Firstly, the Colts don’t have much draft capital to work with in the trade market. No first-round pick in 2027 makes it difficult to justify trading away a second or third-rounder, and with general manager Chris Ballard likely on the way out of his position, the Colts would be wise to hold onto their 2027 picks for Ballard’s successor.
That said, there is a desire to win this season in Indianapolis, so they could choose to throw caution into the wind and see what happens. Considering the options, I don’t think that’s necessary, but there are players available who could be a fit.
We can rule Thomas out right away as the Jaguars would never trade within the division. Jeudy is a realistic candidate to be moved, but I don’t see him being a needle-mover for the Colts.
I personally would steer well clear of Johnston. While a change of scenery could change the entire trajectory of his career, he’s too volatile an option for the Colts to consider when they need proven and consistent production.
Bateman and Jennings are interesting discussions, and the Colts should absolutely do their due diligence on what it would take to make a trade happen. Neither will lead the way as the clear top choice receiver in the Indianapolis offense, but both bring proven experience and solid role-playing production.
Plus, since both contributed to multiple playoff runs with the Ravens and 49ers respectively, Bateman and Jennings both come from a winning culture, which the Colts may be a valuable intangible and something they need to infuse into an otherwise mediocre roster. Still, without a 1,000-yard season between them, the Colts need to try and buy low. With Bateman, I don't think the Ravens would be willing to move him at a low price. With Jennings, it's possible, but he'd most likely be a rental until the end of the season.
All things considered, I wouldn’t rule out any sort of trade on the Colts side of things. The team is in desperate need of pass-catching help. Of the options that are available as of now, none are true building blocks for the long-term, but there are some possible band-aids available to help Indianapolis get through 2026.

title: Week 6 Power Rankings: National Media Sends Clear Message After Steelers Loss
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts suffered a frustrating 34-22 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday. As a result, the picture is becoming clearer on where Indianapolis stacks up against the rest of the league.
At 2-3, the Colts defense has struggled tremendously at times with tackling, coverage and putting pressure on the quarterback. Offensively, injuries at wide receiver have limited the vertical passing game, and red zone struggles have recently been an issue, too.
As a result, Indianapolis has slid down the list in nearly every publication’s Week 6 power rankings. With numerous issues to point to, here's where some of the biggest names in NFL media have the Colts ranked heading into Week 6.
Sports Illustrated: 24th (Week 5: 17th)
“If there is no Jonathan Taylor, there is no Colts offense,” Sports Illustrated’s Conor Orr wrote of the Colts, who come in at 24th, seven spots down from last week and the largest drop by any of the publications listed.
The Colts couldn’t get Taylor going at all against a physical defensive front which held him to just 3 yards per carry on Sunday. If that’s any indication of what’s to come for this Colts offense, then Shane Steichen is in hot water.
ESPN’s team of beat reporters dropped the Colts down two ranking places after the loss over the weekend, pointing to poor tackling as a symptom of a larger defensive dilemma.
“The Colts have a litany of issues on defense, but tackling is a fundamental problem that affects many areas,” Stephen Holder wrote.
Holder added that the Colts rank 28th in the league in yards allowed after contact (482) and are 31st in yards allowed per play (6.2), placing the majority of blame on “the team’s underwhelming linebackers.”
The Colts did sign Germaine Pratt earlier in the week as they look to revive a struggling linebacker core, continuing the trend of bringing in former Lou Anarumo defenders. But considering how that strategy has worked out thus far, I wouldn’t expect Pratt to move the needle.
Pro Football Talk: 23rd (Week 5: 22nd)
Minimal movement for the Colts in Mike Florio’s Week 6 rankings. Florio again kept his analysis brief, but took a powerful stance in the process.
Florio simply wrote, “It feels like an overhaul is inevitable.” Hard to argue with that assessment. The Colts emphasized the fact that this is a must-win season and the levels of urgency are as high as ever. Yet, the product on the field has underwhelmed.
The Athletic: 25th (Week 5: 19th)
Chad Graff and Josh Kendall have the Colts at 25, a steep slide from their No, 19 spot from a week ago. In their eyes, Indianapolis may have made a mistake this offseason they’re not willing to come to terms with.
“They’d never admit it (at least not yet), but perhaps there’s some buyer’s remorse after giving Daniel Jones a two-year, $88 million contract in March,” they said, adding Jones wasn’t the reason for Sunday’s loss, but also hasn’t contributed much to the team’s only two wins so far.
“And when you’re making more than $40 million a season, the expectation is that you’d better be delivering victories.”
Fox Sports: 20th (Week 5: 18th)
After being the highest publication on the Colts in Week 5, Ralph Vacchiano moved Indianapolis down two places this week, leaving a harrowing outlook for this team if problems aren’t corrected quickly.
“The Colts have too much talent on offense to continually come up so empty,” he said. “Maybe things will start clicking when WR Alec Pierce returns…But head coach Shane Steichen is an offensive guy, and he needs to come up with some answers, because he doesn’t have the defense to prop his team up. If the struggles continue, he’s going to find himself on the hot seat long before he gets to their Week 13 bye.”
In Vacchiano’s eyes, things could get late early for the Colts, and if things do go completely sideways, the bye week could be a week of change for the franchise.
NFL.com: 24th (Week 5: 22nd)
Indianapolis drops two spots in Nick Shook’s latest rankings, who still seems a little bit split on the Colts through five games. Like Vacchiano, he thinks the Colts are capable of more.
“There are moments in which you see Indianapolis’ potential,” he wrote. “But each time I watch these Colts, it leaves me wondering what could be.”
Shook cites putting too much stock into a receiving core he deems as “underwhelming” and has some worries about the offensive line as well.
Bleacher Report: 23rd (Week 5: 23rd)
No change for the Colts in Bleacher Report’s rankings, and the lack of change in the rankings seems to align with the current state of the franchise.
“The Colts are stuck in mediocrity,” analyst Maurice Moton writes. “Nonetheless, the Colts must sort out their defensive issues…The Colts gave up 127 rushing yards to the Steelers, who entered Week 5 with the 22nd-ranked rushing offense.”
Like many who share the same defensive concerns, the thought here is until there’s more consistency on that side of the football, the Colts will remain stuck in a cycle of mediocrity.

title: Colts Turn to Familiar Face Germaine Pratt After Rough Start at LB
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts entered the 2026 season with arguably the weakest linebacker room in football, and through five weeks, they haven't done much to prove otherwise.
After another rough defensive performance against Pittsburgh, Indianapolis is turning to a familiar face for help, signing veteran linebacker Germaine Pratt to the practice squad on Tuesday.
Pratt appeared in 12 games for the Colts last season, starting every one of them and recording 101 tackles, five tackles for loss, eight passes defensed, one interception, one forced fumble and two fumble recoveries.
Those are respectable numbers for a player who joined the team midway through the year, but his return says just as much about the current state of this linebacker room as it does about what he brings to the table.
Indianapolis made a pretty significant gamble this offseason by trading Zaire Franklin to Green Bay and electing to address the position primarily through the draft.
So far, that gamble hasn't paid off.
The Colts rank 28th in total defense, allowing 384.2 yards per game, while surrendering 27.6 points per contest. Tackling has been another major concern, with Indianapolis allowing 482 yards after contact through five games.
The problems certainly extend beyond the linebackers, but this group has been one of the biggest contributors to Indianapolis' defensive struggles.
Second-round pick CJ Allen played just 11 defensive snaps through the first four games before finally seeing 24 against Pittsburgh. Bryce Boettcher has received more opportunities, but his early performances haven't exactly inspired confidence, either.
For a team that desperately needed immediate contributions from its rookie linebackers, the lack of production has been disappointing.
The biggest advantage Pratt brings to Indianapolis is his familiarity with defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo.
The two spent six seasons together in Cincinnati before reuniting in Indianapolis last October, meaning Pratt already understands the defensive system and what Anarumo expects from his linebackers.
That familiarity should make his transition relatively straightforward, assuming the Colts eventually elevate him from the practice squad.
But to think Pratt is suddenly going to turn this struggling linebacker room into a strength is probably asking a little too much.
He was a solid contributor last season, and his experience could be especially valuable for Allen and Boettcher, two young players Indianapolis absolutely needs to develop.
At this point, it doesn't particularly matter where the Colts find help at linebacker. Whether it's Pratt, another veteran addition or the development of their rookies, Indianapolis needs better production from a position group that has been a liability through five weeks.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts' 3 Biggest Disappointments Through Five Weeks of 2026
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts entered 2026 betting heavily on internal growth. Five games in, a few of those bets have already become major concerns.
There is still plenty of season left, but these three have fallen well short of expectations so far.
After what looked like a breakout 2025 season, Laiatu Latu was supposed to take another step toward becoming one of the NFL's premier young edge rushers.
Instead, he has been nearly invisible for long stretches.
Latu finished last season with 8.5 sacks, 45 tackles and three interceptions across 16 starts. Through five games this year, he has just one sack and 14 total pressures, while earning a 58.8 pass-rush grade from PFF.
That grade ranks 72nd among 106 qualified edge defenders.
Indianapolis desperately needs more from Latu because this pass rush has been the worst in football.
The Colts own a 23.7% pressure rate through five weeks, according to Next Gen Stats, making them the only defense in the NFL below 30%. Latu is playing plenty of snaps, and he is supposed to be the guy leading the charge in turning this pass rush around.
Simply put, Indianapolis needs him to start wrecking games.
This one is less about how Pierce has played and more about the fact that he simply has not been available.
Indianapolis handed Pierce a four-year, $114 million extension in March after he posted a career-high 1,003 receiving yards in 2025. Shortly after signing, he underwent surgery on the left heel/ankle issue that had bothered him since 2024.
The expectation was that he would be ready for Week 1, and technically, he was.
Pierce caught four passes for 61 yards against Baltimore, then aggravated the heel against Kansas City after one catch for 11 yards. He has been on injured reserve ever since.
The Colts invested heavily in Pierce because his ability to stretch the field is what helps open up this entire offense, particularly for Jonathan Taylor.
Through five weeks, Indianapolis has barely gotten to use it.
The Colts made a pretty significant gamble this offseason when they traded Zaire Franklin to Green Bay and elected to address their linebacker room primarily through the draft.
Through five weeks, that gamble has not paid off.
Second-round pick CJ Allen played just 11 defensive snaps through the first four games before finally seeing 24 against Pittsburgh. Bryce Boettcher has played roughly 80-plus defensive snaps, but his PFF grade sits in the mid-40s.
That lack of immediate impact is hard to ignore considering how badly this defense needed help at linebacker.
Third-round safety A.J. Haulcy has played considerably more, but his start has been rough, particularly in coverage. Still, there have been some flashes of the player Indianapolis believed it was drafting.
There is still plenty of time for this rookie class to turn things around, but the early returns have been anything but encouraging.
And for a general manager in Chris Ballard who entered this season desperately needing results, this rookie group has not given him much help yet.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Rookie Class Rankings After Week 5: Colts Need More from First-Year Players
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts needed an impactful draft class to help elevate their roster ahead of a 2026 season with plenty riding on it. But so far, the returns have been minimal.
In Justin Melo of Sports Illustrated’s recent rankings of all the NFL rookie classes through five weeks, Indianapolis ranked 29th out of 32 teams, receiving a “D” grade, the result of a change in strategy.
Colts general manager Chris Ballard altered his approach to the draft this time around. Instead of taking elite athletes with promising developmental traits and hoping the coaching staff can polish them out, Ballard went for older, more experienced players instead.
The initial indications from the rookie class were good. There were plenty of flashes in preseason and all eight draft picks made the roster, further reinforcing the belief that these rookies could make an instant impact.
Instead, the results so far have been underwhelming. Let’s take a look at each player selected and work out why things haven’t gone to plan so far.
The Colts drafted CJ Allen 53rd overall with the goal of making him the heart of their defense at MIKE linebacker.
Allen differed from some of Chris Ballard's previous linebacker selections in that he wasn't an elite athlete, instead relying on his instincts and football IQ to make plays. He also arrived in Indianapolis with plenty of experience, having appeared in 38 games during his career at Georgia.
The vision of Allen becoming the man in the middle didn't last long, however. The rookie dealt with multiple injuries during training camp that kept him sidelined for much of the summer. Indianapolis subsequently leaned more heavily on veteran Akeem Davis-Gaither, leaving Allen with a difficult path to playing time.
Through five games, Allen has appeared in just three, logging only 35 total snaps. Melo noted that the Colts haven't trusted Allen to play WILL linebacker, and his limited involvement reflects the challenges he's faced earning a role in the defense.
Allen's situation illustrates one of the concerns surrounding Indianapolis' draft class. The Colts targeted experienced prospects with the expectation that they could contribute immediately, yet they've hardly let their second-round pick see the field. His training camp injuries provide important context, but until he earns a larger role and shows what he can do with it, the Colts will struggle to realize the immediate return they envisioned when they drafted him.
The Colts selected A.J. Haulcy 78th overall in the third round, hoping to add an experienced, physical presence to their secondary who could contribute early in his NFL career.
Haulcy came to Indianapolis after a productive season at LSU, where he earned First-Team All-SEC honors after recording 88 tackles and three interceptions in 2025. His experience across three college programs, combined with his ability to make plays against the run and in coverage, gave the Colts reason to believe he could compete for a significant role immediately.
Unlike Allen, Haulcy hasn't had to wait for an opportunity. The rookie has played in all five games, recording 21 combined tackles and two pass breakups. However, his involvement hasn't consistently translated into the kind of dependable play the Colts need from their secondary.
Melo specifically pointed to Haulcy's struggles in coverage, citing a 37.4 PFF coverage grade through the first four weeks. While the rookie has shown an ability to contribute as a tackler, his early coverage performance has been a concern, particularly for a defense counting on him to handle significant responsibilities in the back end.
The Colts have given their third-round pick an opportunity to establish himself, but the early returns have left plenty of room for improvement. Indianapolis drafted Haulcy with the expectation that his experience would help him adjust quickly to the NFL. If he's going to justify that investment, he must become more reliable in coverage and turn his substantial playing time into more consistent production.
The Colts selected Jalen Farmer 113th overall in the fourth round, hoping to add depth and a potential long-term starter to their interior offensive line. Farmer started 24 games at right guard during his final two seasons at Kentucky, continuing the trend of adding experienced prospects who could eventually compete for a starting role.
However, Farmer has yet to establish himself in the Colts' offensive line rotation. Cracking the starting lineup as a rookie was always a long shot for Farmer, as Indianapolis has one of the best starting offensive lines in football. Through five games, Farmer has played just three offensive snaps, with most of his involvement coming on special teams.
While his limited opportunities make it difficult to evaluate his development, his lack of involvement is another example of a rookie class that has yet to provide the immediate contributions Indianapolis envisioned.
The Colts selected Bryce Boettcher 135th overall in the fourth round, adding another experienced linebacker to a position group they wanted to strengthen. Boettcher arrived from Oregon after recording 136 tackles in his final collegiate season, bringing the production and experience Indianapolis hoped would translate to the NFL.
Unlike fellow rookie CJ Allen, Boettcher has found a way onto the field. He has appeared in all five games, recording 20 tackles while earning a larger role on defense.
Boettcher has at least received opportunities to contribute, but the Colts need more consistency from their fourth-round pick if he's to be a part of the future. With Indianapolis still searching for answers at linebacker, if Boettcher is going to establish himself as a dependable part of the defense, he must maintain consistency for the remainder of the year.
The Colts selected George Gumbs Jr. 156th overall in the fifth round, betting on his athletic traits and long-term potential as a pass rusher. In other words, Gumbs was the most Ballard-esque pick of the class. Gumbs recorded 6.5 tackles for loss and 2.5 sacks in his final season at Florida, but his limited starting experience made him more of a developmental prospect than a ready-made contributor.
Through five games, Gumbs has played just 11 defensive snaps, recording two tackles in his NFL debut against Pittsburgh. His limited role isn't particularly surprising given his draft position and developmental profile, but it reinforces the challenge facing Indianapolis' rookie class. The Colts targeted experienced prospects to help immediately, yet Gumbs remains a long-term project who hasn't contributed much so far.
The Colts selected Caden Curry 214th overall in the sixth round, adding another defensive end with experience at a major college program. Curry finished his Ohio State career with 12.5 sacks, showing the pass-rushing ability that made him an intriguing late-round addition.
Curry made a strong impression during the preseason, but that impact hasn't carried over to the regular season. Through five games, Curry has played just 43 defensive snaps with no sacks, though he has contributed regularly on special teams.
With Arden Key now on injured reserve, Curry has an opportunity to earn a larger role. The Colts need to see whether his preseason flashes can translate into more consistent production when given the chance. If there's something to build on there, Curry could be a piece the Cols chose to build around going forward.
The Colts selected Seth McGowan 237th overall in the seventh round, adding an experienced running back to a backfield led by Jonathan Taylor. McGowan rushed for 725 yards and 12 touchdowns in his final season at Kentucky, giving Indianapolis another option behind its star running back.
Through five games, McGowan has arguably been the most effective rookie in the class. He's recorded 61 rushing yards and 10 receiving yards while contributing on kickoff returns. While his role remains limited, he's found ways to maximize…

title: It Is Becoming Clear Which Big-Money Defender the Jaguars Won't Have vs. the Texans
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- It is becoming clear the Jacksonville Jaguars will be without one of their top defenders on Sunday against the Houston Texans, at least based off this week's injury reports.
The Jaguars had two players miss practice for the second day in a row on Thursday with long snapper Ross Matiscik (shoulder) and cornerback Montaric Brown (hamstring). With Brown missing two days in a row, it is becoming clear that the Jaguars will be down one of their top cornerbacks as they face off against the Texans and their passing game.
With the success the Texans have had in the passing game this season, it will be important for the Jaguars' secondary to be at their very best. That looks, as of now, like it will largely be up to Travis Hunter, Jarrian Jones, and Jourdan Lewis to slow down CJ Stroud and Nico Collins . While Brown has struggled at times this season, his last three games have clearly been impacted by his hamstring injury.
Brown missed the Jaguars' Week 4 battle with the Cincinnati Bengals and played just six snaps last week against the Philadelphia Eagles. When healthy, Brown is one of the Jaguars' best defenders thanks to his coverage ability, run defense, and instincts. The Jaguars have a talented secondary that can still make it work and win games without Brown on the field, but they are better when they have their entire unit at 100%.
“Everybody's kind of pulling the rope in the same direction in terms of improvement, and we see that; I've seen that even here in the few days that we've been out here in London. I think the guys are improving, and they're constantly coaching each other on the same stuff, talking about the same stufff," Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said on Thursday.
"And when those things are applied in the practice, it's starting to show up in the game, and their technique has been helping them. They made a bunch of plays the other day. There's plays out there that we certainly want to make but we're making a whole bunch of them, and we're only going to continue to get better. I firmly believe that. And I think it does give us some flexibility, because we got a bunch of guys that have played pretty well for us out there.”
As for those who were limited on Thursday, the Jaguars once again had Tight end Nate Boerkircher (back), right tackle Cole Van Lanen (knee), rookie guard Emmanuel Pregnon (toe), cornerback Jarrian Jones (elbow), cornerback Jourdan Lewis (hamstring), cornerback Jaylon Jones (hamstring) and safety Eric Murray (concussion) listed as limited.
Pregnon is a significant name to watch as we continue through the week. He has started all five games for the Jaguars at left guard and has been a big part of their running game taking a step forward this season. Considering the Jaguars are already missing left tackle Anton Harrison for next month, Pregnon's status entering Sunday against a strong Texans front is critical.

title: 5 Matchups That Will Decide Jaguars vs. Texans: Travis Hunter's Next Challenge
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- For the Jacksonville Jaguars to get past the Houston Texans in Week 6, it will be all about their ability to win matchups.
Matchups are a big reason the Jaguars are 4-1 and leading the AFC South through the first five weeks of the season, and there are several that will decide the result of Sunday's battle with the Texans.
So, which matchups are the most important ahead of the critical AFC South battle with the Texans? We break it down below.
Nico Collins has had some absolutely massive games against the Jaguars in the last few years, and this year it will be up to Travis Hunter and Jarrian Jones to try to slow down the Texans' No. 1 receiver. Each of the Jaguars' cornerbacks has made some big plays over the last few weeks, and they will need to do so again this week against Collins, especially with Montaric Brown injured.
“Nico was at Michigan when I was at Michigan so I kind of know him pretty well. He's a really a big-bodied guy as a receiver, but some of those guys kind of come in the package where they're a possession guy. That's not him," Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said Thursday. "He can run down the field. He can go make plays on nines and eights down the field. He's a guy, they'll hand reverses to him, he's that good with the ball in his hands. And he'll go in there and do the dirty work. He'll block. He’s to me, in every facet, a well-rounded receiver."
Hunter is not bound to travel with Collins, so it will be a team effort to make sure the Jaguars do not see the Texans star make big plays downfield. Collins is going to get his at some point, but the Jaguars' cornerback duo has to provide some resistance.
This one isn't tough to figure out. The Texans are going to rush four and put the onus on the Jaguars to stop Will Anderon, Danielle Hunter and the rest of their pass-rush group. According to NextGenStats, the Texans have sent four or fewer pass rushers on 78.5% of opponent dropbacks this season, the third-highest rate in the NFL, and have recorded 14 sacks with four or fewer rushers, the most. That means pure one-on-ones for the Jaguars' tackles Walker Little and Cole Van Lanen.
“I think how complete their game is as rushers and as run defenders really stands out on tape," Jaguars offensive coordinator Grant Udinski said Thursday. "There are a lot of really good rushers in the league. Now maybe, I don't know if there are as many rushers as good as those two, but there are other good rushers in the league. But it's hard to find two guys who are A, that good at rushing, but B, also that good in the run game, in the screen game. They do all facets of playing defensive end or that position."
The Jaguars' tackles have been up to the Texans' challenge before, but plenty of people probably remember Hunter and Anderson wrecking the Jaguars' offense during the Week 10 loss a year ago. With Anton Harrison out of the lineup, the focus when it comes to stopping the Texans' pass-rush will come down to none other than Little.
If there is a cornerback the Jaguars are going to want to attack this week, I think it is Kamari Lassiter. Parker Washington does a lot of his damage out of the slot, of course, but I think the Jaguars will look to get Washington lined up on the outside against Lassiter when they need to create a shot play downfield. Lassiter has allowed the third-most receiving yards in the NFL this season with 330 yards allowed through five games and s tied for the second-most receptions allowed at 25. Several of these plays have been on explosive downfield passes, and he is the weak link in the Texans' secondary as of right now.
Washington has proven himself as the Jaguars' No. 1 pass-catcher, and he has made big plays against the Texans in past matchups. This is a week for the Jaguars to look to him to make another game-changing play or two, just like he did last week against the Eagles when he scored two touchdowns to lead the way for the win.
Dalton Schultz will not get thrown a million targets like he does in the games Nico Collins misses, but he is still a big piece of the Texans' passing game. I would call him the Texans' No. 2 pass-catcher right now, tying for the team lead in 31 targets while leading the team with 135 routes. The Jaguars will need to make sure they have a good plan for Schultz considering tight ends have had a bit of success against them this year.
Antonio Johnson has been stellar for the Jaguars as a whole this season, but especially in recent weeks. He is the Jaguars' top secondary piece who can effectively stop Schultz from converting first downs and making tough catches for four quarters, and it will be largely up to him and the linebackers to erase Stroud's safety blanket.
“Yeah, we have put a lot on his plate as time has gone by. That started last year, but AJ basically can play a lot of the SAM positions in base. He can do a lot of those things," Campanile said Wednesday. "He does a lot of what the WILL does in base or nickel. He plays the dime position; he plays safety. So, because of that, it kind of lets us do a lot of the same things out of different groupings and hard to tell what position he's actually playing with some of the disguise that those guys have used on the back end.”
The Texans spent a first-round pick on Georgia Tech offensive lineman Keylan Rutledge this April to make him a key piece of their offensive line rebuild. So far, though, Rutledge has had the expected struggles of a rookie offensive lineman. He has allowed the second-most pressures of any Texans' offensive lineman with 14, and this is a matchup that could favor veteran Jaguars defensive tackle Arik Armstead.
Armstead has put together a good stretch of play over the last few weeks, and this game should be one in which he is able to get consistent pressue if the Texans stop attempting to stick to the running game and have to lean on the passing game. Armstead is the key to the Jaguars' interior pass-rush, and they will need him at his best to make Rutledge look like a rookie Sunday.

title: Jaguars Rookie Rankings Entering Week 6: Texans Battle Brings Pressure on 2026 Draft Class
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' rookie class chipped in to another victory on Sunday against the Philadelphia Eagles, and now it is time to look ahead at how the class is shaping up entering Week 6.
So, what have we seen from the Jaguars' rookies so far after the franchise's 4-1 start? We break it down below in this week's rookie power rankings.
Another week, another healthy scratch for fourth-round rookie Wesley Williams. The Jaguars have had undrafted rookie Bryan Thomas Jr. active over Williams for each of the last four games since BJ Green went down with an injury in Week 1. Williams seems unlikely to play much this season unless the Jaguars run into multiple injuries along the edge.
Sixth-round wide receiver CJ Williams was inactive for the fourth week in a row, trailing only Wesley Williams in healthy scratches amongst the rookie class. The Jaguars have rolled with four full-time receivers in recent weeks, in part because they have had three-to-four tight ends and in part because Travis Hunter is also a receiver option. Williams is unlikely to be active unless there are injuries or some kind of trade in the receiver room.
Albert Regis was a healthy scratch for the Jaguars for the first time in Week 5 against the Eagles, though there is a good chance that was due to the Jaguars having to do some gymnastics for the game day roster in terms of special teams and defensive backs due to injuries. We will see if he is active this week, though it does seem like the Jaguars like what they have gotten from their top-four veteran defensive tackles in front of Regis, too.
While Jalen Huskey was active for the first time this season on Sunday, he did not record a single defensive snap. It remains to be seen if this is going to change or if the Jaguars are going to continue to lean on Rayuan Lane and Kaevon Merriweather as their safety depth, but it certainly seems right now like the latter is more likely. Right now, it seems like a redshirt season for Huskey above all else as a rookie.
Bryan Thomas Jr. was ejected on the first play of the game after a scrap on the kickoff return, but I feel like he would have gotten some run on defense had he played the entire game. Look for him to continue to play a special teams and a backup role moving forward in his rookie season as BJ Green recovers.
Tanner Koziol has not seen a pass get thrown his way, but he has played 16 snaps over the last two weeks after just three snaps in the first three games of the season. That does indicate that his role is increasing a bit considering each of the last two weeks have been close one-score games and not blowouts like when he made his debut in Week 3.
We will have to see if the Jaguars have Nate Boerkircher on the field this weekend against the Texans after he popped up on Wednesday's injury report. He has gotten better and better as a pass-catcher in recent weeks, showing after ability to get tough yards after the catch as well as making a nice catch in traffic in the middle of the field last week. He has been a plus-run blocker, too, though he could always get more consistent there.
Josh Cameron has been one of the most productive rookie receivers in the NFL this season despite not even being close to one of the top rookies in terms of snaps and routes. Cameron has played a limited role in terms of official oppurtunity, but he has also thrived with every single pass that has come his way. Cameron has seen a target on a staggering 30.8% of his routes and he ranks No. 1 on the Jaguars' roster in terms of yards per route on a limited sample size. He is averaging just under eight routes a game, a number that must increase moving forward.
Week 5 was not Emmanuel Pregnon's best game as a Jaguars rookie so far, and I would say that Josh Cameron is inching closer to the No. 1 spot. Pregnon actually held his own more than a few times against the Eagles and was far from the offensive line's biggest issue when it came to missed blocks. The penalties have become a bit of a problem, though, with Pregnon now having five penalties through five games. Only two offensive linemen have more this season. Pregnon is also a bit banged up and was limited during Wednesday's practice. Pregnon has played well by rookie offensive lineman standards if you look at the entire season as a whole, however, and the Jaguars will certainly need him this week against the Texans.

title: 5 Bold Predictions for Jaguars' AFC South Battle vs. Texans: Trevor Lawrence vs. CJ Stroud
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- This is a big week for the Jacksonville Jaguars, and the AFC South at large as a whole.
The Jaguars and Houston Texans will face off in London in Week 6 for the most pivotal game of the AFC South's 2026 season thus far. With a win, the Jaguars would be 5-1 going into their bye week while the Texans would be at 1-5 and would need to go, at absolute worst, 8-4 over the last 12 weeks of the season to even have a chance.
But if the Jaguars lose, they could allow the Texans to climb back into the AFC South race at 2-4. The Jaguars would be two games ahead of them entering Week 7, but the Texans have a very easy next month and could easily catch up to the Jaguars.
In short, there is a lot at stake this week. The Jaguars could put the Texans down , or they could let them back into the fight. So, how do we see things playing out? We break it down with this week's bold predictions.
I think everything about this game indicates it is about to be a pure shootout between Trevor Lawrene and CJ Stroud. Two great run defenses, two teams whose best players right now are their quarterbacks, and two offenses who have learned that they can win games by relying on their No. 1 targets in the passing game. Lawrence and Stroud have both played great football to start 2026, and I think this carries over to Sunday's game.
I do think each quarterback will turn the ball over once, which is something Stroud has barely done this season. The Texans still have a ton of defensive talent, and the Jaguars are one of the best teams in the NFL are creating takeaways. With that in mind, I think this becomes a fireworks show between the two passing games and we see each quarterback have a fair amount of success.
I think it is clear to expect the Texans to run the ball against the Jaguars on Sunday. The Texans' offense ranks No. 23 in EPA/Rush and No. 29 in rushing success rate, along with the fourth-highest stuff rate of any running game. Against a Jaguars defense that has allowed an average of 42.66 rushing yards per game over the last three weeks, and this is one matchup the Jaguars should win.
But what about when the Jaguars have the ball? Can Bhayshul Tuten find success against a strong Texans' defense that has stopped a lot of running games along the way? According to NextGenStats, "the Texans defense has allowed the fourth-lowest explosive run rate (7.6%), third-fewest rushing yards per game (78.4), and second-fewest rush yards over expected (-80) this season ... Bhayshul Tuten ranks fifth among qualified RBs in missed tackles forced rate (57.0%) and eighth in explosive run rate (13.4%)."
The Texans are the toughest test Tuten and the Jaguars have had to face on the ground to date. I expect the Jaguars to significantly outpace the Texans on the ground, even if that doesn't lead to a massive day of production.
Few defenses bring the pressure like the Texans' defense. Their pass-rush changed the game a year ago when the Jaguars lost in Houston in Week 10, and it has now slowed down this year. Will Anderson Jr. leads the NFL in sacks and the Texans are second in sacks as a team, ranking third in sack%, 10th in pressures, and No. 12 in pressure %. Anderson and Danielle Hunter will also be facing a Jaguars team without Anton Harrison, who normally plays his best games against Houston.
As a result, I expect for the Texans' edge room to get after Trevor Lawrence quite a bit. With that in mind, I think the Jaguars will have success against the Texans' interior front of Sheldon Rankins, Tommy Togiai, and Logan Hall. The Texans have an elite edge duo, but their defensive tackles are not as good as other ones the Jaguars have faced over the last month in Zach Allen, Milton Williams, Christian Barmore, Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, Jordan Davis, or Jalen Carter.
The Marvin Harrison Jr. trade certainly created some headlines toward the end of last week, and it isn't hard to see why. Harrison is a former top-5 pick who, at one point, was seen as a potentially generational wide receiver prospect. The Texans plan to play Harrison this week, and the Jaguars and head coach Liam Coen have already said that preparing for Harrison and his skill-set is already underway.
With that said, I just do not see him doing much against the Jaguars. The Jaguars give up a decent amount of yards and catches to outside receivers as a function of their scheme, but Harrison is the same receiver who has struggled to get open all year. I like both Jarrian Jones and Travis Hunter in coverage against Harrison this week, which I think will lead to a small day of production for the Texans' new receiver.
I think this is a week where the matchup is going to favor Jakobi Meyers. It was Brenton Strange two weeks ago and Parker Washington last week, but I believe it is going to go in Meyers' direction this week for a few reasons. For one, the Texans have been one of the best defenses in the NFL against tight ends this season. They also do have a potential hole in the slot, which could mean a big day for Washington, but I think they are going to try to roll coverage to him and give him extra attention.
That brings us to Brian Thomas Jr. and Jakobi Meyers on the outside, where the Texans have struggled. The Texans' pair of outside cornerbacks have allowed 16 combined explosive receptions through five games, while the Texans are the worst team in the entire NFL at defending wide receiver targets based on EPA/Play -- even worse than the Tennessee Titans, Detroit Lions, and Miami Dolphins. With that said, I think Meyers is the one who will benefit more so against that matchup this week.
According to NextGenStats, Thomas has been targeted on 2 of his 17 deep routes this season (11.8%), after being targeted on 27 of his 87 deep routes in 2024 (31.0%). Thomas has been targeted on six deep passes with Stingley in coverage in his career and has not caught any of them with Stingley intercepting one. This likely means Meyers draws the better matchups, and he has the kind of tough skill-set that translates to this kind of matchup. I expect a lot of Meyers this week.

title: Ranking the Jaguars Players Most Likely to be Traded Before the Deadline: Brian Thomas Jr. Leads the Pack
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- With the NFL Trade Deadline still a few weeks away, there is plenty of time for the Jacksonville Jaguars to do some shopping ... or selling.
The Jaguars have made their fair share of trades under James Gladstone, shipping out players like Tyson Campbell, Tank Bigsby, Fred Johnson, and Luke Fortner while trading for players like Jakobi Meyers, Greg Newsome, Daniel Faalele, and Quinn Ewers. As a result, it is natural to think the Jaguars could be active again over the next month.
The first five games of the season just haven't seen much production for Brian Thomas Jr. After the best offseason of his career that highlighted some real chemistry on the practice field between him and Trevor Lawrence, Thomas has caught just nine passes for 105 yards and a touchdown through five games, and the last three games have seen him catch just three passes for 25 yards and see just six targets go his way. In short, he has become a background character in the Jaguars' offense.
This doesn't mean he doesn't provide clear value. His deep-threat ability gives the Jaguars a receiver on the field who demands constant attention from the defense, and the stress his skill-set puts on secondaries is a big reason why Parker Washington, Jakobi Meyers, and Brenton Strange have been so productive over the last two seasons. The Jaguars have shown zero intentions of moving on Thomas for that reason, among several others.
But after Marvin Harrison Jr. was traded for a second-round pick, one has to think the Jaguars would at least be open to listening to any calls that would provide similar, if not better, draft cache. Thomas would be by far the most talented player available at the position during this year's trade cycle, which would also inflate his value. The Jaguars clearly do not want to trade him, and chances are they won't. But if a Jaguar gets traded before the deadline, it feels like it would be him.
I am hesitant to place Arik Armstead here since he has been a big part of the Jaguars' run defense and pass-rush all season long, which has been a critical factor toward the Jaguars sitting alone in first-place of the AFC South. The only reason he is actually on here at all is due to the fact that he has a good bit more trade value than any player on the Jaguars' roster not named Brian Thomas Jr. His contract is fairly tradeable, and he is still producing as a disruptive interior defensive lineman -- that is a player with some real trade value.
While Armstead would likely net the Jaguars a fairly significant pick for a player in his career stage, it is still clear the Jaguars would be a worse team in 2026 without Armstead. The Jaguars are playing to compete for a Super Bowl this season, and there is no reason for them to disrupt that window for the sake of a 2027 draft pick, especially when it comes to a pass-rush that relies on Armstead to provide their biggest source of interior pressure.
If the Jaguars feel as if Ruke Orhorhoro is taking the next step, and if they like Albert Regis' development, then maybe this would make more sense. But even though Armstead would have some clear value on the market, this is a move that I would label unlikely. The Jaguars need Armstead right now, even if he would net them some pretty nice draft ammunition. If the Jaguars were not clearly a top AFC team this would perhaps be a bit different, but this is of course not the case.
The Jaguars' offensive line is clearly hurting after left tackle Anton Harrison was placed on injured reserve this week, but this is one that still makes sense to me. The Jaguars have some offensive line depth to weather the storm with Harrison with Walker Little, Wyatt Milum, Jonah Monheim, and Daniel Faalele able to step in and fill several spots along the line. It would be a plus to have Patrick Mekari when he comes off injured reserve, too, but even with Harrison injured I think Mekari has some trade value.
Even if the Jaguars got compensation close to what they gave up to the New York Giants for Faalele (a sixth-round pick). I think the fact that Mekari is a versatile and experienced offensive linemen would give him some trade value as long as he is healthy, which he still remains to be. But if the Jaguars bring him off injured reserve and onto the active roster sooner rather than later, he could give them a chess piece. This leads to the question of whether the Jaguars would actually look for offensive line help of their own, of course, but it still makes sense to me under the right circumstances.
If the Jaguars keep Mekari on their roster, there is a chance he still might be a healthy scratch with Harrison out -- it would be either him, Faalele, or Milum, and it doesn't seem as if the Jaguars would be better with Mekari on the active game day roster instead of any of those three.

title: Jaguars Injury Report: Updates on Eric Murray, While Rookies Get Dinged Up
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are hoping to get healthier by Sunday.
The Jaguars are facing a number of injury issues before their Week 6 battle with the Houston Texans, and that was even before Wednesday's injury report was released to start the week.
The Jaguars had two players miss Wednesday's practice with long snapper Ross Matiscik (shoulder) and cornerback Montaric Brown (hamstring). The Jaguars signed new long snapper Jacob Bobenmoyer to the practice squad this week to give them a chance to have a full-time option at the position after Matiscik got hurt early in last week's game against the Eagles.
Brown missed Week 4 with a hamstring injury before returning last week against the Eagles. Brown played just six snaps last week , however, before leaving the game, making it clear that he is still not 100%. As things stand today, it would appear the Jaguars are on track to miss Brown when they line up against the Texans on Sunday.
As for those who were limited on Sunday, the Jaguars had Tight end Nate Boerkircher (back), right tackle Cole Van Lanen (knee), rookie guard Emmanuel Pregnon (toe), cornerback Jarrian Jones (elbow), cornerback Jourdan Lewis (hamstring), cornerback Jaylon Jones (hamstring) and safety Eric Murray (concussion).
Jones, Lewis, and Jaylon Jones were all limited last week, so not big updates there. Murray was also limited for most of last week's practices, though he did miss Sunday's game against the Eagles following a sustained concussion in Week 4 against the Cincinnati Bengals. The Jaguars started Rayuan Lane in his place, while former practice squad safety Kaevon Merriweather also got a big boost in playing time.
“Yeah, I think we'll see today and tomorrow, be able to see him run around a little bit, see what that looks like, hopeful. But he hasn't been able to do a ton since last week," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said before practice on Wednesday from the United Kingdom.
"Eric just brings a calming confidence. Obviously, the communication being at a premium, it helps take some stuff off Antonio [S Antonio Johnson] as well, which I thought Antonio really stepped up last week and had one of his best games as a Jaguar in terms of just the playmaking, but also the communication and getting us right back there. It's great to have Eric. He's a competitor, he's physical, he brings a standard to everything that we do in the back end, and obviously he's playing against his former team.”
On top of the Murray injury, the Jaguars also saw two rookies added to the injury report in tight end Nate Boerkircher (back) and offensive lineman Emmanuel Pregnon (toe). Boerkircher and Pregnon have each been critical to the Jaguars' success on the running game and in 12 personnel this season, with Pregnon starting all five games at left guard and Boerkircher serving as a significant addition to the rushing attack.
Against a physical, edge-setting defense like the Texans, the Jaguars need as many maulers as they can get. These are two key players to watch this week.

title: 3 Critical Questions Facing Jaguars Against the Texans in Week 5: Are Walker Little, Cole Van Lanen Ready?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have a big, big week ahead of them.
The Jaguars open their AFC South slate in Week 6 against the Houston Texans , and it gives them a chance to put the Texans four games back entering the bye week. If the Jaguars don't succeed, though, they are opening the door wide open for the Texans to crawl back into the thick of things.
So, what are the most critical questions facing the Jaguars after their latest win? We break it down below.
The players with the biggest challenges on Sunday are clearly Jaguars offensive tackles Walker Little and Cole Van Lanen. The Texans pose one of the NFL's best pass-rush duos with Will Anderson Jr., who had three sacks a week ago, and Danielle Hunter. The question now is whether the Jaguars will be ready for the challenge of the best edge rushers they have played to date.
According to Next GenStats, "Anderson Jr. has recorded 7.5 sacks this season, the most in the NFL, and is the only edge rusher with at least five pressures in every game this season. Anderson has also recorded 12 run stops this season, tied for the second-most among edge rushers. He is the first edge rusher since Lorenzo Alexander in 2016 with at least seven sacks and 10 run stops through Week 5 .Danielle Hunter has been chipped 49 times this season, the most among edge rushers, yet has generated 21 pressures (10th most) with three resulting in turnovers, also the most in the league."
The Texans' pass-rushing duo is the top reason the Jaguars did not sweep the Texans a year ago. Now, the Jaguars will need to prevent them from setting a tone early and disrupting the Jaguars' passing game and offense in general.
While CJ Stroud's pure numbers may not be eye-popping, it is clear that he is playing good football right now. He is doing it despite the Texans once again having a woeful running game. This should be the type of game that the Jaguars' run defense is able to dominate like they have in recent weeks, forcing the game into Stroud's hands. Stroud and Nico Collins are the Texans' two best players on offense so they would likely have done that anyways, but shutting down the Texans against the run is how the Jaguars can build their advantages against the pass with longer down-and-distances.
According to NextGenStats, "The Texans have averaged 3.2 yards per designed run this season, the fewest in the NFL, and have posted a 30.4% success rate on designed runs, the second lowest.
 The Jaguars have allowed 2.9 yards per designed run this season, the fewest in the NFL and the fewest by any team through Week 5 since the 2023 Seahawks (2.7), and have allowed a first down on 15.6% of designed runs, the lowest rate."
In short, the Jaguars don't allow anything on the ground, and the Texans can't run the ball worth a lick. The Texans' running game did run the ball for 130 yards in Week 10 last year, though, which amounted to the second-most rushing yards an Anthony Campanile has allowed and the second-highest EPA/Rush. The Jaguars need to make sure this doesn't repeat.
If there is one single player in the NFL who has terrorized the Jaguars over the years, it is Houston Texans wide receiver Nico Collins. In nine career games against the Jaguars, Collins has caught 51 passes for 734 yards and three touchdowns. But over the last two years is when a bulk of that production has happened, with Collins caught 35 passes for 520 yards (14.85 yards per catch) and two of those touchdowns. That averages out to 8.75 catches and 130 yards per game against the Jaguars over the last two seasons.
So, what do the Jaguars do against the Texans and Collins this time? It seems unlikely the Jaguars will be with Montaric Brown against the Texans, which means Travis Hunter and Jarrian Jones will be the two corners tasked with slowing down Collins. The Jaguars do not really follow their cornerbacks, which means Collins will get reps against each. According to NextGenStats, "Travis Hunter has lined up at field cornerback on 75.2% of his 234 defensive snaps this season, while Jarrian Jones has lined up at boundary cornerback on 65.3% of his snaps."
While it is easy to say "Hunter should follow Collins" on paper, that doesn't mean it is quite as easy to execute. I think the Jaguars will simply ask for Hunter and Jones to play their games and match up to Collins with the best of their ability, just like they have against each top receivers they have played this season.
