title: One Key Decision That Changed Week 5 for Raiders
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' poor Week 5 performance against the New England Patriots showed nearly every area that still needs to improve. The Raiders were in Boston but looked like a team mentally in Las Vegas. Then, they simply were outmatched.
With the number of players the Patriots had out, their blowout win over the Raiders was at least as much mental as it was physical, or anything roster-related. There seemed to be little to take from such an ugly loss early in Klint Kubiak's tenure, after the team started the season 3-1.
On the surface, the Raiders' Week 5 loss is primarily a game Kubiak's coaching staff can use to help clean up a long list of mistakes that have continued over the past two weeks. Overall, the entire team performed so poorly that it should be easy for the coaching staff to get their points across.
Yet the Raiders' loss to the Patriots helped the Raiders move their development plan for No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza along. By getting Mendoza on the field late in the game, it gave Mendoza his first taste of a regular-season game at the professional level, without him having to start a game.
The game was out of the Raiders' reach, removing any pressure from the rookie. Las Vegas has been preparing Mendoza to play since he was drafted. Kubiak noted the confidence the coaching staff has in Mendoza, but also confirmed that Kirk Cousins is still the team's starting quarterback.
"That's why he's here. We have a lot of confidence in him. Kirk's [Cousins] the starter, and if Fernando's [Mendoza] called upon, he'll be ready to go just like he was. I just think as an offense we underperformed. We scored on three of 11 possessions. And it starts with all of us. So, we're all in it together. We all did not get it done," Kubiak said after the game.
Kubiak elaborated on Mendoza's brief performance. Mendoza completed his first five passes in a row against a less aggressive Patriots' defense. Still, it was hard not to notice the differences between Cousins and Mendoza on Sunday.
“He was prepared. He played fast. He got through his progressions quickly. He knew his hot issues. It was a solid start for him. I think with any reps that you get, it's going to make you better. The live game reps are the best medicine, but him just getting time with our starting offensive line in an on the road environment was a very positive experience for him. Although it wasn't for us," Kubiak said.
There are few positives, if any, to take from Las Vegas' loss to the Patriots that outweigh Mendoza's quick stint on the field. The Raiders' Week 5 loss reminded everyone that Las Vegas is just beginning its rebuild, in more ways than one.
Mendoza getting playing time was the biggest reminder of how early they are in their rebuild and added value to a loss that otherwise had little value. It was the best part of the game, as it showed what this Raiders offense could look like right now, even with receivers out.
Despite Sunday's ugly loss to the Patriots, Cousins has approached this week's practices the same way he did previously. The veteran quarterback has already started to put the team's poor Week 5 outing behind him.
“Stay the course. Get back to work. You can't have the poor me’s, and you can't brush it off as no big deal. I think it's somewhere in the middle. You have to find that balance of how you come back to work with it hurts, it matters to you, but at the same time, new week,” Cousins said before practice on Wednesday.
Things will be back to normal on Sunday when the Raiders face the Buffalo Bills at home in Week 6. Yet one can only wonder how much more Mendoza will develop in the background, and at what point his development happens more quickly on Sundays than during the week.
Time will tell, but there is no rush for Mendoza to get on the field. It will happen soon enough.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Ranking Players the Raiders Are Most Likely To Trade
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' productive offseason has left little room for general manager John Spytek and the Raiders' front office to work with ahead of the trade deadline. Las Vegas could use additional roster help, but not at the expense of their future or by deviating from a well-thought-out plan of attack.
Entering the season, it was clear the Raiders' roster still needed help at multiple positions. Their two most recent opponents confirmed the team's most significant remaining weaknesses. Whether or not the Raiders make a move before the deadline will largely depend on their playoff chances.
Their roster weaknesses make it fair to wonder if Las Vegas will make a move. Their front office did such a solid job filling out the roster this offseason that a trade seems unlikely, as they'd likely be unwilling to trade any of their young pieces. It also wouldn't make much sense for them to do so.
“In the NFL, there's always people working on your weaknesses at all times. So, the [New England] Patriots did a great job of exposing ours , and all I'm asking them to do is their jobs, and it's our jobs as coaches to get them prepared and put them in position to play successfully. So, they're young guys, they'll keep playing, and we count on them to play at a high level,” Kubiak said before Wednesday's practice.
Logically, their best, aging players on sizeable contracts are most likely to be traded before the deadline. On the other hand, every player who falls into that category for the Raiders is essential to their chances of winning games on Sundays, making the front office hesitant to move them, too.
The Raiders have no player they could trade who wouldn't significantly lower their chances of winning for the rest of the season, or who they just signed to a sizeable contract this offseason. In theory, trade possibilities are everywhere. In reality, possibilities vary for each team based on many factors.
For Las Vegas, the list of players they'd have to choose from is slim, and trading any of those players would essentially be waving the white flag on the 2026 season. Still, they have options, even if they don't have potential suitors. Below are the players Las Vegas is most likely to trade.
While the trade rumors surrounding Crosby have been silenced, it is fair to believe that trading Crosby for anything less than two first-round draft picks is unlikely. It's also fair to believe that, at the moment, no team in the league is willing to trade those picks for him.
Still, Crosby is the Raiders' single-best player on the roster, with the biggest contract, and could fetch the most in return. It seems unlikely he will be traded right now, and although he is their biggest trade piece, another player on the roster might be bigger.
Miller is the team's third-highest player and would be the second-highest paid if not for Tyler Linderbaum's record-breaking contract. Mathematically, it makes more sense for the Raiders to get through the season with Miller and decide their future with the veteran from there.
That is true both mathematically and on the field; even though he has had a few struggles in his first five games back from an injury that sidelined him for most of last season, he is still by far the best left tackle on the team. The Raiders would be hard-pressed to find a better left tackle right now.
The trade deadline is about a month away. They will play four games between now and then. Three of those games will be against three of the league's best teams. If the Raiders lose all three, they will be either 3-6 or 4-5, depending on their road matchup against the New York Jets.
That gives Las Vegas' front office plenty of time to decide how viable a trade is and how much they want to focus on the rest of this season instead of the future. Neither Crosby nor Miller will be as valuable to another team as they are now, and trading one or both would save a ton of money.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Hondo's Raiders Musings: Inside Vegas' Prep for Potential Upset
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-2) host the Buffalo Bills (4-1) on Sunday at Allegiant Stadium, and while the Bills are looking to keep their season rolling, the Raiders are looking to get back on track.
Each Thursday, I offer you my musings from around the team and take you inside where you can’t go. Let’s dig in.
In my previous seven years covering the Raiders , there have been only two reactions when the team takes its first bad loss of the year. Make no mistake, every team has them, but up to this point there have only been two separate reactions.
Panic, and the other is essentially 'We stink again.'
But since the collapse of the 2025 season, things have been and are different.
This week it is resolve, embarrassment, and a sense of individual failure. For the first time since this team arrived in the desert, the Raiders have suffered their first bad loss (documented thoroughly in my report card), and the only finger-pointing is a big thumb back at themselves.
This team knows they aren’t a Super Bowl team; they also know what they represented on the field last week in New England is far from who they are.
They are on a mission to prove that Sunday.
On Tuesday, I watched every snap of the 2025 Seahawks and noticed that even then the NFL stacked the box against Klint Kubiak’s penchant for running the ball; when defenses showed cover zero, Kubiak used a lot of slants and rub routes to defuse it.
We didn’t see that from the Silver and Black on Sunday, so I asked Kubiak whether the Raiders need to add it quickly once teams see the Patriots' success this past weekend on film.
"Absolutely yeah, just trying to attack what the defense gives you. And when you're getting man coverage, that's always an option, yes."
Kubiak mentioned, when I asked him about getting backups, Caleb Rogers and Bryce Cabledue, some reps after the poor play of his guards on Sunday. He elaborated more on that today and went beyond the offensive line.
"Just promoting competition. And whether it's a corner this week or guys on the offensive line this week, there's always competition, and I think that gets the players to play their best. But just telling someone that he's going to go this week, I don't think that's fair to the Raiders or to the players. So, really want to promote competition, especially offensive line and at corner this week."
Darien Porter played very well on Sunday, and Hezekiah Masses struggled, but don’t forget Jermod McCoy is on this roster, and Kubiak spoke on the youth at that CB spot, and what he is expecting this week, specifically from McCoy.
"He certainly can. We're counting on him. We drafted him for a reason. More specifically, I see DP [Darien Porter] and Zeke [Masses] fighting for who's going to start the game, and we know that everybody's going to play."
Kubiak was asked what he is looking for from the Boise State Bronco in terms of his health this week.
"I think Ashton [Jeanty] is really starting to feel a lot better physically. So, excited about giving him even more reps in practice, more full speed reps. And with Mike [Washington] and with Dylan [Laube], all those guys have to factor in for us." Kubiak made it clear that the young man is part of the game plan this week. "He's playing."
The Rams' game plan against the Bills last week shocked me. Rams DC Chris Shula is an elite DC, and it is a matter of when, not if, he becomes an NFL head coach. But the reality is that everyone is paid big money in this league, and Josh Allen, a top-three QB in the NFL, torched the Rams last week.
Kubiak spoke of facing the young superstar.
"Yeah, very difficult. He's an elite athlete, elite thrower, great instincts to know when to run, and definitely between [James] Cook [III] and their quarterback those are two guys that can really hurt you with their legs."
Kubiak didn’t reveal any secrets because it isn’t a secret. The Bills are a legitimate Super Bowl-caliber team, and how you beat them is obvious, but doing it is the hard part.
"Yeah, well, you've got to get first downs to stay on the field. So, going three and out and punting the ball back is not the way to go. So, you've got to sustain drives. A big part of sustaining drives is not being one-dimensional. So, that's a part of our team that we got to improve."
Kubiak was asked if all the turnovers the Raiders' defense produced perhaps hid some of their shortcomings. He took some of that assessment unbridled.
"I think that you do what you got to do to win the game, man. Your weaknesses come out, and what the numbers say that they are, and we're just trying to go win the game. So, we're trying to improve all of our weaknesses. That's offensive, defense, special teams, and the other side of the ball, they're going to come after what you're good at."
"They're going harp on, 'Hey, this team, they've taken the ball away,' so they're going protect it better. So, we've got to continue to take the ball away and just continue to improve as a team."
Kubiak knows his offense has to run the football to work. He also knows that with teams stacking the box, he can’t afford an atrocious offensive line performance like last week. He explained how to fix it.
"Yeah, many areas, and it's coaching, it's playing, and at the end of the day, you kind of go back to the basics and make sure you're focused on the fundamentals and not trying to get too cute with your schemes. And just giving guys a good plan, they can go execute fast."
The NFL and the NFLPA have a CBA. That CBA limits practice time, so how does Kubiak achieve the in-season competition he craves while balancing the CBA rules that dictate practice? Here is a hint: carefully.
"Yeah, well, job's on the line, that fosters it. There are only so many reps, but that's the NFL, and that's why you have training camp. That's why you have the off season, and we got plenty of reps under our belt. So, yeah, there's not a ton during the week, but there's enough to get ready to play a football game."
Brock Bowers is a top-15 player in this league at any position. He is a unicorn. But the Raiders can’t just sit back and expect him to do all the work; other receivers must stand up and make an impact, per Kubiak.
“Yeah, we need everybody to move the ball. We need everybody. So, Brock [Bowers] is doing a good job, his teammates are doing a good job, and they deserve more opportunities. So, that's on myself and the coaching staff of getting them in position."
I have had Klint described as a “Film Junkie,” a “Film Nerd,” and a man in a personal love affair with “Watching plays a million times.” So I asked the first-year coach, who prefers to show his players what they did, good or bad, on film over talking, if the poor film from last week helps even more.
“Yeah, that's the best tool. You know, the guys are visual. You can only tell them so much. If you show them, it definitely helps get your point across. That's definitely something that I like to do, a lot of coaches on our staff like to do. But you got to make the correction somehow, someway. So, whatever hits the player's brain the fastest you got to use that technique.”
The Raiders sophomore WR Dont’e Thornton Jr. needs to show up and out soon, or he could spend the rest of the season back on the IR. Kubiak bluntly assessed his long road back.
“Yeah, he's got to prove to us he's ready to go play in the NFL game. That his conditioning is there. He didn't have a lot of training camp, guys. He's coming back from a lot of time off, but he's worked really hard and he's put himself in position last week to prove to us this week and maybe next week that he's ready to go.”
Are there any certain benchmarks? “Yeah, just with any player coming back from an injury that's been out for a long time, number one's conditioning, and number two is being assignment sound, and number three is making plays.”
One of the many reasons this team loves Klint Kubiak is that he isn’t afraid to go after himself when he feels like he failed. He mentioned…

title: How Raiders Going Back to Drawing Board Ahead of Bills' Arrival
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are on yet another streak. After starting the season with three consecutive wins against three bad teams, the Raiders have lost two straight games to two of the league's top teams: the Kansas City Chiefs and the New England Patriots.
Las Vegas has been on the road plenty, as Week 5 was their third road game in the last four weeks. They now have two consecutive home games against two of the league's best, starting with the Buffalo Bills this Sunday.
The past two weeks have made it clear where the Raiders stand among the league's best, just as the season's first three weeks confirmed that they're no longer the worst team in the league after finishing last season with the No. 1 overall pick in the draft. Las Vegas is somewhere in the middle.
The next month of the season will clarify where Las Vegas falls between the league's best and worst. In the meantime, Klint Kubiak's Raiders have handled their two losses much like their wins, which is a sign of progress inside the locker room.
The team has had an even temperament through the season's first five games. They now turn their attention to a tough Bills team. Both Buffalo and Las Vegas are coming off recent losses to the Patriots and wins over the Los Angeles Chargers. Still, both teams are at very different points.
Las Vegas is working through the first half of the season with new parts across the board. The team's potential and limitations have shown themselves over five weeks. The next few weeks will test the team's ability to battle through extended adversity, as they face a challenging schedule.
Few teams, other than the Chargers, have a four-game stretch as tough as the one the Raiders are working their way through. Yet Kubiak's first year was always going to be about him and his coaching staff working through the remnants of what was arguably the worst roster in the league last season.
The complete rebuild the Raiders began by hiring Kubiak is going through the expected learning curve of a first-year coaching staff with a revamped, but not fully rebuilt roster . The Raiders showed their progress in the first three weeks and where they still needed to improve in the last two.
The Raiders got back to work on Wednesday as they look to shake off the past two weeks and steal one of their next two games before heading to the East Coast to face the New York Jets. Despite two losses, Las Vegas is in position for a strong season, assuming they get back on track.
That will be easier said than done, but not impossible. A productive week of work, along with some changes to the game plan in all three phases, would go a long way. Yet a realistic understanding of where the roster currently stands would help, even after a productive offseason.
The Raiders' coaching staff must make a few tweaks, as the Bills do many things on both sides of the ball that Las Vegas struggles with. Offensively, the Raiders need to run the ball better and sustain drives more consistently. Defensively, Las Vegas' pass rush must rediscover itself.
The past two weeks have been bad matchups for the Raiders, exposing roster holes and deficiencies that most already knew existed. There really have not been any surprises over the past two weeks, other than how quickly their loss to the Patriots got out of hand.
The Raiders' return to Allegiant Stadium might be just what they need to get back on track. Yet the game's location doesn't change the uphill battles they will face at home over the next two weeks. On paper, the Raiders face a roster on the opposite end of the spectrum.
Kubiak and his coaching staff will have to find the right buttons to press throughout the rest of the week, as the Raiders cannot afford another performance like the one they had against the Patriots.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: NFL Trade Deadline: Update From an Executive on Raiders Rumors
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3–2) are barreling toward a matchup Sunday at Allegiant Stadium against one of the two favorites to represent the AFC in the Super Bowl, the Buffalo Bills (4–1).
Later this year, they will also play the three favorites to represent the NFC. To say that their schedule is difficult would be an enormous understatement.
But looming on the horizon for the rebuilding Raiders is the NFL trade deadline on Nov. 10, 2026, at 4 p.m. ET.
Rumors fly around a gigantic fanbase like the Raiders because Silver & Black fans see their fandom more as a way of life than a simple football game. It is personal.
Good, accurate information must reach fans through reputable sources.
Earlier this year, we spoke of the Raiders and Tyler Linderbaum in December of 2025, the Raiders’ interest in Fernando Mendoza early in September 2025, and Brock Bowers as the main target for the Silver and Black in February of 2023.
Earlier this year, erroneous reports claimed the Raiders made head coaching offers. They were rejected by our reporting, including Jesse Minter (now the Ravens' head coach) and Brian Daboll (now the Tennessee Titans' offensive coordinator), neither of whom received an offer from the Silver & Black.
Even more recent rumors claimed the Raiders had “made an offer” for Tampa Bay Buccaneers DT Vita Vea, and had strong interest in WR Marvin Harrison Jr. and were “in it at the end.”
Again, our reporting rejected all of it long before those situations were settled.
As we enter this rebuild, we told you the Raiders saw it as a three-year process. This is a year of implementation; 2027 will be a get-right season, and the expectation is that the Raiders will reach the playoffs in 2028 (if not sooner) and remain there consistently, as the New England Patriots were when Tom Brady led them.
When the Raiders signed Kirk Cousins, we told you he would be the starter, and as long as he played at a high level and the team was truly in contention, he would remain so.
A long-time highly successful GM let us in on Tuesday what the conventional wisdom is around the NFL, and he named names.
“Everybody knew when they saw the contract Tommy (Tom Delaney, Raiders SVP, Director of Football Administration) put together for Cousins, that he was trade bait, once the season went south. Aidan O’Connell staying on the 53-man proved that.”
In a league starved of QBs, he went on, “Kirk is playing great football. That (Male Cow Excrement) in New England wasn’t his fault at all. If the right team needs a QB, once this season goes south, he has great value.”
The executive believes, and I have confirmed with one other team executive, that once the Raiders make the inevitable move to the rookie No. 1 overall QB selected in the NFL Draft, who had executives calling the best QB prospect in the last four years, Fernando Mendoza, Kirk is instantly on the market.
He went on, “The moment they make that move (to Mendoza), as much as they love Kirk, it would be foolish not to trade him, get value in return, and the Falcons paid him for playing for you for free.”
So what does this executive think of Cousins’ value?
“If you are a team that is all in on 2026, like the Rams and you lose Stafford, or whatever QB an all-in contender has, you could maybe even get a fourth (Round pick in the NFL draft) depending on how many other players, but if it is an all-in team, or a contender and maybe only one is looking, a fifth.”
The issue is not just Cousins, but the executive believes that the Raiders are buyers before the deadline for sure, “Everybody knows that,” but added, “If they are out of the hunt (for the NFL Playoffs) I think they are for sure sellers. Why would you not be? You are rebuilding, and you have some assets that won’t be here long-term, or certainly diminished.”
He then added the caveat again, “But they have to be out of it in their mind.”
The Raiders have been buyers all year. The issue is that they are now led by the master of discipline, John Spytek. They aren’t going to make deals that aren’t singularly focused on the plan and the future. No more Raiders futility chasing pipe dreams and overplaying players for a temporary high who, when the price tag comes due, hinder your team.
The Raiders will always be buyers under Spytek. He is aggressive but does not mistake aggression for stupidity. As one NFL coach told me, “I would have to play poker with that (SOB).”
No matter what happens over the coming weeks, the Raiders will always be willing to upgrade and get better. But it must fit the Spytek narrative and doctrine that now lead this organization.
So what would turn the Raiders into sellers, and what could that possibly look like?
Per the executive, “The Raiders aren’t going to sell short their guys if they are in the hunt. No way, (Klint) Kubiak would go ballistic, and so would Spy (Spytek), and Tom Brady is the single-most competitive human being on earth.”
He elaborated, “But the moment they determine 2026 is done from a standpoint of the playoffs, and make the move to Mendoza, I think every veteran is in play that doesn’t fit the narrative.”
He didn’t want to talk about names, so I called another executive and relayed this opinion to him. He agreed and was quick to name names.
The next executive told me, “The Raiders aren’t shopping Maxx (Crosby), and from what I know he isn’t looking to leave, but that trade deadline people are going to call. He burns for a title; he craves it and maybe a contender could make the offer that would make John (Spytek) say yes, and Maxx as well.”
He continued, “Don’t forget (Adam) Butler. He is playing great, is 32, and has the rest of this year and next on his deal at a terrific price. That was a great deal for the Raiders by John.”
Right there are three names. We talked about a few others, and he thought the interest level would have been from nominal to possible, but none were overly substantial.
The Raiders want to keep their promising young players and veterans who fit the long-term narrative. Still, they’ve already decided that the veterans and young players they have aren’t part of the answer, and NFL teams feel strongly that those players are available now.
But around the NFL, they also think veterans who are absolutely part of the dream right now could hit the market the moment the team’s brain trust thinks the dream of the NFL playoffs in 2026 is dead.
Or as one executive said, “If Cousins loses his job because he stinks (not the case presently) moving to the kid (Fernando Mendoza) is a smart move. But if he is playing well, and they replace him, game on. They have moved on to a 2027 mindset, and the Raiders are smart enough to become sellers to the right buyers.”
The Raiders are buyers; they always will be. But with the Bills this Sunday, the Rams next Sunday, the Jets the following week, and the 49ers in the final game before the deadline, the Raiders will quickly assess the reality of the NFL Playoff dream in 2026.
At worst, they would be 3–6, with a good chance at 4–5, and if they play as they did against the Chiefs, they have a legitimate puncher's chance at 5-4.
No matter what, there is plenty of time before the deadline to learn what they are.
The playoffs are looming, but so is a rookie QB who looks the part. Make a playoff push with a veteran in Cousins? Great. Get your rookie in, trade your veteran for quality compensation, and get his play and mentoring for your rookie, with the Falcons paying the bill? Great.
Either way, the Raiders win, or we get a front-row seat to what may be the most exciting NFL trade deadline around the Silver & Black in years.

title: Three Reasons for Optimism at the Bye for the Dolphins
full_text:
If you look hard enough, you can find positives from the Miami Dolphins amid their bye week, even if their winless record is enough to write off their season completely.
The Dolphins have fought through adversity, including critical injuries and some of the NFL's best opponents, just to get to their bye week. It might be lost on some how young and inexperienced this roster and coaching staff are, but they've still battled against top-tier talent like Kansas City, Minnesota, and Cincinnati.
Now, they get a week off to rest and recover before a trip to New York to take on the Jets. Miami is still searching for its first win, but a few positives could help them get the job done sooner rather than later.
Anyone who had doubts that Aaron Brewer was not worth the three-year, $52.5 million contract extension is running out of reasons to doubt. All in all, Brewer has been near-flawless to start this season and should be considered one of the best centers in football.
Having clocked 292 snaps, he's been responsible for zero sacks against Malik Willis and has  committed only three penalties. Pro Football Focus has given Brewer an overall grade of 68.2 - the eighth-best out of 34 qualified centers.
What makes Brewer truly stand out is his ability to run block, being a key creator of space for Ollie Gordon II and Miami's ensemble of running backs. His PFF run grade is a 76 flat - the third-best in the NFL. His most impressive performance came against Minnesota - no QB hits, sacks, or penalties, and only one pressure on 39 snaps.
Even more surprising than Brewer, however, has been the resurgence of Jonah Savaiinaea. Many fans were ready to give up on him following a disastrous 2025 season, but switching him back to right guard has helped him grow exponentially.
Clean is the name of the game for Savaiinaea - he's committed no penalties and is responsible for no sacks so far this season on 244 snaps. His performance against San Francisco was as close to perfect as you can get - zero pressures and hurries on 59 snaps.
That said, Savaiinaea suffered an ankle injury in Miami's loss to Cincinnati, and the week off might be just what he needs to recover, but even MORE surprisingly, his replacement was just as effective. Jarrett Kingston came in and held his own, including a noteworthy pancake block on Dexter Lawrence II on his second snap.
There are some fans who might not agree with the decision to draft Kadyn Proctor in the first round, but Proctor has done nothing but justify his selection. It hasn't always been perfect, but you can't deny that only three penalties and one sack through 292 snaps isn't fantastic for a rookie playing left guard for the first time since his freshman season at Alabama.
The major rookie sensation, however, has been linebacker Jacob Rodriguez. Through Week Five, he leads the NFL in tackles (57). He's also recorded three tackles for a loss, a pass deflection, and is one of 25 linebackers with an interception. These are first-round numbers being done by someone who was picked 43rd overall, and justify consideration for the Defensive Rookie Of The Year Award.
Chris Johnson might have had a shaky start to the season, but he's ramped up his play since Week Three. When playing in man coverage, he's allowed seven receptions (sixth least in the NFL), 29 receiving yards (third least), and 4.1 yards per catch (second least).
Caleb Douglas was looking like the answer the Dolphins needed at wide receiver following a stellar performance against Las Vegas in Week One, racking up 94 yards on five receptions. Unfortunately, an ankle injury he suffered the following week has sidelined him up to this point, and for Miami's sake, they'll want him back as soon as possible.
Douglas, alongside Chris Bell and Michael Taaffe, has been part of a rookie core that has shown potential for years to come, and the Dolphins still have Kyle Louis and Trey Moore in the stash. All in all, general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan did a solid job finding rookie talent in his first season for the Dolphins, which is raising expectations for Miami in a possible make-or-break 2027 Draft.
It would have been easy to write off Miami's running game following De'Von Achane's ACL injury that he suffered against Kansas City. It admittedly looked shaky the rest of the way against the Chiefs, but they got things under control not long after.
The credit goes to the aforementioned offensive line alongside Ollie Gordon II, who has turned into a reliable starter for the Dolphins with 236 rushing yards and three touchdowns, leading the team in both categories. Since becoming Miami's starter, he's averaged 5 rushing yards per attempt, which is the eighth-most in the NFL.
He's been a drive extender, responsible for nine first downs and seven explosive runs, which are runs that net 10 yards or more. He had a brief scare in the Cincinnati game, going to the blue medical tent midway through the game, but returned not long after.
It hasn't all been perfect, however. Jaylen Wright hasn't been an effective backup, with Willis having to do more with his legs to partially compensate. We'll see if the Dolphins continue to stick with Wright as the second option in the backfield or look somewhere else - they missed their opportunity with Jerome Ford, who had a tryout for Miami but ended up signing with Arizona's practice squad.
At the end of the day, the Dolphins average 126.6 rushing yards per game, the 11th-most in the NFL. It could have been much worse considering the loss of Achane, but Gordon has done more than enough to carry the offense on his back at times.

Coming out of college, Jake joined Lemon City Live, where he was able to cover FIU Athletics, the Florida Panthers, NASCAR @ Homestead-Miami Speedway, and the Miami Dolphins, for which he was the beat writer from 2022 to 2024. Jake also works for the Five Reasons Sports Network and is the host of the Shula Bowl Podcast. title: Dolphins Thursday Mailbag: Proctor, Willis (Again), Slowik, and More
full_text:
Part 2 of the bye week Miami Dolphins On SI mailbag:
Alain, why do you think everyone (fans, local media) are so desperate to have an opinion and to prove “they are right” about this team and Malik and who to draft. As bad as it is, it’s just five weeks over one season, no??
Hey Salvador, you are absolutely right in that it’s only been five weeks, but this is 2026 and everybody (myself included) needs to have a take on every important topic, whether it be Malik Willis, Jeff Hafley, anything.
Would love to ask Hafley what he seen in his time in Green Bay in regards to Willis that he is not seeing now because this can’t be the guy he seen on a daily basis & decided to bring here with him.
Hey Dave, it’s possible that the answer would be that he doesn’t have anywhere near the supporting cast he had in Green Bay and therefore figures he needs to do much, and at times is trying too hard to make something happen instead of just settling for the simple decision.
Greetings Alain! Doubting Willis’ ability to be a starting QB. Couple of grumpy old man questions, but always a fan. Is it the previously fired OC? Is it the previously fired passing coordinator? At least Chargers are 0-5 too. Thoroughly enjoyed Monday's Dolphins Collective & All Dolphins Podcast. But still looking forward to both the rest of the week plus always all written content on SI.Com.
Hey Dave, I don’t know if I’d pin the issues Malik Willis has had so far this season on either Bobby Slowik and/or Kevin Patullo, but I totally get fans being skeptical of two coaches who landed in Miami after they were fired by their previous employer — and not because of a regime change, where it’s more understandable. There will come a time, maybe sooner rather than later, where we will have to take a long, hard look at the Slowik, though, if the passing game continues to be this substandard.
Will Slowik make some changes and adjust the offense, or will there be more lip service going forward? I feel oftentimes teams or coaches will say that, we will evaluate things, and then nothing really changes.
I think what’s needed more than schematic changes right now is more time between Malik Willis and his receivers so they’re on the same page way more than they have been. I also think the return of Caleb Douglas could provide a big boost for the offense. Maybe the Dolphins will lean even more on the running game in the next couple of games, but I don’t foresee major changes yet.
Hey Alain! Reflecting on the first 5 weeks, this is about what I was expecting. It hasn't been good, but also not a complete disaster like first quarter of the 2019 season. I'm optimistic we will see continued growth from this team as the season progresses. What say you?
Absolutely agree with you, and I wrote as much in a column I posted Wednesday. The start has been rough, but you can’t tear down the roster, wind up with as many young and/or unproven players as the Dolphins have, and expect the team to win a lot of games. That’s simply not realistic.
I know it’s only one game but Kingston didn’t seem like a problem. Is it possible that when Jonah comes back that inserting him into the lineup, and removing Jackson puts your five best offensive linemen on the field? Yes, that would involve moving Proctor to the RT position.
Hey Dana, while I agree with you with Kingston looked the part against the Bengals and that Jackson (obviously) has struggled, I have a very hard time believing the Dolphins are going to do anything at all with Kadyn Proctor in 2026 in terms of a position switch. And I tend to agree with them. Let him go through the full season at guard and then have him work at right tackle from the start of the OTAs. Now, having said, I wouldn’t necessarily be shocked by a switch at right tackle, but that one would have the Dolphins taking a look at what Caedan Wallace can do at that position.
Who do you think potentially gets traded during the trade deadline? Obviously many are speculating Sieler and Jackson, but do you think there could be a sleeper trade candidate that we aren't talking about? Thank you.
Hey Steve, I addressed the trade candidates in the Wednesday mailbag, and the names included were Sieler, Jackson, Josh Uche and Greg Dulcich. I have a hard time picturing anybody else being a trade candidate because I don’t know who else would be appealing to another team understanding they’re not moving any of their key young pieces.
Hey Alain, is it fair to say that if Malik Willis was already on the roster and under contract and not personally hand-picked by Sully and Hafley, that he would have gotten benched at least once during the first five games to at least get a look at what they have in QB2 (McCord)? Not saying that Willis should be benched completely and lose his job, but in a season in which we are going through a complete rebuild I don't see the harm in giving the backup quarterback a little work here and there. It actually seems like the right thing to do considering the talent or lack thereof on the roster. I really don't want to hear much about the lack of receiver talent that he's working with, because an open receiver is an open receiver, I don't care whose name is on the back of the receiver's jersey. Willis is just not seeing them for some reason. Maybe another quarterback will be able to identify the receiver who's open faster. Also it's kind of sad to see his body language when he's sitting on the bench sulking, instead of talking with Slowik, his receivers and O-linemen about what's going on or having his head buried in an iPad the way you see the All-Pro quarterbacks in this league like Allen, Burrow, Mahomes, etc,, doing. Thank you and keep up the excellent work.
Hey Toby, thanks for the kind words. I don’t think there would have been a change at quarterback regardless under your hypothetical, though maybe McCord would have gotten snaps at the end of maybe the San Francisco game. I don’t necessarily believe it’s generally a great idea to bench a quarterback unless you’re ready to make a change, and even had he been an incumbent I have a hard time believing that Kyle McCord would do much better. I get the fascination with McCord because he’s an unknown commodity and maybe he’ll become the great steal all fans want, but the reality is this a second-year sixth-round pick who hasn’t taken a snap in an NFL regular season game yet. I’ve seen those guys play before, and almost invariably it’s not pretty.
Hi Alain, longtime listener and reader of your work. My question has to do with Kadyn Proctor and his position. The current administration seems pretty set on keeping him at left guard and not cross training him at right tackle (which seems like a more valuable position than LG). One thing that hasn’t come up is the possibility that the Dolphins don’t want to give Patrick Paul a huge contract extension in two years and are banking on letting him leave and replacing him with Kadyn Proctor at left tackle. Is there precedent for this at Green Bay while Sullivan was there? Did they always pay their successful drafted linemen to long-term contracts or try to draft their replacements? Have you heard the coaches or administration actually say they are interested in playing Proctor at right tackle? Would love to hear your thoughts.
Hey Daniel, let me start with the last thing first, and the answer is I've never heard Sullivan or Hafley ever discuss Proctor as a right tackle specifically, they just went with the flow of the questions and talked about his development in general. Forget about two years, Paul becomes eligible for an extension after this season and don't think his agent won't be calling Sullivan if he has a strong 2026 season. The Packers generally have rewarded their drafted offensive linemen if they perform.
Alain Poupart is the publisher/editor of Miami Dolphins On SI, host of the All Dolphins Podcast, and co-host of the Dolphins Collective. Alain has covered the Miami Dolphins on a full-time basis…

title: Why Jeremiah Smith Would Be the Perfect Pick ... For a Team Other than the Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins appear headed for a very early pick in the 2027 NFL draft and the idea of being able to land Ohio State superstar wide receiver Jeremiah Smith is one that's become very popular among fans as well as mock drafters.
It makes sense considering Smith is pretty universallly recognized as the top prospect in college football at this very early stage of the draft process, and we're talking about a Miami Dolphins team in the early stages of a rebuild that could use help at just about every position.
Going strictly with the BPA (best player available) approach, Smith should be a no-brainer if the Dolphins have the chance to draft him and bring home the Miami Gardens native.
Except it's not that simple.
And we'd suggest the Dolphins would be better off going in another direction.
Through Week 5, the Dolphins hold the third position in the 2027 draft because their combined opponent winning percentage is higher than that of the other two 0-5 teams, the Tennessee Titans and Los Angeles Chargers.
But according to ESPN's Football Power Index (FPI) projections, the Dolphins have a 49 percent chance of ending up with that No. 1 overall pick, easily outdistancing Tennessee at 20 percent and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at 8 percent.
Because the Dolphins need volume, maybe a best-case scenario if they do end up with the first overall pick would be to trade a few spots in the first round with a team desperate to land Smith or whoever emerges as the top quarterback prospect by next spring, pick up additional assets and still land a high-end prospect to help build their foundation.
If they stay put, whether at No. 1, 2 or 3, it says here the Dolphins would be better served by taking either a quarterback (if they decide that Malik Willis is not going to be the long-term solution and the jury still should be out on that even though things aren't off to a great start) or a player at a different position.
Based on today's NFL, it's pretty well acknowledged that the most valuable positions are quarterback, tackle, pass rusher and cornerback falling somewhere behind that.
Outside of quarterback, there might not be a position in football that's as dependent on the other 10 players on the field as wide receiver because no matter how great, a wide receiver needs a quarterback to get him the ball and an offensive line (usually) that gives the quarterback enough time to do that.
A wide receiver also touches the ball at most, say, 15 times a game, limiting his ability to make a game-changing play — though there is something to be said for the attention a player can draw, which opens up other things for the offense.
This doesn't necessarily prove anything, but the stats remain pretty vivid when it comes to wide receivers and making Super Bowl champs.
The previous 10 winners — Kansas City three times, Philadelphia and New England twice, Tampa Bay, the L.A. Rams and most recently Seattle — featured in their starting lineup a total of 13 players who entered the NFL as a top 5 pick.
Only one of them was a wide receiver. And that wide receiver, Sammy Watkins of the Kansas City Chiefs in 2019, wasn't drafted by that team, but rather by the Buffalo Bills five years earlier.
The list also included four quarterbacks (Tom Brady, Carson Wentz, Matthew Stafford, Sam Darnold), one running back (Saquon Barkley), one offensive tackle (Lane Johnson), two edge defenders (Chris Long, Von Miller), one defensive tackle (Ndamukong Suh), one linebacker (Devin White) and two cornerbacks (Jalen Ramsey and Devon Witherspoon).
Only four of those 13 top 5 picks who won the Super Bowl in the past 10 years won with their original team: Wentz, Johnson, White and Witherspoon. One quarterback, one tackle, one linebacker and one cornerback.
And there's this other statistical tidbit, which might not mean anything but then again might.
In the 15 drafts between and 2024, 12 defensive ends/edge defenders were selected among the first five picks. Ten of those players made the playoffs with their original team, an 83 percent hit rate.
During that same time period, eight cornerbacks went in the top 5 and six of them made the playoffs with their original team, a 75 pecent clip. That was the same percentage at QB with 18 out of 24.
For wide receivers, the percentage was 57 percent, with four of seven wide receivers taken in the top 5 making the playoffs with their drafting team. Those who did were A.J. Green, Amari Cooper, Corey Davis and Ja'Marr Chase. Those who didn't were Justin Blackmon, the aforementioned Sammy Watkins and Marvin Harrison Jr.
And now Harrison has been traded in his third season in the NFL, going from the Arizona Cardinals to the Houston Texans for a second-round pick along with a late-round swap.
This was the same Marvin Harrison Jr. who was considered almost a sure-fire star prospect when he came out of Ohio State in 2024. He wasn't viewed quite as favorably as Smith is these days, but his failure with the Cardinals still should serve as a warning that there are few sure things.
This is where we bring up Calvin Johnson, as perfect a wide receiver prospect as there ever was with his 6-5 stature, 4.2-4.3 speed and great route-running ability. Johnson absolutely was as good as advertised on his way to becoming a first-ballot Hall of Fame selection.
The Detroit Lions selected second overall in 2007 and had no reason ever to regret the pick.
The Lions made the playoffs twice in Johnson's nine seasons.
They never won a playoff game with him.
None of that is Johnson's fault because it takes way more than one great wide receiver to succeed.
But it does show that a brilliant wide receiver isn't enough, even with Matthew Stafford as the quarterback.
The Dolphins found that out the hard way the past several years because it's difficult to envision a more impactful than Tyreek Hill, who was the embodiment of an explosive player who opened things up for the entire offense because of the attention he demanded.
And with Hill — not to mention a great sidekick in Jaylen Waddle — the Dolphins won exactly zero playoff games in four years.
And this is where Smith supporters and/or Hill detractors will point out that Hill shrunk in big moments or simply didn't have the size to operate when the game got more physical, and there is merit to that argument.
By all indications, this won't be an issue with Smith, who's not only got the athleticism but also the size.
What Smith doesn't have is the right position.
If the Dolphins suddenly found themselves only a wide receiver away from contention by next spring, we'd be on board with taking him at No. 1, No. 2, whatever.
But they won't be, so we're not.
Jeremiah Smith is a fabulous prospect and more than likely will become a great NFL player. The Dolphins still should look elsewhere to max out their anticipated top pick in the 2027 NFL draft.

In addition to being a credentialed member of the Miami Dolphins press corps, Alain has covered three Super Bowls (for NFL.com, Football News and the Montreal Gazette), the annual NFL draft, the Senior Bowl, and the NFL Scouting Combine. During his almost 40 years in journalism, which began at the now-defunct Miami News, Alain has covered practically every sport at one time or another, from tennis to golf, baseball, basketball and everything in between. The career also included time as a copy editor, including work on several books, such as "Still Perfect," an inside look at the Miami Dolphins' 1972 perfect season. A native of Montreal, Canada, whose first language is French, Alain grew up a huge hockey fan but soon developed a love for all sports, including NFL football. He has lived in South Florida…

title: Why This Disappointing Dolphins Season Actually Isn't That Disappointing in the Big Picture
full_text:
It's been a rough start for the Miami Dolphins in this 2026 season, the 0-5 record bad enough in itself but made worse by the fact the team hasn't had a lead for even one second in 300 minutes of game action.
It's absolutely been rough to watch, but there are two questions that need to be asked, or rather two points that need to be made.
The first one is pretty simple: Is the Dolphins' bad start really start surprising?
The second is more important: Has it changed the overall outlook for the franchise at all?
The Dolphins' struggles basically boil down to not having enough talent on their roster and also having an awful lot of inexperience with some players who do have enough talent.
And a roster full of young players usually means the kind of mistakes that veteran teams don't make, whether it be untimely penalties or missed assignments.
It's not a big secret that the roster would be deficient this season became GM Jon-Eric Sullivan himself discussed the lack of depth more than once in the buildup to the regular season.
Most of it, of course, was a conscious decision by the organization to reset the salary cap heading into 2027 and that meant getting rid of most of the front-line players who could have helped the Dolphins win some games this year.
The Dolphins' roster moves this year all have been about trying to unearth some hidden gems in the form of young players looking to break through or failed former high draft picks looking to revive their career.
With all of the player acquisitions other than QB Malik Willis, though, the common them has been operating on the cheap.
And, as the old saying goes, you get what you pay for.
What the Dolphins are experiencing right now is a lot of growing pains and paying the price for blowing up the roster, and head coach Jeff Hafley said more than once this season was about more than wins and losses — maybe in large part because he, Sullivan and the entire organization knew full well there likely would be way more losses than wins.
The 2026 season, as we wrote in the offseason, was about the progress and development of the young players who hopefully will form the core of a contender sooner rather than later — a group that included Miami's entire rookie draft class as well as recent high picks like Chop Robinson, Kenneth Grant and Jonah Savaiinaea.
It also was about building a foundation, identity — or culture, if you prefer that term. It's about the new Dolphins way, not to be confused with the Green Bay way because Hafley and Sullivan want to put their own stamp on the Dolphins.
And it also was about evaluating Willis to see whether he could become the long-term answer at quarterback.
Looking at those three objectives, there have been enough good performances from young players through the first five games to take some encouragement, the list including Jacob Rodriguez, Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Michael Taaffe, Trey Moore in training camp, with Robinson showing some improvement.
In terms of building an identity or foundation, that's going to be a work in progress and it obviously will be easier once there's some success in the form of a win or two, though there have been positive signs already based on how the Dolphins have competed.
With Willis, the early returns haven't been very impressive, but there never was a guarantee he was going to be the guy and there's also a lot of time left in this 2026 season for him to provide those signs — because the Dolphins aren't about to pull the plug on his audition anytime soon. Let's also understand that Willis' performance should improve the more time he spends with his teammates on offense, though he does need to stand out on his own merits.
The bottom line is we stand right now about where we were at the start of the regular season, except with five losses, some good performances from some rookies, not nearly as good a start from Willis as hoped, but in the big picture pretty much in the same place.
So, yeah, the 0-5 start does kind of stink a little bit. But this season always was going to be a starting point as the early part of a rebuilding project.
And all things considered, things aren't so terrible because they're not entirely unexpected. And that, like or not, is a better place to be than constantly underachieving.
Alain Poupart is the publisher/editor of Miami Dolphins On SI, host of the All Dolphins Podcast, and co-host of the Dolphins Collective. Alain has covered the Miami Dolphins on a full-time basis since 1989 for various publications and media outlets, including Dolphin Digest, The Associated Press and the Dolphins team website. In addition to being a credentialed member of the Miami Dolphins press corps, Alain has covered three Super Bowls (for NFL.com, Football News and the Montreal Gazette), the annual NFL draft, the Senior Bowl, and the NFL Scouting Combine. During his almost 40 years in journalism, which began at the now-defunct Miami News, Alain has covered practically every sport at one time or another, from tennis to golf, baseball, basketball and everything in between. The career also included time as a copy editor, including work on several books, such as "Still Perfect," an inside look at the Miami Dolphins' 1972 perfect season. A native of Montreal, Canada, whose first language is French, Alain grew up a huge hockey fan but soon developed a love for all sports, including NFL football. He has lived in South Florida since the 1980s.

title: Dolphins Week 6 Power Rankings Roundup: Race for No. 1 Pick Starting to Form
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins remained winless with their loss against the Cincinnati Bengals, a game that wasn't as close as the 31-24 final score might have suggested, and they now stand as one of three teams with an 0-5 record.
If we're not already there, it won't be long before we start focusing on the 2027 NFL draft and more specifically exactly how high the Dolphins' first-round pick will end up being.
Based on the latest round of national media power rankings, they'll have stiff competition for the No. 1 overall pick from the Tennessee Titans.
The Dolphins came in at 31st in the Week 6 power rankings among our 10 national outlets — Yahoo Sports, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, The Athletic, NFL.com, USA Today, Pro Football Talk, FOX Sports, The Sporting News, CBS Sports — with an average ranking of 31.2 compared to 31.5 for the AFC South team.
For a second consecutive week, the Dolphins did get a ranking as high as 29th, that coming from Nick Shook of NFL.com.
Before we get to our weekly rundown of the Dolphins placement in the rankings with the accompanying commentary, we'll again examine the other winless teams and that race for the No. 1 overall pick.
The Dolphins and Titans were joined at 0-5 this past weekend by the Los Angeles Chargers after their loss against the Denver Broncos.
While the Dolphins have a bye this weekend, the Chargers will face the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium and the Titans will face the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium.
Of the three teams at 0-5, the Chargers obviously are the big surprise considering they went into the season after back-to-back 11-win seasons, while Tennessee won three games each of the previous two seasons.
The Chargers look highly dysfunctional on offense in their first year with Mike McDaniel as their coordinator and now they're dealing with a rash of injuries that had them starting four rookies plus former Dolphins guard Cole Strange against Denver.
Working against the Chargers also is a brutal schedule. After their game at Kansas City, the Chargers will return from their bye to face the Rams, Texans (who probably are on their way to a rebound) and Baltimore, with games against the 49ers, Chiefs and Broncos over the last month.
Tennessee's bigger problem is the team just doesn't look much better than either of the previous two seasons, even if the Titans' schedule is a lot more manageable than that of either the Chargers or Dolphins. After Indy, Tennessee has a home game against Cleveland, followed by a road game against Cincinnati.
The Sporting News (Vinnie Iyer)
Analysis: The Dolphins cannot blame their continued skid on the absence of running back De'Von Achane. Another backfield star has been born, helped by Malik Willis, as Ollie Gordon II has turned 27 carries for 188 yards and 2 TDs the past two games. Gordon will help them finish an upset soon after one-possession losses to the Vikings and Bengals.
Analysis: They stay in their spot as they lost to the Bengals. The question is will they win a game.
Analysis: They're terrible and will remain that way for the duration of this season. But give them credit for fighting for first-year coach Jeff Hafley, which (unexpectedly) gets them out of the power rankings basement.
FOX Sports (Ralph Vacchiano)
Analysis: The Dolphins head into their bye week 0-5, which is exactly what everyone expected. Head coach Jeff Hafley’s defense has been OK, but they’re one of the worst offenses in the league and there isn’t a quarterback anywhere playing as poorly as Malik Willis. Bright sides? There are a few. RB Ollie Gordon has 188 yards and two TDs in two starts since they lost De’Von Achane. And on Sunday, they scored a season-high 24 points and out-gained the explosive Bengals 331 yards to 307. Want another one? When they come out of the bye, they get the Jets twice in a month span, which might be their only two chances for wins this season.
Analysis: First, the good: RB Ollie Gordon II has legitimate juice. The young playmakers out wide (plus TE Greg Dulcich) are fun to watch. LB Jacob Rodriguez is a stud who should be a front-runner for Defensive Rookie of the Year. Now, the bad: QB Malik Willis learned a hard lesson about not playing outside of his limits. Miami’s defensive weaknesses were still evident when Joe Burrow hit big plays and led steady scoring marches. The Dolphins are still winless. But for another week, they competed and didn’t make a ton of mistakes that would suggest a team headed into the abyss. That first win will come eventually.
The Athletic (Chad Graff and Josh Kendall)
Analysis: Hey, at least they fight! That’s more than can be said about the only team behind them in the rankings. The Dolphins don’t have much talent, but one week after keeping it close against the undefeated Vikings, they at least hung around with Cincinnati.
Analysis (on the biggest issue on defense, rushing the passer): It took the Dolphins until the first snap of their fourth game of the season to record their first sack; they have the NFL's second-worst sack rate. Their issues pressuring opposing quarterbacks has compounded into easy completions -- Miami ranks last in both opposing QBR and completion percentage. Going into the season, the Dolphins were thin at pass rusher behind Chop Robinson, but the 2024 first-round pick also started slow. With one of the NFL's youngest secondaries, Miami will continue to struggle against the pass until it can impact opposing QBs more consistently. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques
Pro Football Talk (Mike Florio)
Analysis: 32. Maybe Jon-Eric Sullivan and Jeff Hafley should have waited a year.
Sports Illustrated (Conor Orr)
Analysis: This week’s installment of Jacob Rodriguez corner: He’s leading the league in tackles but he just wants a W. How do you not love this guy?
Yahoo Sports (Frank Schwab)
Analysis: The good news for the Dolphins is they won't lose in Week 6. They have a bye. Good for the Dolphins to lose by only seven points against the Bengals on Sunday, but the true story of the game was a 28-10 deficit after three quarters. The Dolphins have trailed by at least 14 points in four of five games. There are two main goals after the bye: getting one win to avoid the 0-17 questions, and finding out if Malik Willis can be the quarterback of the future. A decision in the 2027 NFL Draft looms. Willis was 1-for-7 passing for 22 yards with a minute to go in the first half Sunday. He threw two interceptions and lost a fumble. It wasn't good enough, and garbage-time stats don't fix that. Of 32 qualified quarterbacks he's 30th in adjusted EPA (expected points added) per play and 29th in success rate. It is hard to judge Willis fairly because there's not much talent around him, but he has to prove he can elevate his teammates.

title: What to Know About New Dolphins WR Jared Wayne and the Latest Wave of Tryout Players
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are in their bye week, but the quest to upgrade their roster never takes a break.
Miami made a swap of wide receivers on their 53-man roster Tuesday when they waived Ryan Miller and claimed Jared Wayne off waivers from the Houston Texans. They also made some moves on the practice squad, signing defensive lineman Jordan Jefferson and releasing former Dallas Cowboys first-round pick Mazi Smith.
Additionally, the team continued its series of tryouts with 10 more players, including Jefferson.
It's been a long time coming for Wayne after he went undrafted in 2023. He made his NFL debut in 2024 but had appeared in only four games before playing in all five games for Houston this season, producing 65 yards on four receptions.
Wayne was waived by the Texans after they acquired Marvin Harrison Jr. from the Arizona Cardinals in a trade Sunday.
At this point, any additions are welcome. The Dolphins currently average 153.6 passing yards per game, the lowest in the NFL. Part of this issue can come from the inconsistency at the wide receiver position. Aside from Malik Washington, who has been reliable enough, the door is wide open for Wayne to become another option for Malik Willis to throw to.
Caleb Douglas showed exciting upside when he's healthy, but he missed the past three games because of an ankle injury. Chris Bell, meanwhile, was almost a non-factor in Miami's loss to Cincinnati , which could partially be his own doing thanks to some struggles creating separation.
Coming out of Pittsburgh, there was upside ahead of the 2023 Draft for Wayne, according to his draft profile. The frame is there at 6-3, 210 pounds. More than anything, though, Wayne is a strong receiver who can battle through contested catches. In addition, something that Miami might want to consider is his ability to serve as an efficient run blocker, which is a welcome attribute in an offense that can live and die on the run.
With that said, the route-running, speed, and acceleration have left a lot to be desired in his skill set, according to his draft profile and his inability to create separation could be reminiscent of Bell's struggles.
The Dolphins have held tryouts for a mix of veterans seeking another chance to get on the field and college graduates looking for an opportunity after being waived during final roster cuts August 30. Still, any chance at improvement is welcome when you're 0-5.
As mentioned at the top, Jefferson joins the Dolphins' practice squad following stops at four different teams: Jacksonville (2024 fourth-round pick), San Francisco, Cincinnati, and the Los Angeles Chargers. He's been waived by every single team he's played for, having only 12 tackles and a sack in his NFL career so far.
One name that stands out is running back Jerome Ford, who is currently in his fifth year in the NFL. He was prominent in 2023 and 2024 with Cleveland, taking over for an injured Nick Chubb before falling to the third-string role in 2025, partly due to a shoulder injury.
Defensive back Cobee Bryant could have potential based on his college resume alone. With Kansas, he showcased impressive longevity, earning three First-Team All-Big 12 Awards. He signed with Atlanta in 2025 after going undrafted, but hasn't had the opportunity to blossom in the league, recording 10 tackles and a pass deflection for the Falcons in 2025.
Tryouts are absolutely no guarantee that a player will be signed. They can simply be a shot for an unproven player to showcase their talent to an NFL coaching staff, and quarterback Jacob Clark did just that. He spent most of his college career at Missouri State, leading the Bears to their first bowl game in their first year in FBS as members of Conference USA in 2025.
Similarly, center Jaren Kump won't be vying for snaps at the position with the Dolphins anytime soon, but he did showcase flexibility at Utah by being a multi-year starter at all five positions in the trenches. He was part of a phenomenal O-line for the Utes, which also featured Cleveland's 2026 first-round pick, Spencer Fano.
Miami Hurricanes fans might recall linebacker Jahfari Harvey, who was a member of the Canes from 2019 to 2023 before transferring to SMU in 2024. He went undrafted and signed with Las Vegas in 2025 before being waived and re-signed to either the practice squad or the active roster three times in that year alone. He showcased solid pursuit and doubled as a pass rusher in college, but he hasn't had the opportunity to make the most of his versatility in the NFL just yet.
Unlike some players on this list, cornerback Dwight McGlothern didn't have trouble finding the field, appearing in 15 games for Minnesota since signing in 2024. However, he only managed a single pass deflection in 2024, and there are no listed stats for 2025. He was remarked as a ball-hawk coming out of college at Arkansas, specializing in zone coverage but being weak against the run.
Linebacker Jeremiah Moon signed with Baltimore as an undrafted free agent in 2022 before being waived, then signing with both Pittsburgh and Carolina not once, but twice from 2024 to 2026. All in all, he's appeared in 25 games and has recorded 31 tackles and two forced fumbles. Strength is his specialty in the NFL, as it was in college at Florida, but if he were to find a home with Miami, it might be for punt coverage, as it was something he was known to do with the Gators.
Likewise, tight end Messiah Swinson's list of NFL teams since 2024 is a bit convoluted, but the bottom line is that he hasn't had an opportunity to record playing time with Green Bay, Carolina, San Francisco, Arizona, or Cleveland. He was a solid target in the red zone at Arizona State, but of all the players on this list, he might have the least chance of landing a spot on Miami, almost solely due to a lack of film and a lack of need at the position.
Offensive tackle Da'Metrius Weatherspoon was a recent release from New England's practice squad. This followed a stellar season for Syracuse in 2025, mainly served as a right tackle but did start one game at left guard. He only allowed four sacks and committed three penalties in 817 snaps, and was the highest-rated player on the Orange's offense, with a 76.5 rating, according to Pro Football Focus.

title: Dolphins Week 5 Report Card: Running Game Delivers, but Mistakes Keep Miami Winless
full_text:
There’s the cliché that numbers never lie, but don’t put too much stock in the final score of this one.
The Miami Dolphins may have lost against the Cincinnati Bengals 31-24, but an impending mistake always felt around the corner.
Cincinnati led 28-10 entering the fourth quarter before Miami’s late touchdowns made things look more competitive.
As the score shows, the Dolphins found ways to produce while rushing for 217 yards and outgaining Cincinnati 331-307 and finishing with more first downs, but three turnovers and another special teams breakdown helped turn any advantages into a loss at Hard Rock Stadium.
Here’s how each position group graded out as Miami fell to 0-5.
After giving Malik Willis some time to adjust to leading a new, inexperienced team, the past couple of weeks have made it clear that pointing to the problems around him can’t explain away his own glaring flaws.
Willis completed 15 of 27 passes for 137 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions, finishing with a 51.0 passer rating. He also fumbled twice, losing one with the Dolphins trailing by 10 late in the fourth quarter.
His first interception came on a tipped pass, when Boye Mafe batted a pass intended for Kevin Coleman Jr., and Jordan Battle came down with the deflection, but the second was a much more avoidable mistake, with Willis throwing back across his body while scrambling and finding Battle again.
And that’s where the feeling of an impending mistake was proven to be correct. Miami had just recovered a Cincinnati fumble near its own goal line, but three offensive plays later, the Bengals had the ball back and were on their way to a 21-7 lead.
The third-quarter goal-line possession was another costly example. After Gordon was stopped for a loss from the 1, Willis took an 8-yard sack on second-and-goal from the 3, a mistake he took responsibility for after the game. Miami eventually settled for a field goal.
He did throw a touchdown, however, rolling to his right and finding Kevin Coleman Jr. in the back of the end zone for a 3-yard score in the fourth quarter, the rookie’s first NFL touchdown.
His legs are still a weapon, as he rushed for 74 yards and a touchdown, including a 39-yard scamper on third-and-13 that helped launch Miami’s first fourth-quarter touchdown drive.
Losing De’Von Achane would have sounded like one of Miami’s biggest potential crises, but Ollie Gordon II looks right at home in an offense that wants to load up on blockers and run through people.
A week after rushing for 100 yards against Minnesota, Gordon followed it up with 88 yards and a touchdown on 18 carries. The Oklahoma State product ranks sixth in rushing yards across Weeks 4 and 5, with 188, through Sunday night.
His 22-yard run on third-and-10 helped keep Miami’s opening possession alive, and he eventually finished that drive with a 1-yard touchdown. He also put together runs of 7, 10 and 13 yards during the third-quarter drive that reached Cincinnati’s 1-yard line.
After Miami got just 2.8 yards per attempt out of the sixth-round pick during his rookie campaign in 2025, Gordon II has thrived off being able to find a rhythm without the one-dimensional predictability that came with being a 6-foot-2, 225-pound back used only in short-yardage situations.
Jaylen Wright continued to struggle, managing 11 yards on six carries. Three of those attempts came while Gordon II briefly was sidelined with an injury early in the fourth quarter.
Malik Washington continues to be Miami’s most reliable receiving option, catching six of eight targets for 43 yards. He also continued to mix in snaps out of the backfield, adding an 18-yard run.
But he averaged just over 7 yards per reception Sunday, and his skill set is better suited to being a reliable, complementary slot option than carrying a team’s entire aerial attack.
Coleman offered more this week, catching three passes for 30 yards, including a 3-yard touchdown and a 23-yard reception that set up Willis’ late rushing score. That said, with Coleman offering a similar but less developed skill set to Washington’s, Miami is yearning for a true No. 1 outside receiver who can put pressure on defenses at every level.
Jalen Tolbert added a 22-yard catch. Chris Bell didn’t record a reception, but his 26-yard reverse helped get Miami into scoring position in the third quarter. His fourth-quarter false start also helped create the third-and-13 that Willis had to escape.
Greg Dulcich caught four of five targets for 37 yards and added the two-point conversion after Coleman’s touchdown.
His 13-yard reception converted fourth-and-1 near the end of the first half, although Miami ran out of time before turning that possession into points. He also moved the chains on third-and-5 during the final touchdown drive.
Will Kacmarek caught just one pass for 5 yards, but on Bell’s 26-yard run, he led the way up the right side of the field before laying a solid block on Bengals cornerback DJ Turner II to help Bell pick up a first down.
Miami averaged 6.4 yards on 34 rushing attempts, with Gordon, Willis, Washington and Bell all producing runs of at least 18 yards.
Willis’ scrambling helped that average, but Gordon’s 88 yards also showed consistency in the ground game.
Unlike last week, no gain was wiped out by a holding penalty.
The protection still had costly breakdowns, however, as Cincinnati finished with three sacks for 23 yards, including Jonathan Allen’s late strip-sack.
That said, Willis’ 8-yard loss near the goal line shows how a quarterback’s decision to keep a play alive can make the protection look worse.
The unit had to adjust after right guard Jonah Savaiinaea left with an ankle injury in the second quarter, with Jarrett Kingston replacing him.
A week after finally collecting their first four sacks of the season, the Dolphins finished with none while also allowing 117 rushing yards
Chop Robinson hit Joe Burrow twice, but Cincinnati’s star quarterback still threw four touchdown passes without an interception.
The Bengals’ rushing total was more a product of volume than efficiency, as Cincinnati ran the ball 31 times for an average of just 3.8 yards per carry. But the bigger problem was how often the Bengals kept possessions alive while converting nine of 13 third downs.
Robinson seemed to come through on a desperately needed fourth-quarter sack with Miami trailing 28-18, only to erase it himself with an offside penalty. Cincinnati received a first down and kept draining the clock. Zach Sieler later turned third-and-7 into third-and-2 with an encroachment penalty, although the defense eventually forced a punt.
Josh Uche did help preserve Miami’s second-quarter takeaway, recovering the ball after Robinson fumbled during his return.
Rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez finished with a team-high 11 tackles, but Mike Gesicki beat him on a double move, selling an inside break just long enough to freeze Rodriguez before catching a red-zone touchdown.
With 11:51 left in the second quarter, he gave up another touchdown after allowing Samaje Perine to cut inside of him on an angle route.
Burrow’s third touchdown pass went to Tanner Hudson with Willie Gay Jr. in coverage.
Cincinnati converted seven of eight third downs in the first half, and its first three touchdowns went to two tight ends and a running back.
The secondary made some of Miami’s most important defensive plays.
Chris Johnson forced Chase Brown’s second-quarter fumble near the goal line, and rookie Michael Taaffe also forced a fumble earlier in that possession, but Miami’s recovery was reversed after the referees determined that Gay Jr. was out of bounds after picking up the ball.
Taaffe left with a chest injury before returning, while JuJu Brents dealt with injuries and eventually was ruled out with a stinger.
Jason Marshall Jr. surrendered the game’s biggest passing play, Chase’s 45-yard touchdown late in the third quarter. The second-year cornerback was close enough to contest the catch, but jumped a step early,…

title: Good NFL News for Johnson As He Continues to Deliver for the Dolphins
full_text:
Things have been moving in the right direction for Miami Dolphins rookie Chris Johnson since a rough start to the season.
His performance keeps getting better every week to the point he's as effective as any rookie on the roster — yes, even on a par with the much more heralded Jacob Rodriguez.
And there's been good news on the field as well for Johnson, who successfully appealed his NFL fine resulting from a tackle against Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty.
In addition to getting back the $17,911 he had been fined for a hip-drop tackle — and remember that there was no flag on the play — Johnson also saw disappear one of his three strikes for that particular violation.
As part of a new rule in 2026, repeat offenders in one of three categories now can be suspended for a game with three violations, and hip-drop tackles is one of them — the other two are blindside blocks and hits on a defenseless player.
So now Johnson has his fine money back and he's again got a clean slate with the league.
On the field, Johnson has come a long way since that opener against the Raiders when he was victimized for a couple of touchdown passes.
His performance in Week 5 against the Cincinnati Bengals might have been his best yet, and it went beyond the forced fumble he produced with a perfectly executed "Peanut punch" in the second half.
While we understand that Pro Football Focus' grades shouldn't be viewed as the ultimate gauge, their game-by-game grades for Johnson have indicated the steady and consistent progress everybody who has watched Dolphins games can plainly see.
PFF gave Johnson an 86.9 overall grade for Week 5, his third consecutive game with at least a 69 mark after he was under 50 for the first two games against the Raiders and San Francisco 49ers.
"I thought Chris had a solid game," Hafley said of Johnson's work against Cincinnati. "There's a couple plays where, just like any of us, I'm sure that he wants back, but I see the confidence overall just growing with him. I mean, you can see it when he's playing out there. Early in the season, when he had some moments where guys caught balls on him, I kind of didn't feel like the response was where we needed it to be. I don't feel that anymore. I thought this was a big test for him with the wide receivers they had as a rookie and overall, I'd say he answered it pretty well and regardless of the outcome of certain plays, I love the confidence and the energy that he's playing with."
What always needs to be mentioned when discussing Johnson  is the fact he continues to split time between the slot and outside, a difficult assignment for any cornerback, let alone a rookie.
Whether inside or outside, what's been consistent about Johnson has been his tackling ability, which would have to be considered high end for a cornerback.
Because he hasn't gotten an interception just yet and because of the bend-but-don't-break style of defense the Dolphins have employed, where they're willing to give up underneath completions to protect against the deep ball, Johnson has flown under the radar a lot more than Rodriguez, who keeps racking up the tackles, but the Dolphins have reason to be as excited right now about Johnson's future potential as that of Rodriguez, with the two making up a good start for a foundation on defense.
