title: Patriots Make Massive Roster Decision on WR A.J. Brown This Week
full_text:
FOXBORO — The New England Patriots just came off a 45-17 thumping of the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 5, where they had three different pass catchers find the end zone. They're now just one step closer to adding another elite weapon to their offense.
Wide receiver A.J. Brown will be out at practice Wednesday as the team prepares to take on the New York Jets in Week 6, head coach Mike Vrabel confirmed. This move begins his 21-day window to be activated off of injured reserve. Brown was placed on IR following the team's 13-10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks in the season opener after suffering a high-ankle sprain.
"A.J. will be out there to practice," Vrabel told reporters ahead of practice. "(We'll) see how that goes."
Brown , the Patriots' top offseason acquisition this year, caught just three passes in his season debut for 26 yards before departing off the field and into the blue medical tent.
He's missed the last four games, but has been spotted a lot more often in the Patriots locker room — often wearing cleats with a slight wrap on his right ankle. He was in a chipper mood last week, chatting with Drake Maye and reporters at his locker.
On Monday, Vrabel didn't shut the door of a possible return for Brown, saying there is a chance that he could be active on the practice field. Today, he doesn't know how much he'll impact the offense out of the gate, but looks forward to getting him up and moving.
"He hasn't been out there, so I can't tell you until we actually see it," Vrabel said. "He's been out for four weeks, so we'll get him back out there practicing and see if he's ready to go in a couple days. And if not, then 21-day window and we'll go from there."
Last week, the Patriots had just four wide receivers active against the Raiders (Kyle Williams, Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism III). This came after Mack Hollins, who injured his calf against Buffalo in Week 4, was placed on IR. The team declined to elevate Kyle Dixon, Cameron Dorner or Chandler Brayboy from the practice squad.
"Those receivers, they, they don't care who catches the ball," Vrabel said Sunday. "They don't care who catches a touchdown. They're just as excited for the next guy if it was them, and I think that that's truly what we wanna build around here, you know? And I gotta get it to be the entire team. I gotta get the entire team to look at it like that."
Once Brown returns to game action, he'll easily be the Patriots' top option in the passing game. His downfield abilities, along with the chemistry that he began to form with Drake Maye during the summer months , can help elevate this Patriots offense that's now starting to find its groove.
After Brown went down in Week 1, the Patriots' offense drastically changed for the worse. Maye, operating efficiently, threw three interceptions in the fourth quarter. While it's been more than a month away, there's no doubt in anyone's mind that adding Brown back into this huddle will help.
"Obviously, a great player. A.J., any time the presence in the huddle and the presence that he carries out there," Maye said after the Seahawks game.
The Patriots don't need to officially activate Brown off of IR this week , but because he's set to return to practice, he'll have three weeks to be added to the active roster. If the Patriots decide not to add him to the 53-man roster, he'll revert back to IR and his season will be over.
There is currently one open spot on the 53-man roster. The Patriots also decided to start offensive tackle Marcus Bryant's 21-day window this week.

title: Most Important Patriots Postgame Quotes From Week 5 — And What They Mean Going Forward
full_text:
FOXBORO — Now sitting at 3-2, the New England Patriots have a sense of confidence around them that they might not have had a few weeks prior. A big win over the Las Vegas Raiders , where the offense put up a season-high 45 points, helped propel them onto a winning streak.
But the team enjoyed the victory for so long before their mindset shifted.
"Last week doesn't matter," Mike Vrabel said after the game. "We're gonna have to focus on the Jets in the division here at home. We still have a lot to improve and to clean up."
Here are some of the biggest quotes following the win, and what they mean for the direction of the Patriots heading into a divisional battle against the New York Jets.
It felt like the Patriots offense could do no wrong. They had their way with the Raiders defense, and Maye — who had struggled really up until Week 4 — looked like a changed man. He threw four touchdowns, ran for another and led the Patriots to their second-straight win. It was a victory that really felt like a more confident group.
Mike Vrabel on where the team has improved: "There's just a lot of things that we have to do to improve, and we have to come back. Again, the players, the effort in which they play with and being able to get stops in the red zone and finish off drives and not let penalties affect us, like, those are all positives. Those are things that crumbled us early in the year, especially offensively, and so we were able to overcome that. But eventually, you're not gonna be able to overcome some of the mistakes that we made and some of the penalties."
Drake Maye on how gratifying it was to score points on nearly every drive: "I'm just proud of these guys for stepping up. I mean, offense, defense, overall as a football team, that's a – I think we talk about identity with Coach Vrabel. I mean, that's a Coach Vrabel football team of stepping up, being ready to take advantage of your opportunity, and he always says when somebody gets their opportunity, he's excited to watch them play, and I think guys are living that."
Efton Chism III on the offense finding a rhythm: "We got so much belief in Drake and that he's one of the best quarterbacks in the league. We just got to continue to prepare each and every day lie that and, you know, not take Monday to Saturday for granted."
Gabe Jacas on his comfort level in the defensive scheme: "I'm 100% comfortable. I just play football. You know, it's a fun thing when you just out there playing free. You got 10 of the guys just willing to play for you and play behind you, and it's a good feeling."
Kindle Vildor on preparing to be signed from the practice squad all week: "I feel like I was able to prepare. Pretty much knew Wednesday when we got in, I knew that I'd be playing. So it was a typical game week for me, just able to watch the film and break it down on my own."
Robert Spillane on Drake Maye on the sideline: "It's fun to see Drake smiling big on the sidelines. That confidence is obviously back, so to be able to watch him lead and move the ball down the field was fun."
Last week's win was something that the Patriots can look back on and use as a defining step in a winning streak. Sure, Vrabel's comments about not going back in the past is true — but with a winnable game against the New York Jets coming up at home next Sunday, the Patriots can start to get this ball rolling.
Really, what kicked it all off was getting Maye to look like his usual self . In the first part of the year, he didn't have the same swagger that he did in 2025. Now that his teammates are commenting about how they've seen his confidence come back, the Patriots can start to ride the performances of their quarterback.
But there was plenty to clean up. Their 12 penalties racked up 116 total yards and they struggled to contain Brock Bowers for most of the game. All things considered, the 28-point win was far from perfect.
Getting some of the players that the Patriots expect to be big contributors rolling, like Jacas and A.J. Brown — who is eligible to be taken off of IR this week — will be major boosts to a team that starts to look like a real playoff contender after a shaky start.

title: Saints Injury Report: Chris Olave Misses Second Straight Practice Before Giants
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints continue to deal with several significant injury concerns ahead of Sunday's Week 6 matchup against the New York Giants , with wide receiver Chris Olave , linebacker Kaden Elliss and defensive tackle Nathan Shepherd among several players who missed practice Thursday.
The Saints did receive some encouraging news, as edge rusher Tyree Wilson and defensive tackle Colby Wooden returned to full participation after being limited Wednesday.
With New Orleans looking to rebound from a disappointing 1-4 start, the availability of several key contributors could play a significant role against the Giants.
Perhaps the most concerning development for New Orleans is the continued absence of Olave, who missed practice for the second consecutive day because of an illness.
New Orleans is coming off a frustrating 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings in which its Tyler Shough and the passing attack failed to generate 100 yards and Shough also threw two interceptions. Losing its best receiver, who is second in the league in receiving yards with 537, creates another challenge for second-year coach Kellen Moore and his offensive staff.
Alvin Kamara 's status also warrants attention after the veteran running back was limited for the second consecutive practice with a back injury.
New Orleans' front seven faces depth concerns as Elliss (calf) and Anfernee Jennings (knee) missed practice for a second straight day, joining sidelined defensive tackle Shepherd (illness) and limited lineman Vernon Broughton (illness). However, Wooden (toe) and Wilson (ankle) returned to full participation Thursday. Those developments provide some encouragement for a defense needing its front seven operating near full strength.
While the Saints have their share of injury problems, the Giants are dealing with several notable absences of their own.
New York had five players miss practice for the second consecutive day, including offensive tackles Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor , both of whom are dealing with injuries.
Thomas is listed with a groin injury, while Eluemunor is battling a calf issue.
Their availability could have major implications for Sunday's matchup, particularly against a solid edge rusher rotation of New Orleans’ Carl Granderson , Chase Young and Cameron Jordan .
New York also remained without linebacker Abdul Carter , who missed his second consecutive practice with a calf injury.
However, the Giants received encouraging news regarding wide receiver Darnell Mooney and safety Jason Pinnock , both of whom improved from limited to full participation Thursday.

title: Gayle Benson Breaks Silence as Saints' 1-4 Start Puts Leadership Under Fire
full_text:
New Orleans Saints owner Gayle Benson declared the team's 1-4 start to the season was “not acceptable" on Monday, issuing a stern warning to leadership and staff as frustration mounts across the franchise and fan base.
Speaking at the Greater New Orleans Quarterback Club following Sunday's 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings , Benson emphasized that accountability extends across the entire organization.
"That is not acceptable to me, and it falls short of what our fans deserve," Benson said. "I hear the frustration directed toward our team and our organization. It is not lost on me."
Benson emphasized that accountability begins with her but extends throughout the organization, specifically identifying General Manager Mickey Loomis , second-year head coach Kellen Moore , the coaching staff, and the players.
"I will not make excuses, and I will not accept this level of performance as our standard," Benson said. "I am committed to making the decisions necessary to improve this team."
While Benson did not say anything straightforward on whether organizational changes were imminent, her comments came nearly two years after she overruled Loomis and fired former coach Dennis Allen following a seven-game losing streak.
In what should have been a year of continued improvement from last season’s second-half success, along with an emerging quarterback in Tyler Shough , this year should have been full of great vibes. Instead, the Saints have been putrid throughout the first five games of the franchise's 60th anniversary season, which has featured several celebrations overshadowed by disappointing performances.
New Orleans suffered an embarrassing 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons during the 20th anniversary celebration of the historic 2006 "Domecoming" game. Six days later, the Saints lost to Minnesota during a ceremony honoring Drew Brees ' Pro Football Hall of Fame induction and his addition to the team's Ring of Honor.
At the end of both games, supporters of the Falcons and Vikings overtook the lower bowl of the stadium as “ATL” chants were heard throughout last Monday night, and “Skol” chants were also heard, but the latter were more audible because there were many Minnesota fans in attendance.
Benson referenced Brees' legacy while emphasizing the importance of restoring the standards that helped New Orleans win Super Bowl XLIV.
"It also includes a standard of preparation, discipline and accountability," Benson said. "The best way to honor that legacy is to uphold those standards today."
She also outlined the responsibilities of the organization's leadership:
"Kellen Moore and his coaches are responsible for preparing our players to perform. Mickey Loomis and our football staff are responsible for building a roster capable of sustained success. Our players are responsible for their preparation and execution. I am responsible for holding this organization accountable."
Despite her strong remarks, Benson acknowledged that public statements alone would not restore confidence in a franchise that has not reached the playoffs since 2020.
"Words will not restore our fans' confidence," Benson said. "Our performance must do that."
The Saints will attempt to end their losing streak Sunday against the New York Giants before traveling to Paris to face the Pittsburgh Steelers .
Benson concluded by reiterating her commitment to the franchise's supporters.
"We cannot change the results of our first five games. We are responsible for what we do next. I expect better. Our fans deserve better. And I am determined to see that we deliver it."

title: Social Media Rips Saints After Loss to Vikings, Lack of Homefield Advantage
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints' frustrating start to the 2026 season continued Sunday with a 23-13 loss to the undefeated Minnesota Vikings , dropping New Orleans to 1-4 and intensifying criticism surrounding second-year head coach Kellen Moore.
What was supposed to be a memorable afternoon celebrating Drew Brees' induction into the Saints Ring of Honor instead became another disappointing chapter in a season rapidly slipping away.
The Saints managed just 142 yards of total offense, while quarterback Tyler Shough struggled against Minnesota's relentless defensive pressure. Even an 87-yard fumble return touchdown by rookie safety Jonas Sanker wasn't enough to prevent New Orleans from suffering its fourth loss in five games.
The defeat also highlighted the Saints' deteriorating home-field advantage, with Vikings fans making their presence felt inside the Caesars Superdome.
As frustration continues to grow, three major talking points have emerged surrounding Moore's coaching, the defense's performance and the team's inability to protect its home field.
Of everyone facing criticism amid the New Orleans Saints' disappointing start, second-year head coach Kellen Moore has arguably received the most.
While Moore faced scrutiny throughout his first season, many fans remained patient, understanding that the franchise was undergoing a rebuild. However, that patience has steadily worn thin, particularly following the Saints' embarrassing loss to the Atlanta Falcons on the 20th anniversary of Domecoming .
The criticism reached a new level following Sunday's loss to Minnesota, marking New Orleans' third consecutive defeat, all coming inside the Caesars Superdome.
Much of the frustration centered on Moore's offensive play calling and his inability to make adjustments against Minnesota's relentless blitz packages.
Offensive sequences don't get much worse than this: MIN 46 1-10: Kendre Miller run (-1) MIN 47 2-11: Holding, Donaldson (-10) NO 43 2-21: False start (-5) NO 38 2-26: INT, Shough, plus, holding Kamara (-10, declined)
Even Saints legend Drew Brees questioned the predictability of Moore's offense during Fox's broadcast, further fueling criticism of the struggling head coach.
Drew Brees has been disgusted with Kellen Moore's play-calling all game. He's just dropping hints without bashing his franchise too hard.
The only reason Brees doesn’t really cut loose on this organization is because he doesn’t want to hurt Loomis or Gayle. But what he just said about our offense is probably the most blunt he can be without trying to offend them.
With New Orleans managing just 142 total yards, including 96 passing, questions continue to mount about Moore's offensive philosophy, game planning and ability to turn the franchise around.
What began as patience during a rebuilding process has increasingly turned into frustration, with fans questioning whether Moore is the right coach to lead the Saints into the future.
Someone threw out a great stat on my show last week.  Not a positive one but… The @Saints have a lower winning percentage post @drewbrees than before him arriving in New Orleans.  That includes the teams first 20 years of ineptness.  Last 5+ years, some lousy football. Not good
In Kellen Moore's 22 games with the #Saints : - 7-15, 3-8 at home. - Have never scored more than 7 in the 1st quarter. - 1 first-quarter lead. - 4 first-half leads. - Fewest 1st quarter points scored (35) - Most 1st quarter 3-and-outs (29) - Third-worst turnover margin (-10)
While the offense received much of the blame, the defense also drew scrutiny after allowing Minnesota to produce its most productive offensive performance of the season.
The Vikings finished with 364 total yards, including 153 rushing, while quarterback Kyler Murray threw for 229 yards and rushed for another 54.
Aaron Jones rushed for 113 yards and a touchdown, while Justin Jefferson added six receptions for 79 yards and a touchdown. He became the third player to rush for over 100 yards or more after Detroit's Jahmyr Gibbs and Atlanta's Bijan Robinson
This isn't the only bad performance as New Orleans allowed Atlanta to have over 420 yards, including 205 on the ground.
While they haven't allowed as many gaudy passing yards (because their opponents are having success running the ball), the Saints secondary isn't any better.
Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry has been a major liability in the Saints' secondary through five games, earning a dismal 55.6 overall Pro Football Focus (PFF) grade and an even worse 51.7 coverage grade. Opposing quarterbacks have completed 60.7% of their passes when targeting him, resulting in 255 yards and a touchdown, while McKinstry has yet to record an interception.
That has earned him the nickame "Sugar Water McKinstry" from ESPN 104.5 radio host Matt Moscona.
LMAO Matt Moscona called Kool-Aid McKinstry “Sugar Water McKinstry” 😭😭 ultimate slander name pic.twitter.com/H2r78MvHk4
Despite forcing two turnovers, including Sanker's fumble return touchdown, the Saints struggled to get Minnesota off the field in critical situations.
That scoop and score was the perfect embodiment of being a Saints fan since Brees has retired. The second you get excited and rejuvenated, they turn right around and kill your vibes.
The performance raised further questions about a defense that has struggled with consistency throughout the early season.
While the Saints’ defense surrendered season-high numbers to a weak Minnesota offense , Sunday's loss highlighted a bigger issue off the field: the Caesars Superdome has lost its elite home-field advantage.
Historically one of the NFL's toughest environments, the venue no longer intimidates visitors. New Orleans has dropped three of four home games this season and sits at 15-21 at home since coach Sean Payton left after 2021, with only one winning home season (5-3 in 2023). The collapse is even sharper recently, with 14 losses in their last 17 home games since 2024.
Compounding the loss, traveling Vikings fans filled the stands with loud "Skol" chants.
Fan frustration continues to grow alongside the home struggles, proving that restoring the Dome's advantage requires winning games, not just past reputation. Until Moore's team delivers, visiting crowds will remain right at home.
It’s bad pic.twitter.com/rrwsCU7nPV
For perspective on how many Vikings fans were in the Superdome today. There was a Saints third down late in the game that you might’ve thought this was a road game. Tough to put into words just how far down the sentiment around this season has fallen in the span of three weeks. pic.twitter.com/Ne8pCQBUDa
In a span of 7 days, you can hear audible ATL chants and SKOL chants. What this franchise has done to our Superdome since Brees retired should be punishable by crime.

title: Drew Brees Questions Kellen Moore's Offense as Saints' Struggles Continue Against Vikings
full_text:
During the second half of the New Orleans Saints' 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings , franchise legend Drew Brees openly criticized head coach Kellen Moore 's offensive approach on a nationwide broadcast.
Working as a Fox analyst shortly after being inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor at halftime, Brees pointed to New Orleans' inability to adjust against Minnesota's relentless blitzing defense .
Specifically, Brees called the Saints' first-down play calling "pretty predictable," questioned the lack of play-action passes, and criticized setup choices that left running back Alvin Kamara in unfavorable matchups.
"You gotta have answers," Brees said, highlighting the team's ongoing struggles in front of a national audience.
Quarterback Tyler Shough suffered through the toughest game of his fledgling career as the Saints (1-4) were held to a paltry 142 total yards—their lowest output since Week 2 of 2021.
Preliminary charting from Pro Football Focus showed Minnesota bringing blitz pressure on 23 of Shough's 27 dropbacks. The second-year passer managed only 16 completions on 25 attempts for 96 yards, throwing two interceptions and posting a career-worst 38.1 passer rating.
Head coach Kellen Moore admitted the team's offensive strategy was ineffective against the Vikings' aggressive scheme.
"I felt like we had a plan (against the blitz)," Moore stated. "Obviously the plan wasn't good enough. They did a better job."
"Obviously, that's on me."
The offensive struggles stemmed from an inability to sustain early momentum and adapt late. New Orleans opened with a promising 15-play, 66-yard scoring drive capped by a 1-yard Kendre Miller touchdown run, but the rushing attack completely stalled afterward. Over their next six drives, the Saints generated a mere 10 yards on the ground as penalties and negative plays continually forced them into obvious passing downs.
A reluctance to adjust the play calling aggravated these issues down the stretch. According to FTN Fantasy, New Orleans entered the contest utilizing play action on just 17.7% of offensive snaps—the fourth-lowest rate in the NFL. Against Minnesota, they called only one play-action pass, which gained 14 yards to Chris Olave .
Special teams miscues and missed chances further doomed the Saints. Jayden Price lost a fumble on the second-half opening kickoff, while Daniel Carlson missed a point-after attempt following an 87-yard fumble return touchdown by Jonas Sanker .
The defense's takeaway went unrewarded, while Minnesota (5-0) anticipated the Saints' aerial concepts, as demonstrated by Byron Murphy intercepting Shough on a late double move intended for Olave.
"They were really prepared for those moments," Shough remarked.
With a 1-4 record through five games, Moore faces mounting criticism during a difficult start to his second year, as New Orleans struggles with preparation, execution, and identity.
"Sometimes, you go through storms," Moore acknowledged. "Inevitably, storms end. But we're going through a little bit of one."

title: Saints vs. Vikings: The Good, Bad and Ugly From New Orleans' 23-13 Loss
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints' struggles continued Sunday as they fell 23-13 to the Minnesota Vikings inside the Caesars Superdome.
The defeat dropped New Orleans to 1-4 for the second consecutive season, further exposing the growing problems facing second-year head coach Kellen Moore and a team that continues to take steps backward .
Here is the Good, Bad and Ugly from the Saints' 23-13 loss to the Vikings.
In one of the few bright spots in the loss to the Vikings, Saints 2nd year safety Jonas Sanker provided a game-changing spark by returning a fumble 88 yards for a touchdown to tie the game at 13-13 late in the second quarter.
Sanker's touchdown demonstrated that New Orleans still has young players capable of making an impact despite a disappointing 1-4 start, though Daniel Carlson subsequently missed the go-ahead extra point.
Fumble 🗣️ Jonas Sanker recovers and takes it to the end zone to tie it up! @MINvsNO on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/W52Ypr6gtT
The second-year defensive back has been tasked with helping rebuild a Saints defense that has undergone significant turnover, delivering an impressive defensive scoring play against Minnesota's undefeated squad.
Ultimately, the Saints' offense failed to capitalize on the momentum, leaving the defense with little margin for error as New Orleans dropped its fourth game of the season.
Shough has been the Saints’ best player throughout the season as he, along with a few others, is the bright spot on what is a bad football team at the moment and if it weren’t for him this season would be a complete disaster.
However, his performance was not good enough for New Orleans to win this game.
Shough had his worst game of the season, completing 16 of his 25 passes for only 96 yards and two interceptions. A lot of his struggles could be placed on the Vikings’ defense and their blitz packages, which present a lot of looks that could deceive a quarterback and his offensive line.
"It was obviously very difficult," Shough said of going up against Minnesota’s defense. "They presented a lot of looks. That's what they're extremely good at. I felt like we were ready for all those looks. We just didn't execute in some of those moments, and now we're second and 20, or third and 15, and — I mean, you're not — those odds are not really in your favor for those situations.
"And we got to be in those third-and-six, third-and-five, third-and-three ranges, where we can convert and dictate tempo. We had a couple good drives and moments, but I don't care who we're playing, we got to be better there. And especially against that team, they're really well coached, really played really well."
While the Saints’ defense allowed a putrid Minnesota offense to put up its best numbers of the season, the most concerning aspect of Sunday's defeat occurred off the field.
The game served as a stark reminder that the Caesars Superdome no longer offers the formidable environment it was once famous for.
Historically, New Orleans boasted one of the premier home-field advantages in the NFL, where deafening crowd noise and an unyielding Saints team made life miserable for visiting opponents.
That distinct edge appears to have vanished.
The Saints have lost all of their four home games this year (including preseason), extending a troubling pattern that began after former head coach Sean Payton left the team following the 2021 campaign.
Since Payton's departure, New Orleans has posted a sub-.500 record of 15-21 at home, managing just a single winning season in the Superdome (5-3 in 2023).
The situation has grown even more dire recently, as the Saints have dropped 14 of their last 17 home contests since the start of 2024.
Yet, the venue's atmosphere on Sunday was perhaps just as unsettling as the loss itself.
A massive contingent of traveling Vikings supporters made their presence felt, filling the Superdome with loud, distinct "Skol" chants.
For perspective on how many Vikings fans were in the Superdome today. There was a Saints third down late in the game that you might’ve thought this was a road game. Tough to put into words just how far down the sentiment around this season has fallen in the span of three weeks. pic.twitter.com/Ne8pCQBUDa
For an organization that built its reputation on creating a hostile environment for opponents, watching opposing fans dominate sections of the stadium underscored the team's ongoing decline.
Understandably, persistent losing eventually takes a toll on crowd enthusiasm and game-day attendance.
With little evidence of progress on the field, fan frustration continues to mount alongside the team's home struggles.
Reestablishing a true home-field advantage will require more than past glory or fan loyalty.
It must be reclaimed by winning football games.
Until Moore and the Saints deliver better results in front of their home crowd, visiting teams and their fans will continue to feel right at home in New Orleans.

The Saints’ offense was abysmal, as it was outgained 364 to 182 yards while Minnesota picked up 18 first downs compared to the Saints’ nine. Tyler Shough had his worst game of the season, completing 16 of his 25 passes for only 96 yards and two interceptions.

title: Saints Must Accomplish 3 Things to End Minnesota's Perfect Start
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (1-3) enter Sunday's Week 5 matchup against the unbeaten Minnesota Vikings (4-0) looking to bounce back from a humbling 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night.
However, getting back on track won't be easy against a Minnesota team that has relied on one of the NFL's most dominant defenses to overcome its offensive struggles.
Sunday's matchup will also be a special occasion for the franchise as legendary quarterback Drew Brees will be inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor, adding even more significance to a game in which New Orleans desperately needs a victory.
For the Saints, the challenge will be giving their former quarterback and the home crowd something to celebrate while avoiding a third consecutive loss at the Caesars Superdome.
Doing so will require significant improvements on both sides of the ball, particularly against a Vikings defense that has consistently overwhelmed opposing offenses.
Here are three keys to victory for the Saints as they look to hand Minnesota its first loss of the season.
The Saints’ matchup against the Vikings will hinge on whether New Orleans can handle Minnesota’s league-leading blitz and pressure package. Minnesota enters Week 5 with arguably the NFL's best defense through four games, allowing a league-low 12.8 points per game while racking up 16 sacks, four interceptions and a plus-five turnover differential, the second-best mark in the league.
That is a major concern for a Saints offense that has struggled with consistency, protection, and turnovers. New Orleans has surrendered 12 sacks through four games, turned the ball over too often and enters Sunday with a minus-five turnover differential. Against a defense that thrives on disguising coverages, generating pressure from different alignments and forcing difficult decisions, the Saints cannot afford to fall behind early or repeatedly find themselves in obvious passing situations.
The biggest individual matchup is quarterback Tyler Shough against Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores ’ blitz-heavy system. Shough has already been sacked a dozen times this, with nine coming against the blitz, and New Orleans will need clear answers built into the game plan to avoid exposing him to the same issues again.
There are reasons for optimism. When Shough has gotten the ball out against blitzing defenses, he has been productive, posting a 105.1 passer rating while completing 71.9% of his passes and throwing for 442 yards, four touchdowns and one interception. But Minnesota has been uniquely effective at creating negative plays, and the Vikings’ No. 2 pressure rate will make life difficult if the Saints cannot keep the pocket clean.
Containing opposing top receivers has plagued the Saints through four games, making Sunday’s matchup against Vikings superstar Justin Jefferson a severe challenge.
Despite Minnesota ranking last in passing and 31st in total offense, Jefferson’s elite route-running, explosiveness, and contested-catch ability threaten New Orleans’ vulnerable secondary.
These defensive struggles were evident in Week 3 when Raiders tight end Brock Bowers posted 10 catches, 119 yards, and a touchdown from Kirk Cousins in Las Vegas' 31-28 win.
They continued Monday against Atlanta, as Drake London caught five passes for 96 yards, including a 37-yarder over Kool-Aid McKinstry , despite the Falcons leaning on the run.
New Orleans' secondary has struggled with missed tackles, blown coverages, penalties, and big plays.
Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. averaged 11.2 yards per attempt, going 15-for-20 for 223 yards and a touchdown.
Cornerbacks Quincy Riley (58 yards, TD allowed; 28.0 PFF grade) and McKinstry (60 yards allowed, two penalties; 29.5 PFF grade) were especially exploited.
These defensive flaws create major concerns facing Jefferson.
Unlike Bowers' versatile tight end mismatches or London's size, Jefferson combines route precision, speed, and versatility across alignments.
Leaving McKinstry or Riley isolated on Jefferson could prove disastrous for defensive coordinator Brandon Staley .
New Orleans must disguise coverages and offer safety help to force Kyler Murray elsewhere.
However, over-committing to Jefferson risks leaving tight end T.J. Hockenson (13 catches, 119 yards last week vs. Miami ) open underneath against an injured Saints linebacker corps.
Ultimately, New Orleans must force Minnesota into long, sustained drives without letting Jefferson dominate.
The four-game difference between these teams centers on protecting the football and capitalizing on errors.
Minnesota's plus-five turnover differential ranks tied for second-best in the NFL, whereas New Orleans ranks among the worst at minus-five. This 10-turnover gap clarifies how undefeated Minnesota overcomes an unproductive offense, while New Orleans loses despite averaging 367 yards and 26.3 points.
The Saints cannot afford to let turnovers, defensive breakdowns, and self-inflicted mistakes ruin offensive output against Minnesota's elite defense. Additionally, the Vikings lead the league in punt return average and rank second in kickoff return average, threatening a Saints squad already struggling with field position.
To succeed, New Orleans must secure the ball, limit penalties, convert in the red zone, force long drives, and avoid slow starts that play into Flores's pressure scheme. Even with Drew Brees honored at halftime and a supportive home crowd, emotional momentum will not offset repeated mistakes.

title: Abdul Carter’s Misses Second Day of Practice with Calf Injury
full_text:
New York Giants outside linebacker Abdul Carter, who is dealing with a calf injury suffered in last week’s game against the Washington Commanders, missed his second day of practice, raising concern about his availability for Sunday’s home meeting with the New Orleans Saints.
In his second NFL season, Carter has played in 92% of the Giants’ defensive snaps , up from 76% last year.
Beyond his production, a potential absence would put a significant crimp in a Giants pass rush already without Brian Burns (season-ending ACL).
Per Next Gen Stats, Carter is tied with Will Anderson Jr. of the Texans for the most quick pressures (14) under 2.5 seconds, and his pressures have come from both sides of the formation.
If Carter can’t play on Sunday, the Giants will likely turn to Trace Ford and also work Arvell Reese, who has primarily been an inside linebacker, on the edge in pass-rushing downs. And if Carter manages to play, it will be worth watching whether his usual heavy workload is reduced because of the injury.
On the other side of the ball, both Giants starting tackles, Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor, also missed a second day of practice.
Thomas has settled into a practice load management plan in which he receives treatment for his painful groin issue on Wednesday and Thursday, then takes part in practice on Friday and the team’s walkthrough on Saturday.
If that continues, he should be good to go for Sunday, though it’s clear that the injury has compromised his play.
Thomas goes through his pregame warmups under the watch of Allison Boudreau, the Giants’ coordinator of rehabilitation and return to play. If he isn’t ready to go, Marcus Mbow will get the start at left tackle.
Eluemunor’s outlook for Sunday is less clear. He will test his injured leg by pushing off in the coming days, and if he does so satisfactorily, he will most likely play. If he cannot, rookie J.C. Davis is expected to get the start at right tackle.

title: Giants Try to Solve Fumbling Problem as “Peanut Punch” Trend Grows
full_text:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh will be the first to admit the team still has plenty to clean up on both sides of the ball.
Among the team’s top priorities is stemming the tide of fumbles. The Giants are tied with Seattle for the league lead in total fumbles (5), three of which they lost, one fewer than Seattle.
“The league is more of a punch-out league than it’s ever been before, and more players are really good at it than they’ve ever been before,” Harbaugh said. “It’s been a major point of emphasis from day one, and it’s still not good enough. So, we’ve got to get a lot better in that area.”
Cam Skattebo, the team’s starting running back, leads the team with three fumbles, including one he lost last week deep in Commanders territory as the Giants were driving toward a potential game-winning score.
On that play, Skattebo, perhaps because of the wet conditions, removed his gloves, which may have made the ball easier to punch out.
His other two fumbles, one each against the Titans and Cowboys, share a common thread. Skattebo, who wore gloves on both of those carries, appeared to bring his elbow just a smidge away from his body as defenders closed in, the running back clearly preparing to throw a stiff arm to ward them off.
The result was a slight gap in the “high and tight” carrying style coaches preach.
Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said Skattebo understands that defenders are looking to separate ball carriers from the ball using what’s called a “peanut punch,” and that the technique has increased league-wide.
“Everyone here is seeing what this NFL has become right now with that peanut punch. It’s across the board. (Defenders) are being taught to punch the ball out.
“Obviously, in that situation, (Skattebo) knows more than anybody that we can’t have that happen, and it’s just unacceptable. He knows that, but that cannot happen again, and it’s not going to happen.”
While Nagy wouldn’t go into specifics about what they uncovered while watching the film of the fumbles, one thing he did mention that should help reduce the likelihood of fumbling is covering the ball with two hands when a defender closes in.
In his quest to squeeze out an extra yard or two on his rushing attempts, Skattebo has used stiff arms to keep defenders off him. But if the arm carrying the ball drifts from his body with the momentum, the ball becomes vulnerable to a punch-out.
“We make sure every practice that we have a bunch of different drills that we work on,” Nagy said.
“You have to speak it into existence. So, that’s the part sometimes that can get frustrating if you end up getting to a point where you practice it, you emphasize it, but yet it still happens. So, you can’t just stop doing that. You have to make sure you keep emphasizing it.”
That, and hoping the continued emphasis finally resolves the problem.

title: Schultz: Harbaugh Effect Could Lift Giants to 9 or 10 Wins
full_text:
One big reason the New York Giants were all over head coach John Harbaugh the moment he became a free agent was their belief that the veteran head coach could quickly turn the floundering franchise’s fortunes around.
So far, Harbaugh has done just that, and he’s done it despite not having starting quarterback Jaxson Dart, a player who is not only essential to the team but around whom the offense was built. Harbaugh has also managed it without last year’s team sack leader, Brian Burns, who is out for the year with a torn ACL.
Somehow, he has even gotten there despite a running game that has averaged just 3.7 yards per carry (24th in the league), and a “feast or famine” run defense whose 5.2 yards per attempt is tied for second in the league.
No, it hasn’t been perfect, but it’s been much better than many critics expected, and the Harbaugh effect is a big reason NFL insider Jordan Schultz believes the Giants are building something special.
“They’re not a pretender,” Schultz told the Locked On Giants podcast this week. “I don’t know if they’re a contender — they’re probably in the middle, like a dark horse. But I think that’s a nine- or 10-win team.”
The 3-1-1 Giants have already tied their 2024 win total of three games, and they are one win away from tying their 2025 win total.
If they finish with nine wins, that would match their 2022 total, the last time they had a winning record and qualified for a postseason berth. And a 10-win regular-season total would give them their first double-digit-win season since 2016, the last year they went to the postseason.
Based on how the NFC East has gone the last several years, a double-digit-win season should not only assure the Giants a spot in the playoffs, but it could be just enough for them to win their first division crown since 2011, coincidentally their last Super Bowl appearance.
Given the current NFL landscape, a double-digit-win season for the Giants isn’t as crazy as it sounds. According to Tankathon , the combined strength of schedule of the Giants’ remaining opponents comes in at .492, 20th in the league.
They’re listed as having four “tough” opponents remaining — the 49ers, Jaguars, Seahawks and Lions.
Of course, at the end of the day, that probably means nothing, as the team needs to go out there and take care of business. But with Harbaugh driving the bus, Schultz believes the Giants are headed for smoother terrain than they have seen in the past.
“There’s a sense of belief and a lightness to them that they haven’t had, and maybe that’s the coach,” Schultz said.
“You gotta give credit to John Harbaugh. But I like the Giants. I’ve probably been about as bullish on them as anyone, just because you can see the DNA of it, and that it’s working.”

title: Why "The Jameis Winston Experience" Has Been Working for the Giants
full_text:
Few, if any, may understand the “ebb and flow” of being an NFL quarterback better than New York Giants starter Jameis Winston.
Since being named the team’s QB1 after incumbent Jaxson Dart’s season-ending knee injury in Week 2, the 32-year-old Winston has thrown for 805 yards, six touchdowns, and three interceptions.
His ability to complete deep, high-risk passes while showcasing his impressive arm strength has made him a key component in the Giants’ NFC East-leading 3-1-1 record.
“It’s tough to just kind of jump in there when the offense is built probably for a different quarterback,” head coach John Harbaugh said. “I think he did a really good job, but it was really tough. It was awkward, and he fought through it, and he kept his confidence. He kept his poise, and he found a way to win football games.”
Winston’s “feast or famine” style of play has often been criticized, specifically in relation to his fit within coordinator Matt Nagy’s methodical, run-centric, and motion-based offense.
For every exciting play, there seems to be a corresponding miscue, from costly interceptions to his frequent difficulty hitting receivers in stride, resulting in what fans and media have come to know as “The Jameis Winston Experience.”
Winston, who seems totally unflappable regardless of the circumstances around him, has leaned on his faith to drive his own definition of “The Jameis Winston Experience.” He continues to lead the Giants’ offense toward their goal of a first winning season since 2022, ideally with a spot in the playoffs.
“My take on the Jameis Winston experience is that I am called to be the light of the world and the salt of the earth,” Winston said. “Every time that I’m around someone, I am driven to increase that man or that woman with every action that I take.
“So, if you’re defining that as the Jameis Winston experience, I’m telling you that is the Jameis Winston experience that I intend to give,” he added. “People can say whatever they want to say. But I intend to be a man of increase. Increase in every man, every woman that I come in contact with, doing unto them as I would want them to do unto me.”
Winston’s leadership has certainly been one of his strong suits. He is not only a member of the team’s eight-man leadership council but also a team captain, both of which are rare honors for a quarterback who began the season as a backup.
In a league where good backup quarterbacks are hard to find, let alone keep on the roster, the Giants made sure to get Winston under contract before the start of the 2026 season rather than let him play out the final year of his initial two-year contract.
And while the results haven’t always been perfect, Winston’s impact has been felt in the locker room, where his teammates look up to him and often seek his guidance on football and life.
“I think that’s the largest platform we get,” Winston stated. “That’s a great testimony to go and be the starting quarterback for the New York Football Giants at MetLife Stadium, to go and play a game, compete with your teammates, fight for each other, be one team, and one heartbeat.”
When seeking the ideal example of the “Jameis Winston Experience,” look no further than New York’s Week 5 matchup with the Washington Commanders at MetLife Stadium.
The Giants erased a 14-point fourth-quarter deficit to tie 27-27 with their division rivals. Winston shook off a subpar first half, in which he completed just 7 of 16 passes for 72 yards, with no touchdowns and one lost fumble, and bounded back to deliver one of his best showings since joining the Giants in 2025.
He finished the game having completed 61 percent of his passes for 326 yards and three touchdowns. He also rushed five times for 27 yards, marking the only time since 1950 that a Giant has thrown for 300+ passing yards, 3+ passing touchdowns, and 25+ rushing yards in the same game.
While the game ended in a tie, Winston appears to be hitting his stride as the Giants head into their Week 6 matchup against the New Orleans Saints. In fact, the former Saints starter is confident that he is improving with each passing day.
“I’m focused on getting better every single day, every single game,” he said. “I think that is the recipe for success: getting one percent better every single day and applying that, being a doer of that as best as we can.
“The consistent striving for greatness is what drives this team. Not opinions, facts, or other people’s perspective. We would love to be our very best. That’s what drives us.”
Harbaugh sees that improvement as well.
“Now we’re starting to get adapted, I think, a little bit to the game plan and what we’re doing and getting reps on the things that are more Jameis-type things,” he said. “So, I think we’re going to keep getting better. That’s the plan, and he’s doing a great job.”
As the Giants look ahead to their next game, Winston remains intent on growing the “experience” in a positive way. Although facing his former team may bring nostalgia, his focus remains squarely on delivering his current team their fourth win of the season.
“I dreamt of it. And now it’s here,” Winston said. “So, I’m grateful for that. Love that (Saints) organization. Man, my heart and soul is with ‘Who Dat,’ but I’m grateful to be a New York Football Giant.
“And the New York Football Giants have given me the privilege to be their starting quarterback. I’m going to honor that and do my very best at that.”

title: PFF Mock Draft Sends Giants a Wide Receiver, and the Numbers Show Why
full_text:
Despite investing a ton of resources in the position during the offseason, the New York Giants are still working to fortify their wide receiving corps and become one of the deepest units in the NFL.
In total, Big Blue doled out $48.34 million in new contracts to veteran pass catchers in free agency, according to Spotrac. Through the first five weeks of the 2026 season, the return on investment has given the franchise the 21st-ranked scoring offense and the 20th-ranked average yards per passing play for a huddle that sought to test the vertical boundaries.
Obviously, a lot changed in head coach John Harbaugh and offensive coordinator Matt Nagy’s plans once their starting quarterback, Jaxson Dart, went down with a season-ending injury. Still, even with a capable backup with a proven arm in Jameis Winston, the Giants felt they had enough options to make some noise through the air.
Pro Football Focus thinks the Giants could still improve the position group beyond this season, and the outlet projected New York to target a pass catcher in its 2027 Mock Draft 1.0 , selecting Florida State wide receiver Duce Robinson with the No. 26 pick.
“The Giants have Malik Nabers but not much else at wide receiver right now,” PFF analyst Gordon McGuinness wrote.
“If they do wind up selecting in the 20s of this draft, they could do a lot worse than take a look at someone like Robinson. His play dipped early in 2026, but he ranked sixth among college wide receivers last season with an average of 3.03 yards per route run.”
McGuinness is stretching it a bit when he suggests the Giants’ arsenal is “Malik Nabers-or-bust.” Yet it’s hard to argue that the team’s leaderboard showcases a bevy of productive weapons for the quarterback.
The Giants’ brass can celebrate an offseason win in acquiring tight end Isaiah Likely, who has come in and quickly shattered franchise records while offering a bigger, more versatile option out of the slot.
Harbaugh and the Giants saw firsthand just how dominant a duo Nabers and Likely can become if they both stay healthy, especially after the two pass catchers combined for 22 receptions, 215 yards and three touchdowns to spark a second-half rally toward a 27-27 overtime tie with the Washington Commanders in Week 5.
Beyond No. 1 and No. 9’s contributions, which are starting to heat up, the same can’t be said for the rest of the receivers, who each have fewer than 10 receptions and 146 yards while accounting for only three of the Giants’ nine passing touchdowns.
Malachi Fields is still a rookie just five games into his pro career, and he’s been effective on limited targets, averaging 14.6 yards per catch and leading the team.
Others like Darnell Mooney and tight end Theo Johnson haven’t had many opportunities to make plays. Still, when they have been targeted, they’ve produced only 12 catches combined and struggled to haul in contested catches that could have swung the results of both of the Giants’ non-winning games.
Injuries have been a factor. The Giants lost veteran kick returner Gunner Olszewski and their projected starting slot receiver, Calvin Austin III, to knee injuries before the season opener. Braxton Berrios suffered his own foot injury in Week 4, bringing the total to three receivers sidelined for the remainder of 2026.
That doesn’t shield any of them from taking some blame. Harbaugh brought each onto his roster as a testament to his belief in their ability to contribute to one of the league’s most versatile aerial attacks.
So far, the offense ranks 13th in EPA per pass play (+0.136), and only 5 of its 21 explosive plays of 20 or more yards have come through the air, good for 28th in the NFL entering Week 6.
With the Giants’ run struggles on full display through five games, it’ll take more than two trick ponies to propel the franchise past the tougher opponents waiting in the second half of their schedule.
Nabers and Likely won’t do it alone, and help isn’t coming soon. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see it arrive early in the draft in April, assuming bigger needs don’t arise down the stretch.

title: Giants’ Early Success Hinges on Winning the Line of Scrimmage
full_text:
Nobody said establishing a new identity overnight would be easy.
Head coach John Harbaugh wanted to transform the New York Giants into a team that would dominate the trenches on both sides of the ball, with an eye on returning the team to playoff contention in his first year on the job. So far, the road has included a few detours, but it’s still being paved in the right direction.
The Giants sit atop the NFC East at 3-1-1 and hold a two-game lead in the loss column over the rest of the division heading into Sunday’s game against the New Orleans Saints at MetLife Stadium. So, yes, they’ve gotten through nearly the first third of the season in good shape. However, they’re unlikely to maintain that course if they don’t win the line of scrimmage on both sides of the ball.
On offense, the running game has gained some traction in alternating games, putting up at least 100 yards in Weeks 1 (win), 3 (win) and 5 (tie). But they ran for just 52 and 87 yards in Weeks 2 (loss) and 4 (win).
“We definitely need more explosives in the run game. That’s definitely something that we’ll be chasing and looking for,” Harbaugh said this week.
“Every play has got its own story that is told. We look back at it and study it. I think everybody in the offense will tell you this play, that play, whatever. There’s always something we can do better. A lot of times it’s the difference in the play. It’s really our execution mostly, usually. Sometimes you’re overwhelmed with numbers or something like that. But there’s definitely been plays where we can get more yards on.”
The Giants lost control of the narrative in last week’s 27-27 tie at Washington, falling behind by 14 points midway through the fourth quarter.
Forced to go to the air, quarterback Jameis Winston went 33-of-54 for 326 yards and three TDs. It was four pass attempts short of his career high. It was the 29th time he’s thrown at least 40 passes in a game, the sixth of those without an interception and his most attempts without being picked off.
The defense is a bigger cause for concern. Opponents have run for 69, 163, 81, 123 and 202 yards through the first five weeks.
“Yeah, I think we’ve had too many chunk plays, overall. We’ve played kind of feast-or-famine run defense,” Harbaugh said.
How well will the Giants’ front fare against New Orleans, given that the Saints, who are weak in the trenches, can be expected to try to turn the day into a passing affair?

title: Giants Injury Report: Abdul Carter, Andrew Thomas Among The "DNPs" on Wednesday
full_text:
New York Giants outside linebacker Abdul Carter is on this week’s injury list.
Carter, who has been simply sensational in his second NFL season, has a calf injury that kept him out of practice. It’s unclear how serious the injury is or if it might keep him out of Sunday’s game against the New Orleans Saints, but it’s certainly worth watching as the new work week begins.
Starting tackles Andrew Thomas (groin) and Jermaine Eluemunor (calf) were also held out of practice. Thomas is clearly having his reps managed from here on out, whereas Eluemunor is considered day-to-day, according to Harbaugh.
Still, if both starters couldn’t play, Marcus Mbow and rookie J.C. Davis would get the start.
“I’ve seen a lot of work. I’ve seen a lot of diligent work,” Harbaugh said of both players. “They’re both very good players who are trying to prove themselves in this league. If and when they get a chance to play, I’m sure that they’ll be very determined to do that and play well. So, we’ll see.”
Safety Jason Pinnock (concussion/non-contact) is trending in the right direction, as he was a limited participant on Wednesday. Tyler Nubin, whom Pinnock initially replaced, did not practice due to a neck ailment.
And in other injury news, the Giants have not yet opened the 21-day windows for cornerbacks Paulson Adebo (knee) and Korie Black (groin), despite each player being eligible to have their windows opened. Both were spotted working with trainers on the side of the field during the part of practice open to the media.

title: Dru Phillips Praises Giants Aggressive Defense: ‘Definitely a Fun Thing’
full_text:
New York Giants cornerback Dru Phillips might have a little “Cobra Kai” in him.
When it comes to pressuring the quarterback, New York’s third-year defensive back makes every effort to “strike first, strike hard, and show no mercy.”
In perhaps his best outing of the season to date, Phillips collected five total tackles, four quarterback hits, two sacks, and two tackles for loss in the Giants’ 27-27 tie with the Washington Commanders.
It’s no surprise that Phillips appears to be enjoying coordinator Dennard Wilson’s aggressive pass-defense style.
“It’s definitely a fun thing, yeah,” Phillips told reporters earlier this week. “It was cool to get out there and blitz a little bit.”
After blitzing at a conservative rate (22 percent of their defensive snaps) for much of the season’s early stages, the Giants have clearly increased the defensive pressure in recent weeks.
Since team captain Brian Burns suffered a season-ending injury in Week 3, the team has blitzed on 56 percent of its defensive snaps against the Arizona Cardinals in Week 4 and 62 percent against the Commanders in Week 5.
In fact, Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels looked as wide-eyed as a pre-Miyagi Do Daniel LaRusso on more than one occasion — thanks largely to Phillips’ heat-seeking style of play.
For as long as Wilson continues his aggressive approach, Phillips will be ready to turn up the pressure.
“Dennard (Wilson) has a way of cooking things up, but I definitely wouldn’t say it is a consistent thing,” Phillips said.
“It’s a week-by-week thing. It goes off of what we’re seeing and the flow of the game. So, you go out there, and if they send me, I’m going to try my best to go get it.”
At his best, Phillips is an elite run defender due to his physical, downhill style. When deployed as a pass rusher, his speed and short-area power let him quickly close on opposing quarterbacks — as shown against Daniels and the Commanders.
Phillips not only earned high praise for his Week 5 effort, but he also performed at a historically high level for the franchise. The 24-year-old became the fifth Giants defensive back since 1982 to record at least two sacks in a game.
He was also the fourth cornerback since 2006 to record four-plus quarterback hits in a single game.
With New York’s Week 6 matchup against the New Orleans Saints fast approaching, Phillips is likely to be an integral component of the club’s defensive game plan once again. Though he may be having a great deal of fun in Wilson’s aggressive system, he also remains aware of his responsibilities to his teammates.
In that regard, Phillips is rapidly becoming the embodiment of a complete football player — one whose value lies not only in his versatile skill set, but also in his commitment to doing what’s best for the team.
“I feel like anybody that blitzes, you have to look out for the people behind you,” Phillips said.
“As a DB as well, when you cover it, you depend on guys to get home. So, when I am blitzing, it’s like, ‘yeah, I got to rush my tail off so I can help these guys in the back.’
“You’ve got to be aware of that. Not trying to ease your way in there … you’ve got guys fighting for their lives behind you.”

title: Giants Open as 1.5-Point Home Underdogs Against Struggling Saints
full_text:
The New York Giants held onto first place in the NFC East despite a 27-27 overtime tie with the Washington Commanders in Week 5.
Now, they return to East Rutherford to face the New Orleans Saints, an opponent that looks like a favorable matchup for extending their lead.
Oddsmakers aren’t sold. FanDuel Sportsbook opened Big Blue as a 1.5-point home underdog in its lines for the NFL’s Week 6 slate.
While the opening spread is an improvement, the Giants are being doubted for the second consecutive week after they were 3.5-point underdogs against Washington. FanDuel also set the total at 45.5 points, up two points from last week.
This isn’t the first time the Giants have been handed an odd opening line, but this week’s number may be the most confusing of the season.
After three gritty performances by John Harbaugh’s group, including two defensive shutdowns that closed out a pair of thrilling victories, the Giants have earned more respect against inferior opponents like the Saints, who arrive in East Rutherford at 1-4.
However, like the Commanders, who went up 27-13 in the third quarter but failed to set up a game-winning field goal in the waning seconds of overtime, the Saints are desperate for a win.
New Orleans opened the season looking like one of the biggest surprises, losing 31-30 on the final play of overtime to the Detroit Lions before stunning the Baltimore Ravens on the road for its only win of 2026.
Since then, the Saints have dropped three consecutive games to fall into last place in the NFC South, a division that has been less than impressive overall. Even so, they sit only two games behind the first-place Carolina Panthers.
The rough stretch, which included their defense allowing a combined 80 points in two weeks, has drawn sharp public criticism from Saints owner Gayle Benson, who challenged her franchise to provide the results its loyal fans deserve.
With the weak state of their division and the outcry from their owner and fanbase, the Saints should arrive motivated to challenge a Giants team that has started slowly in its last few contests.
The Saints offense is not one to overlook, ranking 16th in the NFL in points per game (23.6) and 20th in yards per game (322.0). Its strength is the passing game, led by second-year quarterback Tyler Shough, who is off to a solid start with the seventh-most passing yards and third-most touchdown passes in the league.
Shough and the offense are asked to score often because of the defense, which has allowed the second-most points per game, including at least 23 in each of the last three games.
The ground game is where the Giants could have an edge. The Saints defense has given up an average of 148.8 rushing yards per game and 10 rushing touchdowns, the most in the league through five games.
If the Giants clean up the run game and ball security and get back to playing bully ball in the trenches, they should be able to handle a Saints team still searching for the early-season form that grabbed everyone’s attention. The oddsmakers may be underselling them at home.

title: Giants Jon Runyan, Jr. Credits Coaching Staff for Success Through Adversity
full_text:
In the immortal words of legendary singer-songwriter James Taylor, the New York Giants have clearly seen their share of “fire” and “rain” through the first five games of the 2026 NFL season.
From losing incumbent starting quarterback Jaxson Dart to a season-ending knee injury in Week 2, to defensive team captain Brian Burns suffering both a torn ACL and torn meniscus in Week 3, New York has been forced to push through adversity.
Still, the Giants have endured. Under new head coach John Harbaugh, the team has found renewed vigor. Playing solid, fundamental football, Big Blue sits alone atop the NFC East at 3-1-1.
Though several factors have contributed to New York’s unexpected return to relevance, veteran offensive lineman Jon Runyan Jr. knows the foundation for that success was laid months ago.
“I think it says a lot about our coaching staff and what they’ve tried to build throughout the whole offseason program and into training camp,” Runyan said. “It says a lot about them, the foundation that they’ve built, and a lot of us as players. Because of that, we’re sitting 3-1-1 right now.”
Originally drafted by the Green Bay Packers in the sixth round (No. 192 overall) of the 2020 NFL Draft, Runyan has been with the Giants since signing a free-agent deal with the club in 2024. The 6-foot-4, 307-pound left guard has started all 34 games he has appeared in for the team.
This season, he has played 347 offensive snaps and earned a pass-blocking grade of 78.5, which ranks sixth among 75 qualified offensive guards, per PFF.
While Runyan’s on-field skills have helped the Giants’ offensive line perform at a high level, his veteran leadership remains integral to the unit rising above its middle-of-the-pack preseason rankings. The line has not only provided improved protection for quarterback Jameis Winston, but it has also strengthened its run blocking.
Despite injuries to key starters such as right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (calf) and left tackle Andrew Thomas (groin), the Giants’ O-line continues to press forward. Even as they have weathered the storm through the first five weeks of the season, Runyan has enough experience to know situations can always worsen.
In that regard, Runyan is confident that Big Blue has the structure in place to persevere — even if the club has yet to reach its on-field peak.
“I still feel like we have a long way to go on this team,” Runyan said. “Luckily, we are 3-1-1 at the moment. And as I said, we still have a long way to go. This whole division stacks up how it does, as long as we take care of what we got. Coach Harbaugh has been saying go 1-0 every week, and that’s been our mindset, and it’s been working so far this year.”
With their Week 6 matchup against the New Orleans Saints at MetLife Stadium approaching, the Giants will continue to require a total team effort to return to the win column.
As players begin to hit their stride, Runyan believes the strong solidarity throughout the organization will be the primary reason the Giants accomplish their mission — should they choose to accept it.
“In my opinion, it’s about really good communication back and forth between players and coaches,” Runyan added.
“That is going to help us when we get further down the road in the season. And especially going to be helpful when we face a little bit more adversity, knowing that we have that solid foundation with everybody around us.”

title: It's Crucial for Isaiah Davis to Be a Key Part of Jets' Week 6 Plans to Beat the Patriots
full_text:
Fresh off a hard-fought 17-12 win over the Browns last Sunday, the Jets turn their attention to a Week 6 clash with the Patriots after snapping a three-game losing streak and injecting a little optimism into an upcoming schedule that presents some opportunities.
While a pitiful trend of going 25-65 against AFC East opponents since 2011 and just 4-26 against the Patriots during that same stretch is not exactly encouraging, the Jets did some positive things in the Week 5 win over Cleveland and have a division opportunity in front of them to build off that and make some proper tweaks.
With Breece Hall sidelined due to a right quad injury, Braelon Allen brought his best with a career-high 116 yards on 24 carries and the game-winning 22-yard touchdown. Although his stock is certainly skyrocketing after a long-awaited breakout performance , there is no reason that fellow RB and 2024 draftee Isaiah Davis should not be more involved in the offense on Sunday.
Davis hasn't been used all that often this season, but that needs to change for the Jets' offense to be a problem for the Patriots' defense.
While Hall's return is of the utmost importance in terms of getting their versatile RB1 back on the field, ESPN Jets reporter Rich Cimini noted on Thursday that he "is working with trainers on the side field" and is "considered week-to-week."
Breece Hall (quad) is working with trainers on the side field. That’s progress. He’s considered week to week. #Jets
As Hall continues to make progress, that could obviously impact the amount of playing time that Davis receives.
The Patriots are coming off back-to-back wins, including a signature win over fellow AFC East rival Buffalo in Week 4. That said, their defense hasn't been perfect; tied for the 11th-most catches allowed (24) and tied for the fifth-most receiving yards allowed (200) to RBs this season. That is definitely an area to exploit for a Jets team that is still trying to get healthy.
If Hall can't play, it makes sense to use Davis as a receiving option out of the backfield since he averages an impressive 8.7 yards per catch in his career. He only had two carries for eight yards and one catch for nine yards last week, but the fact that he played a season-high 10 offensive snaps adds to the idea that the Jets are ready to put more on his plate.
As good as Allen has been, he is only averaging 2.7 yards per catch this season with a career-worst 63.6% catch rate. He averages 6.6 in that department for his career, and his lackluster pass-catching production could open the door for Davis to get an uptick in snaps as early as this weekend.
Davis has been productive in his young NFL career and has scored three total TDs without fumbling the ball until this past Sunday, although quarterback Geno Smith recovered it, and it did not result in a turnover. It made sense for New York to get Davis more involved in the game plan while Hall has been out of action and for him to take on a more important role .
Head coach Aaron Glenn shared a conflicting injury update that only raised more questions than answers , specifically regarding the availability of wide receiver Adonai Mitchell. For weeks, this wideout group has been without two of its top-three targets—Mitchell and rookie Omar Cooper Jr.—though Cooper is nearing his crucial return from an ankle injury that he suffered in the opener.
Those depth concerns, along with rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq entering concussion protocol after suffering a head injury in the Week 5 win over Cleveland, have left holes in the passing game behind WR1 Garrett Wilson. Is Davis ready to step up when Gang Green needs him most?
At the same time, Davis has primarily been used on special teams and could find himself on the trade block before the month is over , especially if the Jets continue to shy away from him when the opportunity is right in front of the 2024 fifth-rounder. That's why it's crucial for him to capitalize on every chance he gets, whether it leads to a bigger role with the Jets or elsewhere.
At the end of the day, the Patriots have clearly struggled to contain pass-catching backs so far this season. If the Jets want to put themselves in position to pull off the upset and earn a rare divisional win, Davis should be a key part of those plans, especially if Hall is out for another week.

title: Job's Not Over: David Bailey Still Has Plenty to Prove to Jets Despite Winning AFC Defensive Player of the Week
full_text:
It's good to be David Bailey right now.
The Jets' second-overall pick in the 2026 draft has been highly productive through his first five games, becoming just the third rookie since 2000 to accomplish that feat. He was aided by a three-sack effort in Gang Green's 17-12 win over the Browns last week, as well as a season-high nine pressures , according to Pro Football Focus .
Bailey was the best player on the field in that game, resulting in him being awarded major NFL honors : AFC Defensive Player of the Week.
AFC Players of the Week! (Week 5) @Nunless2 | @gregrousseau pic.twitter.com/wsavBPaARN
Not Defensive Rookie of the Week. Player. Bailey was that good on Sunday.
But as the Texas Tech product moves forward beyond his breakout game, the Jets know that one game does not make or break a prospect, meaning Bailey still has plenty more to prove.
Transcendent draft picks often get misassociated with great ones. Myles Garrett was a transcendent talent. Aidan Hutchinson was a great one. Bailey's moniker falls somewhere in the middle between what Garrett was and what Hutchinson became when they were both drafted.
But through sheer production, his motor, and willingness to improve, the Jets have known for a while now how special Bailey can be for their team.
"(Bailey is) everything you'd want in an edge," Jets cornerback AZ Thomas said on Monday. "We can go into stats and stuff like that, but I mean, like he's a rookie, and it's going to be a learning curve just like I had last year. … David Bailey is David Bailey, and he put that on display last night (h/t NFL). I just look forward to seeing more of that."
David Bailey was a man on a mission in Week 5 🔥 @Pepsi pic.twitter.com/DKOYWjlsLg
That's the ticket going forward. More. New York wants to see more from Bailey.
Fellow teammate Will McDonald IV is a good example of a player who can get to the quarterback in bunches. He has the talent of a first-round pick. Yet he is too inconsistent as a pass rusher to be trusted the way the Jets want to trust Bailey.
Already they are seeing that trust pays off.
Bailey's motor and pass-rushing skills are apparent. But another factor that has made him an everydown player is the one skill that was considered a detriment to him coming out of the draft: defending the run.
"The other things that really showed up in the game was (David's) ability to play the run," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said of Bailey's performance. "He just had an all-around game as far as affecting the quarterback and playing the run."
Before the draft, the big weakness to Bailey's game was his inconsistencies against the run. Teams were worried that he wouldn't be able to become the three down player that someone like Arvell Reese could be.
Through five games, though, Bailey's run defense has been the best part of his game. Pro Football Focus grades him as the 16th-best run defender of all edge rushers. His grade (76.1) is also two points higher than Reese's (74.0) so far in that category.
Winning defensive player of the week is certainly an achievement to celebrate, especially for a rookie making just his fifth start. His latest effort has made him DraftKings Sportsbook's current +200 favorite to be named the 2026 Defensive Rookie of the Year , but the mark of a special player is performing at a high level each and every week.
Garrett, Hutchinson, and T.J. Watt are all great examples of that. If Bailey wants his name to be thrown into the groups of the elite, he'll need to show that last week's performance against the Browns was not a mirage.
It was a sign of things to come.

title: Adonai Mitchell Injury Is Easily Jets’ Biggest Concern Heading Into Week 6 vs. Patriots
full_text:
Thanks to Braelon Allen’s career-high 116 rushing yards and a dominant pass-rush effort, the Jets ended their losing streak with a much-needed win over the Browns in Week 5. Star wide receiver Garrett Wilson once again provided the main spark through the air, recording 104 of the Jets’ 182 passing yards.
Despite finally returning to the win column, Gang Green’s passing attack continued to struggle in the sloppy conditions. Some of these struggles can be attributed to the absence of receiver Adonai Mitchell, who has missed the last three games with a finger injury .
The severity of the former 2024 second-round pick’s injury had been unknown, adding more frustrating to his absence.
When asked last week about Mitchell’s injury, head coach Aaron Glenn said he didn’t know whether his finger was sprained or fractured , but that he didn’t have surgery on it. Turns out things can change quickly, because on Wednesday, Glenn told reporters that Mitchell underwent a "small procedure" last week.
“ (Adonai) did have a small procedure on his hand ,” Glenn said. “But the good thing is, man, that he’s moving his hand really, really well.”
With the former Texas Longhorn not at practice Wednesday and Glenn keeping his status as week-to-week, Mitchell appears unlikely to suit up against AFC East rival the Patriots.
Naturally, that makes his looming absence a major concern in Week 6.
Mitchell quickly established himself as New York’s WR2 during the summer workouts, and the former Texas Longhorn has given the Jets another vertical threat alongside Wilson.
He’s been Smith’s favorite target downfield, receiving four targets on passes of 20-plus yards , according to NFL Next Gen Stats . He hauled in one catch for 40 yards against the Titans in Week 1.
Standing at 6'2" and 205 lbs with a blazing 4.34-second 40-yard dash time , this shouldn’t come as much of a surprise. His physical frame and athleticism, combined with his ability to win 50/50 balls, make him an enticing target.
After the first two games, Mitchell ranked second on the team in receptions (9), targets (15), and receiving yards (123).
Since his injury, the rest of the receiving corps hasn’t provided consistent production. While tight end Kenyon Sadiq exploded for seven catches and 105 yards against the Lions in Week 3, he posted two catches for three yards over the next two games. He's also currently battling through the NFL's concussion protocol , leaving his outlook uncertain.
Granted, the Jets were also without Breece Hall, Tim Patrick and Mason Taylor at various points during this stretch, further complicating their passing attack.
Still, New York has tried to fill Mitchell’s void on the outside by giving Isaiah Williams a larger role in Weeks 3 and 4 before turning to Patrick in Week 5. While both receivers have their own strengths, neither has been as intimidating downfield as Mitchell.
Williams showcased his big-play ability against the Bears, hauling in a 58-yard touchdown in the team’s 23-12 loss. However, much of his production has come at or near the line of scrimmage. Patrick, like Mitchell, is a big receiver, standing at 6'5" and 210 lbs, though he is more of a run-blocking, red-zone threat receiver.
Mitchell’s value isn’t limited to deep plays downfield. He’s also proven he can add value in the intermediate areas and win matchups with his route-running, logging three catches (four targets) for 47 yards at these levels.
With Mitchell out, the Jets are missing a receiver who can take pressure off Wilson and give their passing game another dimension. Through five games, the five-year veteran from Ohio State leads the team in receptions (31), receiving yards (373), and touchdowns (3).
Williams and Patrick can’t replicate Mitchell's production , as each brings a different skill set to the table. Until New York can consistently find ways to create plays at multiple levels, opposing defenses can afford to focus all their attention on Wilson.
That makes it abundantly clear why Mitchell’s continued absence a significant concern heading into Week 6 and beyond.
